```{.r .cell-code}
source(here::here("scripts", "paths_and_packages.R"))
p_load(see, backbone, kableExtra, DT)

# Loading Data
# bert_df <- arrow::read_feather(file.path(
#   data_path,
#   "top1pct_sentences_by_year.feather"
# ))

# setDT(bert_df, key = "sentence_id")
# bert_df <- bert_df[between(year, 1900, 2010), ]

metadata_jstor <- read_rds(file.path(
  jstor_data_path,
  "jstor_constellate_merged_metadata.rds"
))

# keep only relevant lines, columns and rename them for consistency
metadata_jstor <- metadata_jstor %>%
  filter(
    refined_sub_type == "research-article",
    languages == "eng",
    publication_year < 2010
  ) %>%
  select(
    id = url,
    journal = is_part_of,
    title,
    authors = creators_string,
    year = publication_year,
    ID_Art = id_wos_matched
  ) %>%
  mutate(url = str_c("https://", id)) |>
  arrange(year)

# same for scopus metadata
metadata_scopus <- read_rds(file.path(
  elsevier_data_path,
  "scopus_economics_articles.rds"
))

metadata_scopus <- metadata_scopus %>%
  mutate(
    year = as.integer(str_sub(prism_cover_date, 1, 4)),
    url = str_c("https://doi.org/", prism_doi)
  ) %>%
  filter(
    full_text == TRUE,
    subtype_description == "Article",
    year < 2010
  ) %>%
  select(
    id = scopus_id,
    title = dc_title,
    authors = dc_creator,
    journal = prism_publication_name,
    year,
    url,
    ID_Art = id_wos_matched
  )

metadata <- bind_rows(metadata_jstor, metadata_scopus) |> 
  filter(!is.na(year) & !is.na(title))

sentences <- arrow::read_feather(file.path(
  data_path,
  "sentences_intertemporal_cluster.feather"
)) %>%
  filter(between(year, 1900, 2009)) %>%
  select(-year) %>%
  left_join(metadata, by = "id") %>%
  arrange(id, sentence_id)
setDT(sentences)

rm(metadata, metadata_jstor, metadata_scopus)

backbone_network <- read_rds(file.path(
  data_path,
  "backbone_network_of_sentences_clusters.rds"
)) |> 
  filter(window != "2010-2019") # we don't have sentences from 2010 onward

list_clusters <- sentences %>%
  pull(backbone_community) %>%
  unique() |>
  sort()
```

```{.r .cell-code}
tokens <- extract_ngrams(
  sentences[, .(
    sentence,
    window,
    HDBSCAN_cluster,
    backbone_community
  )],
  ngrams = 2L,
  grouping_cols = c(
    "HDBSCAN_cluster",
    "backbone_community",
    "window"
  ),
  text_col = "sentence",
)

tokens_count_hdbscan_cluster <- compute_tf_idf(
  tokens,
  token_col = "token",
  document_col = c("backbone_community", "HDBSCAN_cluster", "window")
)

# Top tf-idf terms
top_terms_hdbscan_cluster <- tokens_count_hdbscan_cluster[order(-tf_idf)][
  corpus_tf > 20,
  head(.SD, 15),
  by = .(backbone_community, HDBSCAN_cluster, window)
]

# Labels per decade
labels_hdbscan_cluster <- tokens_count_hdbscan_cluster[order(-tf_idf)][
  corpus_tf > 20,
  head(.SD, 5),
  by = .(backbone_community, HDBSCAN_cluster, window)
]

labels_hdbscan_cluster <- labels_hdbscan_cluster[,
  .(label_hdbscan_cluster = paste0(token, collapse = ", ")),
  by = .(backbone_community, HDBSCAN_cluster, window)
]

labels_hdbscan_cluster[,
  label_hdbscan_cluster := paste0(
    backbone_community,
    "_",
    HDBSCAN_cluster,
    "_",
    window,
    ": ",
    label_hdbscan_cluster
  ) # we save the backbonne community number to see difference in top terms depending on kmean cluster
]

sentences <- merge(
  sentences,
  labels_hdbscan_cluster,
  all.x = TRUE,
  by = c("backbone_community", "HDBSCAN_cluster", "window")
)
```

```{.r .cell-code}
tfidf_mean_community <- tokens_count_hdbscan_cluster[
  corpus_tf > 50,
  .(mean_tf_idf = mean(tf_idf)),
  by = .(token, backbone_community)
][order(-mean_tf_idf)]

# Top tf-idf terms
top_terms_cluster <- tfidf_mean_community[,
  head(.SD, 20),
  by = backbone_community
]

# Get top 4 tf-idf tokens per cluster
labels_backbone_community <- tfidf_mean_community[,
  head(.SD, 4),
  by = backbone_community
][, .(backbone_community, token)]
labels_backbone_community <- labels_backbone_community[,
  .(label_backbone_community = paste0(token, collapse = ", ")),
  by = backbone_community
]
labels_backbone_community[,
  label_backbone_community := paste0(
    str_extract(backbone_community, "\\d+$"),
    ": ",
    label_backbone_community
  )
]

sentences <- merge(
  sentences,
  labels_backbone_community,
  all.x = TRUE,
  by = "backbone_community"
)
```

```{.r .cell-code}
# Adding references
sentences_art <- sentences[
  !is.na(ID_Art),
  .N,
  .(id, HDBSCAN_cluster, window, backbone_community, ID_Art)
]
setnames(sentences_art, "N", "nb_sentence")

data_ref <- open_dataset(
  here::here(wos_data_path, "all_ref.parquet"),
  format = "parquet"
)
refs <- data_ref %>%
  filter(ID_Art %in% unique(sentences_art$ID_Art)) %>%
  distinct(ID_Art, ItemID_Ref, Annee, Nom, Revue_Abbrege) %>%
  collect()

top_refs <- sentences_art %>%
  left_join(refs, by = "ID_Art", relationship = "many-to-many") %>%
  filter(ItemID_Ref != 0) %>%
  group_by(
    HDBSCAN_cluster,
    window,
    backbone_community,
    ItemID_Ref,
    nb_sentence
  ) %>%
  summarise(absolute_cluster_cit = n(), .groups = "drop") %>%
  mutate(weighted_cluster_cit = absolute_cluster_cit * nb_sentence) %>%
  arrange(
    backbone_community,
    HDBSCAN_cluster,
    window,
    desc(weighted_cluster_cit)
  ) %>%
  group_by(backbone_community, HDBSCAN_cluster, window) %>%
  slice_head(n = 20) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  filter(weighted_cluster_cit > 1) %>%
  left_join(
    refs %>% distinct(ItemID_Ref, Nom, Annee, Revue_Abbrege),
    by = "ItemID_Ref",
    relationship = "many-to-many"
  ) %>%
  distinct(
    backbone_community,
    HDBSCAN_cluster,
    window,
    ItemID_Ref,
    absolute_cluster_cit,
    weighted_cluster_cit,
    .keep_all = TRUE
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    absolute_cit = sum(absolute_cluster_cit),
    all_sentences = sum(nb_sentence),
    weighted_cit = absolute_cit * all_sentences,
    .by = c(ItemID_Ref, backbone_community)
  )

top_refs_without_id <- sentences_art %>%
  left_join(refs, by = "ID_Art", relationship = "many-to-many") %>%
  filter(ItemID_Ref == 0 & Annee != 0 & Nom != "") %>%
  group_by(backbone_community, HDBSCAN_cluster, window, Nom, Annee) %>%
  mutate(
    absolute_cluster_cit = n(),
    weighted_cluster_cit = absolute_cluster_cit * nb_sentence
  ) %>%
  filter(weighted_cluster_cit > 1) %>%
  distinct(
    ID_Art,
    backbone_community,
    HDBSCAN_cluster,
    window,
    .keep_all = TRUE
  ) %>%
  arrange(
    backbone_community,
    HDBSCAN_cluster,
    window,
    desc(weighted_cluster_cit)
  ) %>%
  group_by(backbone_community, HDBSCAN_cluster, window) %>%
  slice_head(n = 20) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  select(
    backbone_community,
    HDBSCAN_cluster,
    window,
    Nom,
    Annee,
    Revue_Abbrege,
    nb_sentence,
    absolute_cluster_cit,
    weighted_cluster_cit
  ) %>%
  distinct(
    backbone_community,
    HDBSCAN_cluster,
    window,
    Nom,
    Annee,
    .keep_all = TRUE
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    absolute_cit = sum(absolute_cluster_cit),
    all_sentences = sum(nb_sentence),
    weighted_cit = absolute_cit * all_sentences,
    .by = c(Nom, Annee, Revue_Abbrege, backbone_community)
  )

rm(refs)
```

```{.r .cell-code}
# Here, we find the sentences the closest to "rational" and "rationality" per kmean cluster
# We would then be able to extract the closest per backbone community later on
top_sentences_rationality <- sentences %>%
  select(
    id,
    sentence_id,
    sentence,
    similarity = similarity_rv,
    year,
    window,
    backbone_community,
    HDBSCAN_cluster
  ) %>%
  group_by(HDBSCAN_cluster, window) %>%
  slice_max(similarity, n = 20) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(similarity = round(similarity, 3))
```

```{.r .cell-code}
# Here, we find the sentences the closest to the centroid of the hdbscan cluster.
# The embedding of the sentence is in embedding; the centroid of the cluster is in centroid. We just need to calculate the distance for each row:
sentences[,
  similarity_hdbscan_centroid := map2_dbl(
    embedding,
    centroid,
    ~ {
      num <- sum(.x * .y)
      den <- sqrt(sum(.x * .x)) * sqrt(sum(.y * .y))
      if (den == 0) NA_real_ else num / den
    }
  )
]

# optional: round similarity for display
sentences[,
  similarity_hdbscan_centroid := round(similarity_hdbscan_centroid, 3)
]

# Select the top 20 sentences for each backbone community
top_sentences_hdbscan_cluster_centroid <- sentences[, .(
  id,
  sentence_id,
  sentence,
  backbone_community,
  HDBSCAN_cluster,
  window,
  similarity_hdbscan_centroid
)]
top_sentences_hdbscan_cluster_centroid <- top_sentences_hdbscan_cluster_centroid[order(
  -similarity_hdbscan_centroid
)][,
  head(.SD, 10),
  by = .(backbone_community, HDBSCAN_cluster, window)
]
```

```{.r .cell-code}
# compute centroid (mean embedding) per backbone_community and attach to sentences,
# then compute cosine similarity of each sentence to its backbone centroid

# 1) centroid per community: bind embeddings into a matrix then colMeans
community_centroids <- sentences[,
  {
    m <- do.call(rbind, embedding) # matrix: rows = sentences in group
    list(backbone_centroid = list(colMeans(m))) # store centroid as a list-column
  },
  by = backbone_community
]

# 2) merge centroids back into sentences (preserve sentence_id order)
sentences <- merge(
  sentences,
  community_centroids,
  by = "backbone_community",
  all.x = TRUE
)
setorder(sentences, id, sentence_id)

# 3) cosine similarity between each sentence embedding and its community centroid
sentences[,
  backbone_centroid_similarity := map2_dbl(
    embedding,
    centroid,
    ~ {
      num <- sum(.x * .y)
      den <- sqrt(sum(.x * .x)) * sqrt(sum(.y * .y))
      if (den == 0) NA_real_ else num / den
    }
  )
]

# optional: round similarity for display
sentences[,
  backbone_centroid_similarity := round(backbone_centroid_similarity, 3)
]

# Select the top 20 sentences for each backbone community
top_sentences_backbone_community_centroid <- sentences[, .(
  id,
  sentence_id,
  sentence,
  backbone_community,
  backbone_centroid_similarity
)]
top_sentences_backbone_community_centroid <- top_sentences_backbone_community_centroid[order(
  -backbone_centroid_similarity
)][,
  head(.SD, 20),
  by = backbone_community
]
```

# General Description of the Method

We start from JSTOR economics articles, split them into sentences, and embed each sentence with Sentence-BERT. To target discourse about the future, we build year-specific “query” embeddings for *rational* and *rationality* using a 5-year sliding window, which limits present-day bias in meanings. For every year, we compute cosine similarity between each sentence and that year’s query vector and retain the top 1% most similar sentences. 

Within each decade, we cluster the selected sentences with k-means and compute cluster centroids. We then form intertemporal clusters: we start from the matrix of cosine similarity between clusters centroids. Then, we use backbone statistical disparity function to find the most significant links between clusters. Finally, we build a network connecting k-mean clusters with these links and identify communities thanks to Leiden algorithm. 

We label backbone community (the meta-clusters) and k-mean clusters with high-TF-IDF unigrams and bigrams and summarize them with indicators: centroid-closest sentences, “future(s)” exemplars, temporal distributions, and top contributing articles. The report is structured along backbone communities, but we also provide disaggregation by k-mean clusters within each backbone community.

The next visualisations shows the overall network of kmean clusters connected by similarity links, coloured by backbone community.

```{.r .cell-code}
# 3) hierarchical clustering on scaled community-centroid matrix

  rbind,
  community_centroids$backbone_centroid
) |>
  as.matrix()
mat_scaled <- scale(backbone_centroid_matrix) # scale so features comparable
d <- dist(mat_scaled, method = "euclidean")
hc <- hclust(d, method = "average")

# 4) order communities along the dendrogram
comm_levels <- community_centroids$backbone_community[hc$order]

# 5) build a smooth palette so adjacent communities are visually similar
names(cluster_colors) <- comm_levels
```

```{.r .cell-code}
sentences[, size_window := .N, by = window]
sentences[,
  proportion_hdbscan_cluster := .N / size_window,
  by = .(HDBSCAN_cluster, window)
]
backbone_network <- backbone_network %>%
  activate("nodes") %>%
  left_join(
    sentences %>%
      distinct(
        cluster_id,
        HDBSCAN_cluster,
        backbone_community,
        label_hdbscan_cluster,
        label_backbone_community,
        proportion_hdbscan_cluster
      ),
    by = "cluster_id"
  )

backbone_network <- backbone_network %>%
  activate("edges") %>%
  mutate(
    community_from = .N()[["community"]][from],
    community_to = .N()[["community"]][to],
    edge_community = if_else(
      community_from == community_to,
      community_from,
      NA_character_
    ),
    edge_community = factor(edge_community, levels = comm_levels)
  )

# compute layout and community centroids
set.seed(89)
layout <- ggraph::create_layout(backbone_network, layout = "fr")

community_average <- layout %>%
  as_tibble() %>%
  group_by(community) %>%
  summarize(
    x = mean(x, na.rm = TRUE),
    y = mean(y, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  left_join(
    layout %>% as_tibble() %>% distinct(community, label_backbone_community),
    by = "community"
  )

# plot: edges coloured by edge_community when endpoints share same community, otherwise grey
backbone_network_plot <- ggraph(layout) +
  geom_edge_link(
    aes(colour = edge_community),
    alpha = 0.6,
    width = 2,
    show.legend = FALSE
  ) +
  geom_node_point(
    aes(fill = community, size = proportion_hdbscan_cluster),
    show.legend = FALSE,
    shape = 21
  ) +
  geom_label(
    data = community_average,
    aes(
      x = x,
      y = y,
      label = str_wrap(label_backbone_community, 30),
      fill = community
    ),
    size = 3,
    fontface = "bold",
    alpha = 0.8,
    show.legend = FALSE
  ) +
  scale_edge_width(range = c(0.2, 3)) +
  scale_size_continuous(range = c(1, 25)) +
  labs(edge_width = "Avg similarity") +
  scale_edge_color_manual(values = cluster_colors, na.value = "grey80") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = cluster_colors) +
  theme_void()

ggsave(
  here("pictures", "backbone_communities_network.png"),
  backbone_network_plot,
  units = "cm",
  width = 30,
  height = 30,
  dpi = 300
)

knitr::include_graphics(here("pictures", "backbone_communities_network.png"))
```

```{.r .cell-code}
p_load(ggiraph)

set.seed(89)
backbone_network_ggiraph_plot <- ggraph(layout) +
  geom_edge_link(
    aes(colour = edge_community),
    alpha = 0.6,
    width = 2,
    show.legend = FALSE
  ) +
  # interactive node points: tooltip = label_hdbscan_cluster, data_id = cluster_id
  geom_point_interactive(
    aes(
      x = x,
      y = y,
      fill = community,
      size = proportion_hdbscan_cluster,
      tooltip = str_c(
        label_hdbscan_cluster,
        "\nPeriod:",
        window,
        "\nProportion of sentences in window: ",
        round(proportion_hdbscan_cluster * 100, 2),
        "%"
      ),
      data_id = cluster_id
    ),
    show.legend = FALSE,
    shape = 21
  ) +
  scale_size_continuous(range = c(1, 20)) +
  labs(edge_width = "Avg similarity") +
  scale_edge_color_manual(values = cluster_colors, na.value = "grey80") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = cluster_colors) +
  theme_void()

# create interactive girafe object with sensible hover/tooltip styling
girafe_obj <- ggiraph::girafe(
  ggobj = backbone_network_ggiraph_plot,
  width_svg = 16,
  height_svg = 10,
  options = list(
    ggiraph::opts_selection(type = "single"),
    ggiraph::opts_zoom(min = 1, max = 12), # wheel to zoom, drag to pan
    ggiraph::opts_toolbar(position = "topright")
  )
)
```

:::



The next visualisation takes the same nodes and edges but repositions the nodes in a temporal layout, with time on the x-axis and communities stacked on the y-axis. It allows to see how backbone communities evolve over time.



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# per-window equally spaced y to avoid overlap
nodes_pos <- backbone_network %>%
    activate("nodes") %>%
    as_tibble(.name_repair = "minimal") |>
    mutate(x = as.integer(factor(window, levels = window_levels))) |> 
  group_by(window) %>%
  arrange(desc(community), .by_group = TRUE) %>%
  mutate(
    n_in_window = n(),
    y = ifelse(n_in_window == 1, 0, seq(-1, 1, length.out = n_in_window))
  ) %>%
  ungroup()

# distribute nodes vertically within each (community, window) cell to avoid overlap
# compute per-(community,x) offsets without calling seq() on a vector
# compute required band per community (max nodes in any x for that community)
comm_band <- nodes_pos %>%
  mutate(community = factor(community, levels = comm_levels)) %>%
  group_by(community, x) %>%
  summarise(n_in_cell = n(), .groups = "drop") %>%
  group_by(community) %>%
  summarise(
    max_in_column = max(n_in_cell, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  arrange(community) %>%
  mutate(
    max_in_column = pmax(max_in_column, 1L),
    pad = 0.7, # vertical padding between community bands
    band = max_in_column + pad # total vertical band height for the community
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    baseline = cumsum(lag(band, default = 0)) + band / 2 # center y for each community band
  ) %>%
  select(community, band, baseline)

# assign nodes within their community/x band
nodes_pos <- nodes_pos %>%
  mutate(community = factor(community, levels = comm_levels)) %>%
  left_join(comm_band, by = "community") %>%
  group_by(community, x) %>%
  arrange(window, cluster_id, .by_group = TRUE) %>%
  mutate(
    n_in_cell = n(),
    # centered offsets inside the community band; works for n_in_cell == 1 as well
    offset = (row_number() - 0.5) * band / n_in_cell - band / 2,
    y = baseline + offset
  ) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  select(cluster_id, x, y, community)

# join positions into the graph nodes (match keys exactly)
temporal_backbone_network <- backbone_network %>%
  activate("nodes") %>%
  left_join(nodes_pos, by = c("cluster_id", "community"))

# compute label positions for communities (uses comm_band and layout from above)
community_label_positions <- comm_band %>%
  left_join(
    layout %>% as_tibble() %>% distinct(community, label_backbone_community),
    by = "community"
  ) %>%
  arrange(match(community, comm_levels)) %>%
  mutate(label = str_wrap(label_backbone_community, 40))

temporal_network_plot <- ggraph(
  temporal_backbone_network,
  layout = "manual",
  x = x,
  y = y
) +
  geom_edge_link(
    aes(colour = edge_community),
    alpha = 0.5,
    show.legend = FALSE,
    width = 2
  ) +
  geom_label(
    aes(
      x = x,
      y = y,
      label = cluster_id,
      fill = community,
      size = proportion_hdbscan_cluster
    ),
    label.padding = unit(0.12, "lines"),
    show.legend = FALSE,
    alpha = 0.9
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = cluster_colors) +
  scale_edge_color_manual(values = cluster_colors, na.value = "grey80") +
  scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = seq_along(window_levels),
    labels = window_levels
  ) +
  # y axis showing community labels at their baseline positions
  scale_y_continuous(
    breaks = community_label_positions$baseline,
    labels = community_label_positions$label,
    expand = expansion(add = c(1, 0.8))
  ) +
  scale_size_continuous(range = c(3, 10)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    panel.grid = element_blank(),
    axis.title.y = element_blank(),
    axis.text.y = element_text(size = 8, hjust = 1),
    axis.ticks.y = element_line(color = "grey50"),
    axis.line.y = element_line(color = "grey50"),
    axis.line.x = element_line(color = "grey50"),
    axis.ticks.x = element_line(color = "grey50"),
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1, vjust = 1, size = 9)
  )

ggsave(
  here("pictures", "temporal_network_plot.png"),
  temporal_network_plot,
  units = "cm",
  width = 30,
  height = 30,
  dpi = 300
)
```

```{.r .cell-code}
  temporal_backbone_network,

  x = x,

  geom_edge_link(
    aes(colour = edge_community),
    alpha = 0.5,
    show.legend = FALSE
  ) +
  geom_point_interactive(
    aes(
      x = x,
      y = y,
      fill = community,
      size = proportion_hdbscan_cluster,
      tooltip = str_c(
        label_hdbscan_cluster,
        "\nPeriod:",
        window,
        "\nProportion of sentences in window: ",
        round(proportion_hdbscan_cluster * 100, 2),
        "%"
      ),
      data_id = cluster_id
    ),
    show.legend = FALSE,
    shape = 21,
    alpha = 0.9
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = cluster_colors) +
  scale_edge_color_manual(values = cluster_colors, na.value = "grey80") +
  scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = seq_along(window_levels),
    labels = window_levels
  ) +
  # y axis showing community labels at their baseline positions
  scale_y_continuous(
    breaks = community_label_positions$baseline,
    labels = community_label_positions$label,
    expand = expansion(add = c(0.9, 0.9))
  ) +
  scale_size_continuous(range = c(2, 15)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    panel.grid = element_blank(),
    axis.title.y = element_blank(),
    axis.text.y = element_text(size = 10, hjust = 1),
    axis.ticks.y = element_line(color = "grey50"),
    axis.line.y = element_line(color = "grey50"),
    axis.line.x = element_line(color = "grey50"),
    axis.ticks.x = element_line(color = "grey50"),
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1, vjust = 1, size = 9)
  )

# create interactive girafe object with sensible hover/tooltip styling
girafe_obj_time <- ggiraph::girafe(
  ggobj = temporal_network_ggiraph_plot,
  width_svg = 16,
  height_svg = 10,
  options = list(
    ggiraph::opts_selection(type = "single"),
    opts_tooltip(use_fill = TRUE),
    ggiraph::opts_zoom(min = 1, max = 12), # wheel to zoom, drag to pan
    ggiraph::opts_toolbar(position = "topright")
  )
)

girafe_obj_time
```

## Description of the clusters: a reader’s guide {#sec-description}

A series of indicators are produced for each clusters. Here are some explanations on how to read them.

### Header summary
::: {.callout-note}
**What this shows**: size, time span, and main sources of the cluster.  
**How to read**:  
- **Sentences and share**: number of sentences in this cluster and its share of all analysed sentences.  
- **Period**: first and last window where this cluster appears.  
- **Recurring authors/journals**: most frequent contributors by sentence count.  
**Notes**: counts are sentence-level. Long papers can contribute many sentences.
:::

### Top TF-IDF terms describing the community
::: {.callout-tip}
**What this shows**: words or two-word phrases most specific to this intertemporal backbone community over the full period, in comparison to all other backbone communities.  
**How to read**: higher TF-IDF = greater within-cluster distinctiveness. Compare terms within this table.  
**Use**: quick topic fingerprint.  
**Caution**: This is not an "absolute" TF-IDF: to take into account the fact that more recent periods have more sentences, we average TF-IDF calculated at the window level.
:::

### Top TF-IDF terms by kmean cluster
::: {.callout-tip}
**What this shows**: the kmean cluster’s distinctive vocabulary.  
**How to read**: compare kmean clusters within the same backbone community to see terms that appear or fade.  
**Use**: detect shifts in focus, methods, or cases across time, as well as diversity within a backbone community.
:::

### Distribution of sentences over time
::: {.callout-note}
**What this shows**: yearly counts of sentences in this cluster.  
**How to read**: bars = activity level. Peaks = years with more writing on this theme.  
**Caution**: absolute counts, not shares. Later years may have more total publishing.
:::

### Closest sentences from "rationality" and "rational" embeddings within the backbone community
::: {.callout-note}
**What this shows**: sentences that have the highest cosine similarity with the "rational"/"rationality" embeddings  
**How to read**: examples of how this community talks about the future.  
**Caution**: ranked by the proximity with "rational"/"rationality" embeddings, not by the proximity with the centroid of the cluster (i.e. the average point in the cluster).
:::

### Closest sentences to the backbone community centroid
::: {.callout-note}
**What this shows**: sentences most representative of the backbone community's core meaning.  
**How to read**: scan to grasp the cluster’s center. These sentences help to grasp what's the cluster is about, but not necessarily how it talks about the future.
**Caution**: this has been calculated by averaging the embeddings of all sentences in the backbone community, and then finding the sentences closest to this centroid. May be biased towards more recent periods when the community grew over time.
:::

### Closest sentences to the kmean cluster centroids
::: {.callout-tip}
**What this shows**: centroid-closest sentences split by window.  
**How to read**: compare phrasing across clusters to see stability or change, as well as diversity in the community.
**Caution**: this has been calculated by calculating the distance of each sentence to the centroid of its kmean cluster. Here, we look at the lowest values (low distance) rather than highest values (high similarity).
:::

### Top articles (most sentences) of the backbone community
::: {.callout-note}
**What this shows**: works contributing the most sentences to this cluster.  
**Columns**: **Number sentences** and **Work Similarity**.  
— **Number sentences**: volume contributed by the work.  
— **Word Similarity**: mean of the cosine similarity to "rationality"/"rational" for that work’s sentences in this cluster.  
**How to read**: Most representative articles of the cluster. Worth clicking on the link to see more about what the article is about. Often a good way to understand how it talks about rationality.
:::

### Top articles (most sentences) of each kmean cluster
::: {.callout-note}
**What this shows**: same as above, but split by kmean cluster.  
**How to read**: see which articles contribute to which kmean clusters within the backbone community
:::

### Most cited references in the backbone community
::: {.callout-note}
**What this shows**: the references most often cited by the articles that contribute sentences to this community.

**Columns**  
- **First Author / Year / Journal**: metadata from the reference list.  
- **Citation by article**: number of *distinct articles in this cluster* that cite the reference.  
- **Citation by sentence**: **Citation by article** weighted by how many sentences those citing articles contribute to the cluster (higher = the reference is cited by more central articles in this cluster).

**How to read**: prefer **Citation by sentence** to identify anchors of the cluster; use **Citation by article** to see breadth of citing articles.

**Caveats**  
- The second table lists references *without stable IDs*. This helps recovering books but may be inaccurate.  
- Weighting captures cluster centrality of the *citing articles*, not the number of in-text mentions.  
- Abbreviated journal names may vary.
:::

### Most cited references in each kmean clusters
::: {.callout-tip}
**What this shows**: decade-level leaders by the same two indicators.
**How to read**: compare decades and clusters in same decate to see which references anchor the community at different times.
:::

### Column legend
- **Sentence**: quoted sentence.  
- **Title**: clickable article title.  
- **Year**: publication year.  
- **Journal**: outlet.  
- **Authors**: as listed.  
- **Words Similarity**: cosine similarity to the embeddings of "rational"/"rationality".  
- **Centroid Similarity**: cosine similarity to the cluster's centroid.  
- **Distance to centroid**: distance to the kmean cluster's centroid.
- **Number sentences**: sentences from that work in this cluster.  

### General cautions
- Similarity values lie in \[0,1]. Near-top differences can still matter.  
- TF-IDF is comparative within this dataset.  
- All counts reflect the top-1% sentences set used here.


# Description of the Clusters




```{.r .cell-code}
for (cluster in list_clusters) {
  cluster_data <- sentences %>%
    arrange(window) |>
    filter(backbone_community == !!cluster) %>%
    mutate(title = glue("<a href='{url}' target='_blank'>{title}</a>"))

  cluster_name <- cluster_data %>%
    pull(label_backbone_community) %>%
    unique

  hdbscan_clusters <- cluster_data %>%
    distinct(HDBSCAN_cluster, window, cluster_id)

  # extracting the first year and last year of the community
  window <- c(
    first(unique(cluster_data$window)) %>% str_extract("^\\d{4}"),
    last(unique(cluster_data$window)) %>% str_extract("\\d{4}$")
  )

  ################ Beginning of the template ######################
  cat(sprintf("  \n## Intertemporal cluster _%s_ \n\n", cluster_name))

  ############# General Info ##################
  cat(paste0(
    "  \nThe cluster gathers ",
    nrow(distinct(cluster_data, sentence_id, id)),
    " sentences from our corpus. It represents ",
    round(
      nrow(distinct(cluster_data, sentence_id, id)) /
        nrow(distinct(sentences, id, sentence_id)) *
        100,
      2
    ),
    "% of all the sentences selected over the whole period.\n"
  ))

  cat(paste0(
    "\nThe community exists from ",
    window[1],
    " to ",
    window[2],
    ". \n\n"
  ))

  recurring_authors <- cluster_data %>%
    filter(!is.na(authors)) %>%
    select(authors, id) %>%
    separate_longer_delim(authors, delim = ", ") %>%
    # unnest(authors) %>%
    add_count(authors, name = "nb_sentences") %>%
    distinct(authors, id, nb_sentences) %>%
    add_count(authors, name = "nb_articles") %>%
    distinct(authors, nb_sentences, nb_articles) %>%
    slice_max(order_by = nb_sentences, n = 15)
  cat(paste0(
    "The most recurring authors are ",
    paste0(
      recurring_authors$authors,
      " (",
      recurring_authors$nb_sentences,
      " sentences; ",
      recurring_authors$nb_articles,
      " articles)",
      collapse = ", "
    ),
    ".\n\n"
  ))

  recurring_journals <- cluster_data %>%
    select(journal, id) %>%
    add_count(journal, name = "nb_sentences") %>%
    distinct(journal, id, nb_sentences) %>%
    add_count(journal, name = "nb_articles") %>%
    distinct(journal, nb_sentences, nb_articles) %>%
    slice_max(order_by = nb_sentences, n = 6)
  cat(paste0(
    "The most recurring journals are ",
    paste0(
      recurring_journals$journal,
      " (",
      recurring_journals$nb_sentences,
      " sentences; ",
      recurring_journals$nb_articles,
      " articles)",
      collapse = ", "
    ),
    ".\n\n"
  ))

  ############# TF-IDF ##################
  cat("\n### Top TF-IDF terms describing the community\n\n")
  # Extracting top terms in general and for window
  top_terms_cluster %>%
    filter(backbone_community == !!cluster) %>%
    select(token, mean_tf_idf) %>%
    kbl(col.names = c("Token", "TF-IDF")) %>%
    kable_styling(
      bootstrap_options = c("striped", "condensed"),
      font_size = 15
    ) %>%
    print()

  if (nrow(hdbscan_clusters) > 1) {
    cat(
      "\n### Top TF-IDF terms describing the different k-means clusters\n\n"
    )

    for (hdbscan_id in hdbscan_clusters$cluster_id) {
      time_window <- hdbscan_clusters %>%
        filter(cluster_id == hdbscan_id) %>%
        pull(window)

      hdbscan <- hdbscan_clusters %>%
        filter(cluster_id == hdbscan_id) %>%
        pull(HDBSCAN_cluster)

      cat(
        glue(
          "#### Top terms {cluster_data[cluster_id == hdbscan_id,]$label_hdbscan_cluster |> unique()} ({time_window})\n\n"
        ),
        sep = ""
      )

      top_terms_hdbscan_cluster %>%
        filter(window == time_window, HDBSCAN_cluster == hdbscan) %>%
        select(token, tf_idf) %>%
        kbl(col.names = c("Token", "TF-IDF")) %>%
        kable_styling(
          bootstrap_options = c("striped", "condensed"),
          font_size = 11
        ) %>%
        print()
    }
  }

  ############# Distribution sentences ##################
  cat("\n### Distribution of sentences over time \n\n")

  plot(
    cluster_data %>%
      count(year) %>%
      ggplot(aes(x = year, y = n)) +
      geom_bar(stat = "identity") +
      scale_x_continuous(expand = c(0.01, 0), n.breaks = 10) +
      scale_y_continuous(expand = c(0.01, 0)) +
      theme_light(base_size = 20) +
      labs(y = "Number of sentences", x = NULL, title = NULL)
  )

  ####### Top Sentences ###################
  top_sentences_rationality_filtered <- top_sentences_rationality %>%
    filter(backbone_community == !!cluster) %>%
    left_join(distinct(
      cluster_data,
      title,
      journal,
      authors,

  top_sentences_hdbscan_cluster_centroid_filtered <- top_sentences_hdbscan_cluster_centroid %>%
    filter(backbone_community == !!cluster) %>%
    left_join(
      distinct(
        cluster_data,
        title,
        year,
        journal,
        authors,
        id,
        sentence_id,
        url
      ),
      by = c("sentence_id", "id")
    ) %>%
    mutate(title = glue("<a href='{url}' target='_blank'>{title}</a>"))

  top_sentences_backbone_community_centroid_filtered <- top_sentences_backbone_community_centroid %>%
    filter(backbone_community == !!cluster) %>%
    left_join(
      distinct(
        cluster_data,
        title,
        year,
        journal,
        authors,
        id,
        sentence_id,
        url
      ),

    ) %>%
    mutate(title = glue("<a href='{url}' target='_blank'>{title}</a>"))

  ############# Top sentences rationality ##################
  cat("\n\n")
  cat(
    "\n### Closest sentence from 'rational' and 'rationality' of the backbone community\n\n"
  )

  top_sentences_rationality_filtered %>%
    slice_max(similarity, n = 20, by = backbone_community) %>%
    select(
      sentence,

        "Sentence",
        "Title",
        "Year",
        "Journal",
        "Authors",
        "Words Similarity"
      )
    ) %>%
    kable_styling(
      bootstrap_options = c("striped", "condensed"),

    ) %>%
    column_spec(2, "3.5cm") %>%

  ############# Top sentences centroid ##################
  cat("\n### Closest sentences of the backbone community's centroid\n\n")

  top_sentences_backbone_community_centroid_filtered %>%
    slice_max(backbone_centroid_similarity, n = 15) %>%
    select(

        "Authors",
        "Similarity to Backbone Centroid"
      )
    ) %>%
    kable_styling(
      bootstrap_options = c("striped", "condensed"),
      font_size = 13
    ) %>%
    column_spec(2, "3.5cm") %>%
    print()

  if (nrow(hdbscan_clusters) > 1) {
    cat(
      "\n### Closest sentences of each HDBSCAN cluster's centroid composing the backbone community\n\n"
    )

    for (hdbscan_id in unique(cluster_data$cluster_id)) {
      time_window <- hdbscan_clusters %>%
        filter(cluster_id == hdbscan_id) %>%
        pull(window)

      hdbscan <- hdbscan_clusters %>%
        filter(cluster_id == hdbscan_id) %>%
        pull(HDBSCAN_cluster)
      cat(
        glue(
          "#### Top terms {cluster_data[cluster_id == hdbscan,]$label_hdbscan_cluster |> unique()} ({time_window})\n\n"
        ),

      )

      top_sentences_hdbscan_cluster_centroid_filtered %>%
        filter(window == time_window, HDBSCAN_cluster == hdbscan) %>%
        slice_max(similarity_hdbscan_centroid, n = 10) %>%
        select(
          sentence,
          title,
          year,
          journal,
          authors,

          escape = FALSE,
          col.names = c(
            "Sentence",
            "Title",
            "Year",
            "Journal",
            "Authors",
            "Similarity to HDSBSCAN Centroid"
          )
        ) %>%
        kable_styling(
          bootstrap_options = c("striped", "condensed"),

        ) %>%

        print()
    }
  }

  ############# Top articles ##################
  cat("\n### Top articles (most sentences) of the backbone cluster\n\n")
  # Extracting top terms in general and for window
  cluster_data |>
    mutate(
      mean_similarity = mean(similarity_rv) %>% round(3),
```

## Intertemporal cluster _1: bounded_rationality, rationality, rationalism, bounded_ 

  
The cluster gathers 15387 sentences from our corpus. It represents 4.64% of all the sentences selected over the whole period.

The community exists from 1900 to 1999. 

The most recurring authors are Frank H. Knight (178 sentences; 37 articles), Robert Sugden (117 sentences; 12 articles), O. H. Taylor (80 sentences; 8 articles), Talcott Parsons (74 sentences; 8 articles), Pingle M. (74 sentences; 4 articles), J. W. Fedderke (70 sentences; 1 articles), Oliver E. Williamson (65 sentences; 19 articles), Nicholas Levis (65 sentences; 6 articles), <suffix>Jr.</suffix> (63 sentences; 43 articles), Machan T.R. (62 sentences; 4 articles), Herbert A. Simon (61 sentences; 9 articles), Joseph A. Schumpeter (58 sentences; 3 articles), Etzioni A. (58 sentences; 3 articles), Tilla Siegel (57 sentences; 3 articles), Paul T. Homan (54 sentences; 11 articles).

The most recurring journals are The American Economic Review (1025 sentences; 547 articles), The Quarterly Journal of Economics (906 sentences; 364 articles), Journal of Political Economy (698 sentences; 374 articles), The Economic Journal (679 sentences; 347 articles), Journal of Economic Issues (553 sentences; 219 articles), Economica (505 sentences; 210 articles).

   <td style="text-align:left;"> From a purely theoretical standpoint, there are good reasons for assuming rationality. </td>

   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1909635" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1909635" target="_blank">Rational Expectations and the Theory of Price Movements</a> </td>

  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Intuitively we expect every considered judgment or decision of a serious person to be rational in some definite sense. </td>

   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1884325" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1884325" target="_blank">Distortion of Subjective Probabilities as a Reaction to Uncertainty</a> </td>

   <td style="text-align:left;"> However, the implications of more "rationality" will be considered, as well as whether the label is always being correctly applied.4 Two related ideas will be presented. </td>

   <td style="text-align:left;"> "26 A number of controversies in the social sciences, especially as it pertains to the problem of rationality, are due to the making of elliptical judgments on the respective rationality or irrationality of certain actions without defining the term itself or, if it is done, in terms of inapplicable praxiological rules. </td>

   <td style="text-align:left;"> We use the overall concept of selective rationality to designate a set of psychological postulates which suggests that individuals behave neither "fully rationally," nor "irrationally," but choose some degree of rationality as this term is used by econiomists.5 Although individuals come in a variety of psychological types, we try to designate an essential element of behavior behind this variety by assuming that in general individuals behave on the one hand (a) as they like to, and on the other hand, (b) as they feel they must. </td>

  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> First, I would like to expand on the theme that almost all human behavior has a large rational component, but only in terms of the broader everyday sense of rationality, not the economists' more specialized sense of maximization. </td>

   <td style="text-align:left;"> This paper will analyze views of rationality that could underlie such claims. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://doi.org/10.1017/S0266267100005095" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://doi.org/10.1017/S0266267100005095" target="_blank">On the possibility of rational dilemmas: An Axiomatic Approach</a> </td>

   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.877 </td>

  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Thus, a critic of the rationality assumption faces the following well-fortified position: (i) a definition of rationality which appears to be overly permissive in some important respects; (ii) a willingness of choice theorists to make the theory even more permissive, as needed to accomodate apparent violations of its requirements; (iii) a methodological position that treats rationality as a maintained hypothesis, making it very difficult to disprove; (iv) an apparent readiness to assume that behavior that has not been proved to be irrational is highly intelligent. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/40753012" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/40753012" target="_blank">New Challenges to the Rationality Assumption</a> </td>

  </tr>
  <tr>

   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/0167-2681(92)90077-O" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/0167-2681(92)90077-O" target="_blank">Costly optimization: an experiment</a> </td>

   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.862 </td>

  <tr>

   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2235528" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2235528" target="_blank">Bounded Rationality, Indeterminacy, and the Theory of the Firm</a> </td>

   <td style="text-align:left;"> It is hoped that this paper can give a contribution to such a rethinking of the notion of ra tionality by pointing out why and how making the traditional approach to rationality behaviorally consistent entails a fatai loss of generality and of practical relevance of the analysis. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/23247010" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/23247010" target="_blank">INSIDE RATIONAL EXPECTATIONS: THE INDIVIDUAL VIEWPOINT</a> </td>

  </tr>

   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01079204" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01079204" target="_blank">The epistemic structure of a theory of a game</a> </td>

   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.859 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Some commentators relate this form of decision making to Simon’s concept of “bounded rationality” (1955), in which case it does not challenge or supplant rationality but, rather, takes a position on a rational‐irrational spectrum. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://doi.org/10.1108/03068299810212414" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://doi.org/10.1108/03068299810212414" target="_blank">If planning is about anything, what is it about?</a> </td>

  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Rationality, it is said, is viewed as a matter of choosing efficient means for the attainment of given ends; but there are situations in which a person who acts on the prescriptions of the theory will do less well than one who does not. </td>

  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> and are seen as optimal dynamic decision rules of rational agents, as both can be rationalised in terms of equilibrium theory.3 If expectations about p, are formed as postulated by the rational expectations hypothesis, the system of and implies that no monetary policy rule can affect the behaviour of real output. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/S0014-2921(82)80056-1" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/S0014-2921(82)80056-1" target="_blank">Unanticipated money, output and prices in Greece</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1982 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> European Economic Review </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Alogoskoufis G.S. </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.784 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> I find particularly objectionable the postulate that all rational agents believe the quantity theory of money holds instantly, because there is no reason in the world that this should be true, [in Klamer, 1983, 125-26] * As has been noted numerous times (Hoover [1988] is one example), the two hypotheses of rational expectations and market clearing are not logically connected. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/40326404" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/40326404" target="_blank">Modigliani's Expectations</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 2004 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Eastern Economic Journal </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> James E. Hartley </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.767 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> he key element underlying this strong implication of 'rational' expec-, for the role of monetary policy is that 'rational' expectations, by !G definition, yield predictions of future events which differ from the eventual outcomes only by errors which are themselves ~~dc~ndent of the variables used to generate the predictions. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/0304-3932(79)90022-9" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/0304-3932(79)90022-9" target="_blank">Optimal expectations and the extreme information assumptions of 'rational expectations' macromodels</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1979 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Journal of Monetary Economics </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Friedman B. </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.765 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Thus, rational expectations concerning future actions of the monetary authorities can have anticipatory effects; but unlike some models, where these attempt of one party to gain at the expense of the other. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/0014-2921(92)90084-A" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/0014-2921(92)90084-A" target="_blank">Capital markets and economic fluctuations in capitalist economies</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1992 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> European Economic Review </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Stiglitz J.E. </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.763 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The connection between the rational and adaptive models should not be overemphasized in this case because it relies on some rather specific assumptions about the inflation process and because our earlier results rejected rationality as an adequate model of expectations formation with these data. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1924211" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1924211" target="_blank">The Formation of Inflationary Expectations</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1981 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The Review of Economics and Statistics </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Stephen Figlewski, Paul Wachtel </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.763 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> If one believes that anticipations are formed rationally, then this evk!ence iur';her implies that adaptive: antic!ipations were not in fact rational in at least three of the hyperinflations. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/0304-3932(82)90049-6" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/0304-3932(82)90049-6" target="_blank">An alternate method of estimating the Cagan money demand function in hyperinflation under rational expectations</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1982 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Journal of Monetary Economics </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Goodfriend M. </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.759 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> A key result of this procedure is that we cannot reject the joint hypothesis that agents' expectations are rational and that ex ante real rates are exogenous, or Granger-causally prior, relative to a universe containing money, prices, nominal rates, and output. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1911728" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1911728" target="_blank">Money, Real Interest Rates, and Output: A Reinterpretation of Postwar U.S. Data</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1985 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Econometrica </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Robert B. Litterman, Laurence Weiss </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.758 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> "2 Let us allow, furthermore, that where inflationary anticipations are concerned economic agents base their behavior exclusively on "rationally-formed" expectations. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/4537789" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/4537789" target="_blank">Non-Positive Market-Clearing Real Rates of Interest</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1983 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Journal of Post Keynesian Economics </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Paul Beckerman </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.757 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Conversely, all but the rational expectations monetary model (D) are capable of rejecting at least one other specification. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/135076" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/135076" target="_blank">Empirical Models of the Exchange Rate: Separating the Wheat from the Chaff</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1984 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The Canadian Journal of Economics / Revue canadienne d'Economique </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> David Backus </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.757 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Another branch of the literature examines the effects of alternative specifications for rational expectations which leads to the consideration of learning processes, peso problems and rational bubbles. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/S0261-5606(99)00036-4" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/S0261-5606(99)00036-4" target="_blank">Uncovered interest parity, monetary policy and time-varying risk premia</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1999 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Journal of International Money and Finance </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Anker P. </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.754 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Hence forming rational expectations in this model includes forming a rational expectation of the monetary authority's policy action. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1058483" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1058483" target="_blank">Rational Expectations of Government Policy: An Application of Newcomb's Problem</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1982 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Southern Economic Journal </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Roman Frydman, Gerald P. O'Driscoll, <suffix>Jr.</suffix>, Andrew Schotter </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.754 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> According to rational expectations theorists, instead, private agents, and a fortiori the monetary authority, have complete knowledge of the "true" model of the economy; a discretionary policy will increase the variance of output because, by conveying wrong signals to agents, it blurs the assessment of relative prices. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1803937" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1803937" target="_blank">The Rational Expectations Hypothesis in Retrospect</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1983 </td>

  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> In models of this class, expectations of monetary policy are often assumed to be rational. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1058483" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1058483" target="_blank">Rational Expectations of Government Policy: An Application of Newcomb's Problem</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1982 </td>

   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.752 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Rational expectations implies that agents understand the connection between money and the price level and that they correctly anticipate the systematic components of government monetary policy. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2725227" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2725227" target="_blank">Two Types of Monetarism</a> </td>

  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Contrary to advocates of the rational expectations hypothesis, we conclude from the theorem that money is generally non-neutral under perfect information and rational expectations. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/40439311" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/40439311" target="_blank">Rational Expectations and Non-Neutrality of Money</a> </td>

  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> In its most recent form, this proposition has been expressed as the rational expectations hypothesis, proponents of which' argue, in the context of the standard "ad hoc" macro model, that not only the level but the entire probability distribution of output is independent of the deterministic parameters of the monetary policy rule. </td>

  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The latter finding not only illustrates a potential benefit from intransparency under discretion, it also addresses a critique that has been made of the “inflationary bias” outcome under the assumption of fully rational agents (see, e.g., McCallum, 1997). </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ejpoleco.2006.07.002" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ejpoleco.2006.07.002" target="_blank">The value of central bank transparency when agents are learning</a> </td>

  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> However, whatever its merits as a description of the way expectations are formed in the real world, the rationality assumption gives policymakers a useful insight into the qualitative properties of prices and exchange rates when their objective is to guide the economy along paths of self-fulfilling expectations. </td>

  </tr>

   <td style="text-align:left;"> In that case it would be irrational for economic agents to continue to form their price expectations adaptively.12 The rational expectations approach assumes that economic agents use all the information available to them and learn that the actual development of inflation is conditioned by the structure of the economy and the policies applied (see [18, 25]). </td>

   <td style="text-align:left;"> The idea that we can have a stable unit of money leaves out of sight that the bounty of Nature varies, that man's industrial activities do not exactly coincide with human requirements, that the vagaries of taste disturb his wants, and that the standard of his desires perpetually alters. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1823606" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1823606" target="_blank">Consideration of the Proposal to Stabilize the Unit of Money</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1919 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The American Economic Review </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> G. H. Knibbs </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.808 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> This difference between money and other commodities ought to make it apparent that the value of money cannot be accounted for by precisely the same phase of the law of supply and demand as will account for the value of other commodities. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1884906" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1884906" target="_blank">The Concept of an Economic Quantity</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1907 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The Quarterly Journal of Economics </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> T. N. Carver </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.799 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The obvious importance of this consideration to the discussion of the quantity theory of money will at once appear, and it leads to some of the following considerations. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1884906" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1884906" target="_blank">The Concept of an Economic Quantity</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1907 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The Quarterly Journal of Economics </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> T. N. Carver </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.798 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Money also he claitns does not derive its purchasing power from the natural qualities of the metals of which it is composed, but from the agreemellt of people to employ thetn as instruments of exchange. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://www.jstor.org/stable/10.2307/2485740" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://www.jstor.org/stable/10.2307/2485740" target="_blank">The Theory of Value before Adam Smith</a> </td>

  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> 553 it is proposed to show here that by changes in the volume of money there are set in operation, in the very nature of the case, other influences which make it impossible that other things should remain the same, thus destroying one of the premises of the theory. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1882416" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1882416" target="_blank">What Determines the Value of Money</a> </td>

  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> These remarks upon the metaphysics of monetary theory, and upon the nature of the "truth" attainable in that field, have been prompted by a single paragraph in this little book by a writer whose own definitive contributions toward our understanding of the non-metaphysical parts of his subject are so numerous and important as to forbid the suggestion that he himself, despite his obviously deep and earnest interest in its metaphysics, will allow himself to be drawn into controversies which from their very nature are bound to be futile. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1885369" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1885369" target="_blank">Hawtrey's the Gold Standard in Theory and Practice</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1927 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The Quarterly Journal of Economics </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Arthur W. Marget </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.828 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> It is consequently somewhat disconcerting to be told by the best-known English monetary theorist 1 that the doctrine of limitation of currency is obsolete, and has been replaced by the doctrine that due limitation of credit is what is necessary, and if that is present, currency will somehow manage to be of the right magnitude. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2222618" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2222618" target="_blank">Limitation of Currency or Limitation of Credit?</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1924 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The Economic Journal </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Edwin Cannan </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.828 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> When money is conceived as a valuable thing employed as a medium of exchange, the quantity of money is not increased by a mere multiplication of the evidences of debt without an increase of the resources available for honoring the promises, which resources are the real substance of the money. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1822583" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1822583" target="_blank">The Quantity Theory Scrutinized</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1921 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Journal of Political Economy </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Hugo Bilgram </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.817 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> In practical life recognition of the truth of the proposition is of enormous importance, because it explains the fact that private persons and the banks in which private persons pool their immediate resources can and do raise or lower the value of a currency of a given magnitude by trying to increase or diminish their holdings, and can and do by actual alteration in their holdings nullify or partially counterbalance or aggravate the effect which increase or decrease of the total of currency would otherwise have. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2222618" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2222618" target="_blank">Limitation of Currency or Limitation of Credit?</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1924 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The Economic Journal </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Edwin Cannan </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.811 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Under this general head of "metaphysical" themes in monetary theory are to be placed such topics as the definition of money, discussions of the " essential nature" of money, the "functions" of money, and similar questions. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1885369" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1885369" target="_blank">Hawtrey's the Gold Standard in Theory and Practice</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1927 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The Quarterly Journal of Economics </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Arthur W. Marget </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.809 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> There is a branch of the theory of money which might be called loosely, for want of a better name, the metaphysics of monetary theory.4 The Germans, as might have been expected in view of their traditional inclination for this type of speculation, have concerned themselves much more with this branch of the subject than have the more terrestrially minded Englishmen - whether entirely to good purpose remains yet to be seen. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1885369" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1885369" target="_blank">Hawtrey's the Gold Standard in Theory and Practice</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1927 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The Quarterly Journal of Economics </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Arthur W. Marget </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.789 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> We continue, of course, to speak of the value of money, but the catallactic meaning we give to this expression, while somewhat abstract, is neither abstruse nor vague. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1807500" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1807500" target="_blank">A Revaluation of Traditional Economic Theory</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1921 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The American Economic Review </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Carl E. Parry </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.787 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> "This is the famous Quantity Theory of Money. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2548167" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2548167" target="_blank">Recent Theories of Currency Reform</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1924 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Economica </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> T. E. Gregory </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.786 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> It is easy to argue that any attempt even to consider the problems which are suggested by what has been called the "metaphysical" branch of monetary theory is to be rejected once for all as fruitless, on the ground that one opinion upon such subjects is just as good as another. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1885369" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1885369" target="_blank">Hawtrey's the Gold Standard in Theory and Practice</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1927 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The Quarterly Journal of Economics </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Arthur W. Marget </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.785 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> This fact gives a peculiar importance to the theoretical question whether it is possible to establish an economic system without money, or whether it is possible to substitute for our monetary arrangements an improved method. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2223209" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2223209" target="_blank">The Monetary Economy of Bolshevism</a> </td>

   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.776 </td>

  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Even if it may be grasped, it is then necessary to take as the premise that money itself does not contain this " something," in order to consider the value of money in the sense of general purchasing </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://www.jstor.org/stable/10.2307/43217264" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://www.jstor.org/stable/10.2307/43217264" target="_blank">THE SUBJECTIVE THEORY OF VALUE AND THEORIES OF THE VALUE OF MONEY</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1931 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Kyoto University Economic Review </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Kei Shibata </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.825 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> So that on the one hand we have the more or less explicit idea that to have the right definition of money is to possess the key to the " right " monetary policy, while on the other hand controversy on empirical problems, which by reason of the multiplicity of factors involved admit of no general solutions, acquires the character of an unbridgeable "logical " contradiction.' </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2548905" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2548905" target="_blank">On the Subject-Matter and Method of Economic Science</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1933 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Economica </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Felix Kaufmann </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.817 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> For, when the point at issue is whether - in the study of the mechanism decisive of the value of money, in which it has been made clear that in all the objects of exchange to be admitted into this mechanism the subjective value, not given them for the first time by the exchange community, is required - money which, unlike ordinary goods, does not possess value in use can possibly possess such subjective value, it is only proper that the reasons for its possession of such subjective value should be given, and, indeed, by so doing only can it explain the matter effectually. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://www.jstor.org/stable/10.2307/43217264" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://www.jstor.org/stable/10.2307/43217264" target="_blank">THE SUBJECTIVE THEORY OF VALUE AND THEORIES OF THE VALUE OF MONEY</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1931 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Kyoto University Economic Review </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Kei Shibata </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.817 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> For, whereas the subjective value of money (not the function) must be regarded as unalterable, if such necessity is to be justified, our basic experience does not approve </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://www.jstor.org/stable/10.2307/43217264" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://www.jstor.org/stable/10.2307/43217264" target="_blank">THE SUBJECTIVE THEORY OF VALUE AND THEORIES OF THE VALUE OF MONEY</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1931 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Kyoto University Economic Review </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Kei Shibata </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.813 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Nevertheless, there remain very serious grounds for asking, first of all, whether the analysis under discussion does not itself ignore some of the considerations which we found it necessary to adduce in our attempt to refute what has been characterized as the simpler form of the doctrine alleging that there is a necessary equivalence in the movements in the velocities of circulation of money and of goods. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1822850" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1822850" target="_blank">The Relation between the Velocity of Circulation of Money and the "Velocity of Circulation of Goods:" II</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1932 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Journal of Political Economy </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Arthur W. Marget </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.810 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The existence of money and the possibility of changes in its total amount (as well as changes in the amounts held by particular individuals or desired to be held by them) was thus supposed to overthrow the tautology or at least its applicability to a monetary economy, and so to admit the possibility of un- </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1806964" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1806964" target="_blank">The Relation of Wage Policies and Price Policies</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1939 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The American Economic Review </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> A. P. Lerner </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.808 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Our first problem, therefore, is to meet on its own ground the rigid form of the argument alleging the necessity for a precise equivalence in the movements of the velocity of circulation of money and of goods, and to discover the fallacy underlying that argument, if it be unsound. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1824154" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1824154" target="_blank">The Relation Between the Velocity of Circulation of Money and the "Velocity of Circulation of Goods"</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1932 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Journal of Political Economy </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Arthur W. Marget </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.807 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Just as, in the Theory of Value, the supply-and-demand mechanism is used to analyse the forces determining the value of a single commodity, so in the traditional Theory of Money the supply-and-demand mechanism, with some necessary modifications, is used to analyse the forces determining the value of money. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2967434" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2967434" target="_blank">The Theory of Money and the Analysis of Output</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1933 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The Review of Economic Studies </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Joan Robinson </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.804 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> In consequence, the equation of exchange is not, as is often supposed to be, predicated on the a priori quantity theory of money ; nor does it prove that theory .32) And the meanings possessed by all the terms included in the equation of exchange such as M, V, T, and P are essentially determined by the foregoing circumstance. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://www.jstor.org/stable/10.2307/43217271" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://www.jstor.org/stable/10.2307/43217271" target="_blank">AN EXAMINATION OF PROFESSOR CASSEL'S QUANTITY THEORY OF MONEY</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1932 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Kyoto University Economic Review </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Kei Shibata </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.801 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Cherished in contemporary monetary discussion is the classical doctrine that money is concrete and definable in terms both of the "medium" and "standard" functions. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1801987" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1801987" target="_blank">What Is Money?</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1937 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The American Economic Review </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Raymond H. Lounsbury </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.799 </td>
  </tr>
</tbody>

  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Since this conclusion itself seems necessary to the successful integration of the general theories of money and price and to putting both bodies of doctrine "on the same side of the moon,"2 the objections will be considered in considerable detail. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1884572" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1884572" target="_blank">Some Fundamentals in Liquidity Theory</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1945 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The Quarterly Journal of Economics </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> M. Bronfenbrenner </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.821 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The function of some kinds of money as a reserve for others is obviously not a function of money in general and it may as well here be said that, in the writer's opinion, the social interest would be served if there were no difference between the powers possessed by any of the several forms of money which it may be convenient to keep in circulation. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1814476" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1814476" target="_blank">The Primary Functions of Money and their Consummation in Monetary Policy</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1940 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The American Economic Review </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Frank D. Graham </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.820 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> At any rate, where the quantity theory of money occuppies an important position, it is only too natural that monetary quantity should be held in great importance, forming the issue of arguments. " </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://www.jstor.org/stable/10.2307/43216917" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://www.jstor.org/stable/10.2307/43216917" target="_blank">ON THE MONETARY IDEAS AS SEEN IN THE RECORDS OF ECONOMIC AND FINANCE IN THE SUNG HISTORY</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1942 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Kyoto University Economic Review </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Fumio Hozumi </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.814 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> I am convinced that an appropriate type of money will either maintain full economic activity, without alterations in the value of the monetary unit, or that this cannot be done by any monetary manipulation whatever and that the problem must be attacked by other means such as the direct stimulation of investment, reduction of saving, or both. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1814476" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1814476" target="_blank">The Primary Functions of Money and their Consummation in Monetary Policy</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1940 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The American Economic Review </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Frank D. Graham </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.801 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> What is usually desired is not a mere change in what has been defined as money, but rather a change in what money is supposed to do, but which this money will not do. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2663455" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2663455" target="_blank">The Supply of Bank Money in England and Wales, 1920-1938</a> </td>

   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.799 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> This does not mean a belief that the value of money depends solely on its quantity, nor that a permanently fixed volume of money would result in a stable value of money. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/3484132" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/3484132" target="_blank">Monetary Policy in the United States in World War II</a> </td>
