  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The two characteristics of money, viz., the facts that its utility depends on prices and that it is not consumed where it is demanded, have proved not to present insuperable difficulties. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1909263" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1909263" target="_blank">The Consumer's Demand for Money</a> </td>

   <td style="text-align:left;"> C. E. V. Leser </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.798 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Likewise they must not fall into the error of depending on the quantity of money alone as an adequate regulator of economic developments, or adopt the reverse doctrine that the amount of money is an unimportant and irrelevant condition with little or no bearing on prices or the course of events. </td>

   <td style="text-align:left;"> If a clearly understood policy of increasing the quantity of money at a reasonable rate were to be established these reasons for variation in monetary velocity would disappear, and with them the usual basis for the belief that changes in the quantity of money should be used to offset changes in monetary velocity. </td>

   <td style="text-align:left;"> Nevertheless, most economists will admit, on consideration, that those economic phenomena bear no definite relationship to the amount of money in the above mentioned sense, and that they could not be controlled in any definite way by manipulating the quantity of money defined as </td>

  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The real issue, then, is not the existence of vested interests which will compel inflation but the adequacy of unconditional ex ante compensatory policies.9 V Let us now consider the relation of monetary theory to the prevailing pessimistic conclusions about the future value of money. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1826438" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1826438" target="_blank">Keynesianism and Inflation</a> </td>

  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> What has been said above is not to be construed as disparagement of monetary theory, though it is critical of the apotheosis of particular doctrines or dogmas. </td>

   <td style="text-align:left;"> It is possible to take a simpler but not outright contradictory approach: to observe that it is convenient to hold assets in order to bridge the gap between the receiving and making of payments and to note that there is a wide variety of assets that could be used for this purpose.5 Money then comes to be defined as that asset or set of assets which is best adapted for this purpose in the sense that it is easy to store, cheap to realize and relatively riskless as far as its market value is concerned.6 Though it is readily granted that time deposits 4 Though it is sometimes argued that monetary theory is properly confined to dealing only with the transactions motive since other motives affect the demand for a far wider class of assets than anyone would think of classifying as money. </td>

  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> If we believe that the demand for money is a stable function around which there is very little variation, that the interest-elasticity of the demand for money is low, and that the direction of causation runs from the stock of money to the arguments on the right- </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1817196" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1817196" target="_blank">Lessons for the Present from the Great Depression</a> </td>

   <td style="text-align:left;"> Peter Temin </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.802 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> While a credible long-run commitment to a specified quantitative rule concerning the rate of increase in the money supply would have the advantage of relating price-level expectations to an objective factor, the relationship between observing such a rule and observing a specific price-level objective is apt to be too loose. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2722802" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2722802" target="_blank">Lessons From the Failure of Demand-Management Policies: A Look at the Theoretical Foundations</a> </td>

   <td style="text-align:left;"> William Fellner </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.802 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> However, if as assumed throughout this paper the money stock can be set at exactly the desired level, then the money stock may as well be called an instrument of monetary policy rather than a proximate target. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1883009" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1883009" target="_blank">Optimal Choice of Monetary Policy Instruments in a Simple Stochastic Macro Model</a> </td>

   <td style="text-align:left;"> William Poole </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.799 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> If monetary theory provides no rationale for the holding of money, many of the conclusions of currently accepted monetary theory, which derive from treating money like any other good or factor in the utility function or the production function, become unacceptable. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2552841" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2552841" target="_blank">The Roles of Money in an Economy and the Optimum Quantity of Money</a> </td>

   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2230624" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2230624" target="_blank">Inflation: A Survey</a> </td>

   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/134472" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/134472" target="_blank">The Demand for Money in Canada: Some Additional Evidence</a> </td>

   <td style="text-align:left;"> The theoretical work of , and , suggests that in an economy in which agents have rational expectations, anticipated changes in the money supply have no effect on real output, but are simply translated into price level changes. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/S0014-2921(82)80056-1" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/S0014-2921(82)80056-1" target="_blank">Unanticipated money, output and prices in Greece</a> </td>

   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.864 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> If anticipated money matters for the real economy, a fixed monetary rule is not necessarily a safe rule. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2232830" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2232830" target="_blank">The Superiority of Contingent Rules Over Fixed Rules in Models with Rational Expectations</a> </td>

  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Elementary theoretical models seem to show, finally, that the special role of money that is (or should be) the basis of present-day monetary policies may not persist forever. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/0378-4266(82)90016-4" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/0378-4266(82)90016-4" target="_blank">Innovation in monetary policy. Challenge and response</a> </td>

   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.816 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> In particular, the following results will be shown: the fundamental implication of the rational expectations hypothesis, that is, that only unexpected changes in the money stock influence the real sector of the economy, is a basic tenet of classical monetary theory as well and is founded upon the very argument according to which agents efficiently use the available information in order to take account of the consequences of policy measures (Section I). </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1803937" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1803937" target="_blank">The Rational Expectations Hypothesis in Retrospect</a> </td>

   <td style="text-align:left;"> Filippo Cesarano </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.815 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> A rational expectations monetarist perspective makes large unpredictable movements in the money stock evidence of bad monetary policy, and it implies that if the money stock could be made to grow in a smoothly predictable way, real fluctuations would be smaller. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1816846" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1816846" target="_blank">Is There a Monetary Business Cycle?</a> </td>

   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.814 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> But even here the differences may be more apparent than real, if expected future rates of money growth cannot be perfectly predicted, and are probably themselves strongly conditioned either by current and past rates of inflation or current and past rates of money growth, a plausible component of Z in (8).5 Hence no finding about money growth, current or past, and its relationship to expected inflation can distinguish well between adaptive and rational expectations economic models of the inflation process. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1992397" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1992397" target="_blank">Models of Inflation Expectations Formation: A Comparison of Household and Economist Forecasts</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1983 </td>

   <td style="text-align:left;"> Edward M. Gramlich </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.812 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Introduction is the basic proposition advanced by the rational expectations hypothesis that, if an economy is free of money illusions, monetary policy is effective only because of a lack of information on the part of private individuals that keeps them from perceiving monetary changes perfectly. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/40439311" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/40439311" target="_blank">Rational Expectations and Non-Neutrality of Money</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1985 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Weltwirtschaftliches Archiv </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Kiyoshi Otani </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.810 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> These points cast doubt on the proposition that, in a rational expectations f samework, short run monetary policy should be based on the objective of maintaining a predetermined value of the money stock. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/0304-3932(84)90015-1" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/0304-3932(84)90015-1" target="_blank">Optimal monetary policy, endogenous supply and rational expectations</a> </td>

   <td style="text-align:left;"> It remains true that only unanticipated monetary movements matter for deviations in market output, in the sense that rational expectations do preclude any stabilizing influence of Eft iMt+r, that portion of nominal money balances in any period t + r that is predictable on the basis of full information in period t - 1. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/135398" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/135398" target="_blank">The Neutrality and Optimality of Counter-Cyclical Monetary Policy in Equilibrium Models with a Wealth Effect</a> </td>

  </tr>

   <td style="text-align:left;"> A new monetary rule would change inflation in a way that would be unpredictable using equations (7) and (8), but eventually predictable using the money demand function (2). </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1805776" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1805776" target="_blank">The Short-Run Relation between Growth and Inflation in Latin America: A Quasi-Rational or Consistent Expectations Approach</a> </td>

   <td style="text-align:left;"> INTRODUCTION A popular criticism of rational expectations models of exchange rate determination is that recent movements in exchange rates have been too volatile to be justified by movements in "fundamental" economic conditions. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2648797" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2648797" target="_blank">Rational Expectations and the Volatility of Floating Exchange Rates</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1983 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> International Economic Review </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Richard A. Meese, Kenneth J. Singleton </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.885 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The last result highlights the general significance of rational expectations for modelling exchange rates; the assumed behaviour of exogenous variables influences critically the path of the expected and hence actual exchange rate (see . </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/0261-5606(83)90009-8" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/0261-5606(83)90009-8" target="_blank">The asset market model of the balance of payments and the exchange rate: A survey of empirical evidence</a> </td>

   <td style="text-align:left;"> Horne J. </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.880 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Two types of exchange rate expectations are considered: rational and adaptive. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/0165-1889(88)90018-8" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/0165-1889(88)90018-8" target="_blank">Asymmetrical effects of monetary policy between the US and Europe</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1988 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Journal of Economic Dynamics and Control </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Karakitsos E. </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.878 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Expectations regarding the future course of the exchange rate are formed rationally2 and economic agents are assumed to be risk neutral. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2232353" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2232353" target="_blank">Currency Management and Economic Stability</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1984 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The Economic Journal </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Slobodan Djajić </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.878 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> We show below that expectations formed in this manner can be rational in the sense that they correctly predict the actual path of the exchange rate. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/0014-4983(82)90005-5" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/0014-4983(82)90005-5" target="_blank">Did speculation destabilize the French Franc in the 1920s?</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1982 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Explorations in Economic History </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Eichengreen B. </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.868 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The recent rational-expectations models of exchange-rate determination test the systematic response of expectations to the stochastic processes generating the fundamental determinants of the exchange rate. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1925538" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1925538" target="_blank">A Comparison of the Stochastic Processes of Structural and Time-Series Exchange-Rate Models</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1987 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The Review of Economics and Statistics </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Francis W. Ahking, Stephen M. Miller </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.868 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Rational expectations and the exchange rate. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/4623711" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/4623711" target="_blank">Are Exchange Rates Excessively Variable?</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1987 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> NBER Macroeconomics Annual </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Jeffrey A. Frankel, Richard Meese </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.867 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Summary In this paper it has been shown when exchange-rate expectations are rational within the context of the 'structural theory' of the foreign exchange market that 1. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/S0261-5606(83)80006-0" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/S0261-5606(83)80006-0" target="_blank">Rational expectations and the effect of exchange-rate intervention on the exchange rate</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1983 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Journal of International Money and Finance </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Beenstock M. </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.865 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> 2 The role of rational expectations in models of exchange rate dynamics has been analysed by Calvo and Rodriguez (I977), Dornbusch (I976), Frenkel (I976), Kouri (I976) and Mussa (I976), to name just a few. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2232353" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2232353" target="_blank">Currency Management and Economic Stability</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1984 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The Economic Journal </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Slobodan Djajić </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.862 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> In the former case, we have a "rational expectation" explanation of the exogenous speculative disturbance on the exchange rate as put forward and used by Dornbusch [1976, p. 269]. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/40439497" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/40439497" target="_blank">Expectations and Niehans' Exchange Rate Dynamics</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1986 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Weltwirtschaftliches Archiv </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Sukesh K. Ghosh </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.858 </td>
  </tr>

  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Thus, rational expectations concerning future actions of the monetary authorities can have anticipatory effects; but unlike some models, where these attempt of one party to gain at the expense of the other. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/0014-2921(92)90084-A" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/0014-2921(92)90084-A" target="_blank">Capital markets and economic fluctuations in capitalist economies</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1992 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> European Economic Review </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Stiglitz J.E. </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.815 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> In fact, if individuals choose their money holdings on the basis of (rational) expectations concerning the future evolution of real income, interest rates and inflation, the instability of the estimated feedback equations may be due to shifts in the expectations generating processes. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/0378-4266(92)90018-U" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/0378-4266(92)90018-U" target="_blank">Money demand instability, expectations and policy regimes: A note on the case of Italy: 1964-1986</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1992 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Journal of Banking and Finance </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Bagliano F.C. </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.807 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Rational expectations, in both theory and practice, has placed an ever-growing emphasis on the importance of unanticipated changes in the money supply as a major transmission mechanism through which monetary policy can have an effect on the real economy. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/0164-0704(91)90056-Z" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/0164-0704(91)90056-Z" target="_blank">Another source of money supply announcement surprises</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1991 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Journal of Macroeconomics </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Cunningham T.J. </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.802 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> In other words, rational expectations in themselves do not imply that the real economy will be invariant to inflation policy in either the short-run or long-run—such claims rely upon the additional, and far more questionable, as sumption of a unique market clearing equilibrium. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/23606154" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/23606154" target="_blank">THE ASSESSMENT: INFLATION POLICY</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1990 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Oxford Review of Economic Policy </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> TIM JENKINSON </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.800 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Some commentators on an earlier draft of this paper seemed to believe that this possibility of monetary irrelevance depends on the assumption that the central bank is expected to defend a future price-level target, as opposed to an inflation rate target-that money becomes irrelevant only because the central bank creates expectations of future deflation. </td>

### Closest sentence from 'rational' and 'rationality' of the backbone community

<table class="table table-striped table-condensed" style="font-size: 12px; margin-left: auto; margin-right: auto;">
 <thead>
  <tr>
   <th style="text-align:left;"> Sentence </th>
   <th style="text-align:left;"> Title </th>
   <th style="text-align:right;"> Year </th>
   <th style="text-align:left;"> Journal </th>
   <th style="text-align:left;"> Authors </th>
   <th style="text-align:right;"> Words Similarity </th>
  </tr>
 </thead>
<tbody>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> It is a useful unifying principle in economics, but all implications of rationality depend on the conditions constraining decision makers, and often this knowledge is precisely what is lacking. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/S0014-2921(98)00002-6" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/S0014-2921(98)00002-6" target="_blank">Why not cut pay?</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1998 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> European Economic Review </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Bewley T. </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.811 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Indeed this theory suggests that (a) for the standard problems and kinds of analysis in which economists trade, rationality is both insufficient and unnecessary and (b) that the term rational is grossly abused when it is applied to certain economic theories of expectation formation and decision making. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2663084" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2663084" target="_blank">The Nature of Rational Choice and The Foundations of Statistics</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1991 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Oxford Economic Papers </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Paul Anand </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.811 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> As much as economists would like to purge all normative considerations from their conception of rationality, this exercise merely empties the term “rationality” of its essential meaning. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/S1053-5357(99)00045-1" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/S1053-5357(99)00045-1" target="_blank">The volunteer's folly and socio-economic man: Some thoughts on altruism, rationality, and community</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1999 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Journal of Socio Economics </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Knox T.M. </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.767 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Since the role of economic rationality in market exchange and all economic actions is a function of definite sociohistorical–institutional conditions, it becomes an institutionalized value that is “something more than a psychological postulate—i.e., a standard of behavior to which people conform or from which they deviate” (Smelser, 1976, p. 34). </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/S1053-5357(99)00020-7" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/S1053-5357(99)00020-7" target="_blank">A socio-economic approach to market transactions</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1999 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Journal of Socio Economics </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Zafirovski M. </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.761 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> For economists habitually evaluate the rationality of actions, even actions having merely incidental economic aspects, according to their “economic efficiency.” (Unfortunately, the efficiency bias has been adopted outside the economics profession by those who want similarly to endow their judgments with an air of scientific objectivity.) </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/S1053-5357(99)00045-1" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/S1053-5357(99)00045-1" target="_blank">The volunteer's folly and socio-economic man: Some thoughts on altruism, rationality, and community</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1999 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Journal of Socio Economics </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Knox T.M. </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.757 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Economic rationality is not only ultrarelative, but also dependent upon seemingly arbitrary distinctions between means and ends. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/S1053-5357(99)00045-1" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/S1053-5357(99)00045-1" target="_blank">The volunteer's folly and socio-economic man: Some thoughts on altruism, rationality, and community</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1999 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Journal of Socio Economics </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Knox T.M. </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.746 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> If the methodological assumption of economics that people do act rationally is to be maintained, rationality cannot require that which I am not motivated to do, because I will not do it. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/S1053-5357(99)00045-1" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/S1053-5357(99)00045-1" target="_blank">The volunteer's folly and socio-economic man: Some thoughts on altruism, rationality, and community</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1999 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Journal of Socio Economics </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Knox T.M. </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.744 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> In addition, the critique may fail empirically if "irrational," strongly rule- governed behavior satisfies the abstract consistency requirements that constitute the neoclassical paradigm's most fundamental characterization of rational choice. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1061094" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1061094" target="_blank">Morality, Maximization, and Economic Behavior</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1997 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Southern Economic Journal </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Alan G. Isaac </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.743 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Despite the probable unreality of the rationality assumption it can be defended on a number of grounds within the neoclassical framework. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/3487158" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/3487158" target="_blank">Belief: Its Role in Economic Thought and Action</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1993 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The American Journal of Economics and Sociology </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> J. Barkley Rosser, <suffix>Jr.</suffix> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.742 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Studying systems competition under the assumption of rational states is the same as studying private competition under the assumption of rational individuals. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/S0047-2727(97)00043-1" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/S0047-2727(97)00043-1" target="_blank">The selection principle and market failure in systems competition</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1997 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Journal of Public Economics </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Sinn H.W. </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.739 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> In this literature, the decision makers typically behave less than fully rational in the neoclassical sense. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/S0304-4068(97)00031-1" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/S0304-4068(97)00031-1" target="_blank">When is rational behavior consistent with rules of thumb? a link between evolutionary terminology and neoclassical methodology</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1999 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Journal of Mathematical Economics </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Blonski M. </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.739 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The above argument and evidence suggest that orthodox explanations of market exchange and other economic phenomena “in terms of rational and given individuals are not as robust as is often supposed” (Hodgson, 1998, p. 175). </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/S1053-5357(99)00020-7" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/S1053-5357(99)00020-7" target="_blank">A socio-economic approach to market transactions</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1999 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Journal of Socio Economics </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Zafirovski M. </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.734 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Economists have often expostulated over the excessive rationalism of the eighteenth century, and it is certainly true that mankind is not the perfect calculator of classical theory. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1807783" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1807783" target="_blank">Fifty Years' Developments in Ideas of Human Nature and Motivation</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1936 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The American Economic Review </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> C. E. Ayres </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.733 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> , in contrast, holds that 'there is no general principle that prevents the creation of an economic theory based on hypotheses other than that of rationality'. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://doi.org/10.1017/S0266267100003229" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://doi.org/10.1017/S0266267100003229" target="_blank">A Critique of Instrumental Reason in Economics</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1995 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Economics and Philosophy </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Stewart H. </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.724 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> One might argue, then, that economic rationality may harmlessly coexist with alternative definitions, with the understanding that rationality in economics is limited to little more than technical efficiency in the production of goods, services, and utility. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/S1053-5357(99)00045-1" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/S1053-5357(99)00045-1" target="_blank">The volunteer's folly and socio-economic man: Some thoughts on altruism, rationality, and community</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1999 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Journal of Socio Economics </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Knox T.M. </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.723 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> So with these brief remarks, my critique of economic rationality advances beyond the ultrarelativism of revealed preference theory and progresses toward a deeply embedded and infrequently challenged tenet of economic analysis: the rationality of efficiency. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/S1053-5357(99)00045-1" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/S1053-5357(99)00045-1" target="_blank">The volunteer's folly and socio-economic man: Some thoughts on altruism, rationality, and community</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1999 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Journal of Socio Economics </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Knox T.M. </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.722 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> And Lucas adds: In situations of risk, the hypothesis of rational behavior on the part of agents will have usable content, so that behavior may be explainable in terms of economic theory. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/4538115" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/4538115" target="_blank">Probability and Uncertainty in Economic Analysis</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1988 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Journal of Post Keynesian Economics </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Tony Lawson </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.720 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> This is not the only way economists misunderstand rationality. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://doi.org/10.1108/03068299510764235" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://doi.org/10.1108/03068299510764235" target="_blank">Reason In Economics Versus Ethics</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1995 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> International Journal of Social Economics </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Machan T.R. </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.720 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> In sum, while there is no logically necessary conflict between rule-governed behavior and rational choice modeling-given the restricted criteria of rationality informing the neoclassical paradigm-reconciliation of actual rule-governed behavior with rational choice modeling appears problematic. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1061094" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1061094" target="_blank">Morality, Maximization, and Economic Behavior</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1997 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Southern Economic Journal </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Alan G. Isaac </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.717 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>

   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.756 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> So long as economics was political economy, so long as a statement of principles was conditioned upon a consideration of problems, so long as the building of systems had to wait upon popular concern, the subject was a capricious and vacillating one. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1822591" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1822591" target="_blank">The Place of Value Theory in Economics: II</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1918 </td>

   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.755 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> tion it is doubtful whether at this stage of the development of economics he could have covered the matter satisfactorily. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1820538" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1820538" target="_blank">An Appraisal of Clay's Economics</a> </td>

  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> If it is insisted that these forerunners of classical doctrine had no distinct speculations upon value, the obvious reply will be that this fact alone proves that they were not systems of economic thought-that they were tangled and I It is evident, of course, that the terms "productive" and "unproductive" carry the connotation, "toward something." </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1821866" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1821866" target="_blank">The Place of Value Theory in Economics: I</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1918 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Journal of Political Economy </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Walton H. Hamilton </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.747 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Not that he did not consciously accept and utilize certain established economic doctrines, such as the theory of land rent, but rather that all such had to be wrought over in his own thinking and thoroughly amalgamated with his own theoretical departures. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1804593" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1804593" target="_blank">Jevons' "Theory of Political Economy."</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1912 </td>

   <td style="text-align:left;"> Allyn A. Young </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.742 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Yet whatever hope may have been entertained as to the positive utility of the historical method in constructing a body of economic doctrine was-it is now seen- born of reaction. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://www.jstor.org/stable/10.2307/2999963" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://www.jstor.org/stable/10.2307/2999963" target="_blank">The Present State of the Theory of Distribution</a> </td>

   <td style="text-align:left;"> Jacob H. Hollander </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.740 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> But the "postulates" of the classical political economy, while restricted and scanty enough, were not as hypothetical or "assumed" as was supposed by the economists who formulated them. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1819612" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1819612" target="_blank">Some Problems of Logical Method in Political Economy</a> </td>

   <td style="text-align:left;"> J. Viner </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.738 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> If anyone chose to compare these doctrines with reality, he was at perfect liberty to do so, but in doing so he was stepping beyond the bounds of economic science, and indeed of any science. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1819612" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1819612" target="_blank">Some Problems of Logical Method in Political Economy</a> </td>

   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.737 </td>

  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> But it would be to disregard all Adam Smith's antecedents as a philosopher; all that we know of the history and transformation of the conception of " Nature " from the Greek thinkers downward; all the evident affiliation of Smith with his predecessor Hutcheson, and of both with Shaftesbury; and in particular it would be to ignore the essential unity of the Wealth of Nations with Smith's other work, the Theory of Moral Sentiments, to refuse to recognise that Smith took over the doctrine of Natural Liberty from current theology and moral philosophy. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2223376" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2223376" target="_blank">A Retrospect of Free-Trade Doctrine</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1924 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The Economic Journal </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> William Ashley </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.899 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> It is a commonplace among the authorities on Adam Smith that it is impossible fully to understand the Wealth of Nations without recourse to the Theory of Moral Sentiments. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1823421" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1823421" target="_blank">Adam Smith and Laissez Faire</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1927 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Journal of Political Economy </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Jacob Viner </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.865 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> ter's doctrine against Mandeville, and went so far as to make the pure, disinterested love of mankind the only virtuous motive in our natures.8 Finally, Adam Smith himself, before writing the Wealth of Nations, wrote upon our Moral Sentiments; and in the earlier book analyzed the mental processes by which we build up out of our experience a knowledge of the moral rules, obedience to which yields conduct conducive to the common welfare; finding in this social beneficence of our moral faculties the same proof of providential design of our natures, which he afterward saw also in the social beneficence of economic (acquisitive) ambition.4 If the two books are read together, it is clear that Smith agreed with Shaftesbury, that self-centered economic ambition is socially beneficent, so long as it is limited, as it normally is, by the beneficent dictates of our moral faculties. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1884888" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1884888" target="_blank">Tawney's Religion and Capitalism, and Eighteenth-Century Liberalism</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1927 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The Quarterly Journal of Economics </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Overton H. Taylor </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.852 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> It is quite possible that Smith carried into The Wealth of Nations from The Theory of Moral Sentiments some of the indiscriminate worship of Nature and the Law of Nature which characterised the eighteenth century. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2222682" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2222682" target="_blank">A Retrospect of Free-Trade Doctrine</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1925 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The Economic Journal </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> A. A. Mitchell </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.849 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> "27 To the extent that Smith in the Wealth of Nations does expound a, doctrine of a harmonious order in nature, he accounts for it, as a rule, and perhaps even invariably, by reference to "more familiar causes [and] to such as mankind were better acquainted with, than the agency of the gods." </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1823421" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1823421" target="_blank">Adam Smith and Laissez Faire</a> </td>

   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.847 </td>

  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> THE HARMONIOUS ORDER OF NATURE An endeavor to make a just appraisal of Adam Smith's original contributions to economic doctrine would even today be a task of extraordinary difficulty. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1823421" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1823421" target="_blank">Adam Smith and Laissez Faire</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1927 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Journal of Political Economy </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Jacob Viner </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.833 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> All governments which thwart this natural course, which force things into another channel, or which endeavor to arrest the progress of society at a particular point, are unnatural, and, to support themselves, are obliged to be oppressive and tyrannical.3 In his Theory of Moral Sentiments, Smith develops his system of ethics on the basis of a doctrine of a harmonious order 'Rae, Life of Adam Smith, p. 62. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1823421" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1823421" target="_blank">Adam Smith and Laissez Faire</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1927 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Journal of Political Economy </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Jacob Viner </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.833 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> In the political body the wisdom of nature has fortunately made ample provision for remedying many of the bad effects of the folly and injustice of man, in the same manner as it has done in the natural body for remedying those of his sloth and intemperance Adam Smith's reasons for believing in the reality of this "natural order" were partly empirical, but mainly, it is safe to say, a priori. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1822052" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1822052" target="_blank">Adam Smith: Moralist and Philosopher</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1927 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Journal of Political Economy </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Glenn R. Morrow </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.832 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Nowhere in the Wealth of Nations does Smith place any reliance for the proper working of the economic order upon the operation of benevolence or sympathy, the emphasis upon which was the novel feature in the account of human nature presented in the Theory of Moral Sentiments. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1823421" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1823421" target="_blank">Adam Smith and Laissez Faire</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1927 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Journal of Political Economy </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Jacob Viner </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.832 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> His philosophical speculations about a harmonious order in nature undoubtedly made it easier for him to reach a laissez faire policy, though I believe that the significance of the natural order in Smith's economic 60 Cf. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1823421" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1823421" target="_blank">Adam Smith and Laissez Faire</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1927 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Journal of Political Economy </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Jacob Viner </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.825 </td>
  </tr>

  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> So the doctrine of economic harmonies, while definitely misleading in some of its implications and childish in its extreme forms, was not necessarily a hindrance in the early stages of the search for regularities or laws, and natural processes of adjustment, in society's economic life. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1885439" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1885439" target="_blank">Economics and the Idea of Natural Laws</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1929 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The Quarterly Journal of Economics </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> O. H. Taylor </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.777 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> So it would be true to say that if economics as a science were to be confined to the analysis of market phenomena, denying the significance of these phenomena as evidences of the nature of human conduct, the generalizations arrived at must be confined to mechanistic explanations of how things happened after they had come to pass. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1822708" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1822708" target="_blank">Human Nature in Economic Theory</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1922 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Journal of Political Economy </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Rexford G. Tugwell </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.776 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> He feels that whereas economic science has perhaps been too much a deductive and static science, and needs to give greater consideration to the facts and institutions of economic life, economic history has consisted too greatly of a description of facts, without serious consideration of the theoretical problems. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1822053" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1822053" target="_blank">Tendencies in Swedish Economics</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1927 </td>

   <td style="text-align:left;"> Bertil Ohlin </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.766 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> But the difficulty, if not the complete of data external to man and of human behavior in its strictly objective manifestations, he later found this position untenable, and has reached the conclusion that economics, like even the physical sciences, though in greater degree, must deal with the metaphysical entities which lie behind the objective regularities which can be observed in the external world. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1822261" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1822261" target="_blank">The Utility Concept in Value Theory and Its Critics</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1925 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Journal of Political Economy </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Jacob Viner </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.763 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> cal economists and their seventeenth- and eighteenth-century predecessors used the ideas of physical science to explain economic actions and events in a way that logically precluded the application to them of ethical criteria. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1884888" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1884888" target="_blank">Tawney's Religion and Capitalism, and Eighteenth-Century Liberalism</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1927 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The Quarterly Journal of Economics </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Overton H. Taylor </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.762 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The consequences and variants of their views have been developed in philosophy, sociology, and in economic history itself, though not always with a common aim. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1822056" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1822056" target="_blank">The New Realism and Economic History</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1927 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Journal of Political Economy </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Abbott Payson Usher </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.759 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> His intention was less to promulgate a set of doctrines or to discover and expound a system of economic laws than to portray the economic situation in its totality in a way which would furnish an organon of thought for those engaged in the analysis of narrower problems. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1822132" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1822132" target="_blank">The Impasse in Economic Theory</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1927 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Journal of Political Economy </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Paul T. Homan </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.759 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> And as I study the history of economic thought it seems to me that the most worth while theory has been the by-product of attempts to solve practical, everyday problems. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1814858" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1814858" target="_blank">Land Economics</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1926 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The American Economic Review </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> B. H. Hibbard, L. C. Gray, Richard T. Ely </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.751 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> And as I study the history of economic thought it seems to me that the most worth while theory has been the by-product of attempts to solve practical, everyday problems. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1814859" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1814859" target="_blank">The Federal Reserve System</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1926 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The American Economic Review </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Owen D. Young </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.751 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> If it perchance outlaws most of our more ambitious doctrines, what, it may be asked, has become of the "pure" science of economics? </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1884782" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1884782" target="_blank">Issues in Economic Theory: an Attempt to Clarify</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1928 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The Quarterly Journal of Economics </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Paul T. Homan </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.750 </td>
  </tr>

  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> But these two statements are not yet sufficient to condemn the classical methods of mathematical economics as an arbitrary transgression of the limits of human reason. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2967553" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2967553" target="_blank">II</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1934 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The Review of Economic Studies </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Harro Bernardelli </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.784 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Economists have often expostulated over the excessive rationalism of the eighteenth century, and it is certainly true that mankind is not the perfect calculator of classical theory. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1807783" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1807783" target="_blank">Fifty Years' Developments in Ideas of Human Nature and Motivation</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1936 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The American Economic Review </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> C. E. Ayres </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.781 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> This general principle applies with especial force to economics, if we grant that it is highly desirable to keep economics " scientific." </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2548228" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2548228" target="_blank">"Economic Welfare"</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1930 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Economica </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> F. C. Benham </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.773 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Now unfortunately economic theory for the most part consists of the unlovely and inanimate skeletons of economic controversies of the past. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://www.jstor.org/stable/10.2307/136556" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://www.jstor.org/stable/10.2307/136556" target="_blank">Review of Economic Text-Books for Use in Canadian High Schools</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1934 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Contributions to Canadian Economics </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> A. E. Gilroy, A. F. W. Plumptre </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.756 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> This not merely begs the question (to which we shall return) whether a precise definition of the subject-matter of economics is possible or necessary, but it makes no attempt to justify the definition advocated in its own right. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2223780" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2223780" target="_blank">How Do We Want Economists to Behave?</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1932 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The Economic Journal </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Lindley M. Fraser </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.755 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The sterility of much ecohomic theory has been due, I think, to the attempt to amplify into a body of theory a single dominating principle, in terms of whiclh all economic phenomena might be interpreted. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1805658" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1805658" target="_blank">The Theory of Economic Dynamics as Related to Industrial Instability</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1930 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The American Economic Review </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Frank W. Taussig, Frederick C. Mills, F. B. Garver, Frank H. Knight, R. W. Souter, Lewis L. Lorwin, Mordecai Ezekiel </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.753 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> This does not mean that we find them all equally well founded, or even that his central idea, namely, that in price movements lies the cause of economic progress, seems to us so solidly established as to be unassailable. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2967444" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2967444" target="_blank">François Simiand's Theory of Economic Progress</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1938 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The Review of Economic Studies </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Robert Marjolin, G. Jaffé, W. Jaffé </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.751 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> On the contrary, the existing body of economic principles is the result of careful thinking based upon a few facts of general observation. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1824178" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1824178" target="_blank">The Scope and Definition of Economics</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1939 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Journal of Political Economy </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Raymond T. Bye </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.749 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> One may doubt, however, that the economic theorists of today will subscribe to this characterization of their general systems of economics. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1885790" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1885790" target="_blank">Equilibrium Economics and Business-Cycle Theory</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1930 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The Quarterly Journal of Economics </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Simon Kuznets </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.749 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> More and more the statement can be found that economics is but another name for politics, there being no line of demarcation between the two, and that the writing of history became scientific only when formulas were discovered which could be used to interpret historical events in terms of the economic environment. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1823170" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1823170" target="_blank">Marxian, Liberal, and Sociological Theories of Imperialism</a> </td>

   <td style="text-align:left;"> E. M. Winslow </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.745 </td>
  </tr>

  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> In justice to Mill it must be remembered that he safeguarded himself by regarding his statement as a hypothesis, but Cairnes took Mill's statement as a positive premnise, qualifying it by saying that it was incomplete but not indicating the possible importance of that incompleteness.3 It is evident, of course, that it was much easier for Senior than for Mill to bring the premises of the desire for wealth out of the realm of hypothesis since he included immaterial goods in wealth, while Mill excluded them. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2549222" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2549222" target="_blank">Nassau Senior's Contribution to the Methodology of Economics</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1936 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Economica </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Marian Bowley </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.787 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> As long as wealth was confined to material goods the necessity of the hypothesis of the economic man, though unperceived by anyone before J. S. Mill, was a fact, since it is impossible to deny the influence of desires other than the fundamental desire for wealth on values. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2549222" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2549222" target="_blank">Nassau Senior's Contribution to the Methodology of Economics</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1936 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Economica </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Marian Bowley </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.786 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> With Mill again the problem as to which line of conduct will yield "the greater portion of wealth" is not mentioned as existing, and his principle that men "naturally" prefer this to a smaller portion, only begins to have sense when it is assumed that people can foresee perfectly which line of conduct leads to the greater portion,- an assumption which Mill apparently tacitly slips in. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/41793308" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/41793308" target="_blank">Expectation and Rational Conduct</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1937 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Zeitschrift für Nationalökonomie / Journal of Economics </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> T. W. Hutchison </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.771 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> For Adams believed that a large proportion of mankind is irrational and imprudent in respect to the preservation and acquisition of wealth; that but a small proportion possesses property whereas the vast majority of every nation is virtually destitute.44 Apparently Adams did not expect this state of affairs to change appreciably, for in a letter to John Taylor of Virginia, a Jeffersonian, Adams expressed a Malthusianism to which he seems to have subscribed long before Malthus ever wrote his Essay. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1807805" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1807805" target="_blank">Malthusianism In Late Eighteenth Century America</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1935 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The American Economic Review </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> J. J. Spengler </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.764 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> than a philosopher he did not share Adam Smith's interest in the ethical significance of a labor theory of value, but when he came to work out the principles of his own economic system he was naturally attracted to an idea which fitted into it so nicely. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1883868" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1883868" target="_blank">A Re-Interpretation of Ricardo on Value</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1935 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The Quarterly Journal of Economics </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> John M.Cassels </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.754 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Mill claims for himself not "the original conception, but only the elaboration" of the part played by the "law of reciprocal demand." </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/40415959" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/40415959" target="_blank">The Doctrine of Comparative Costs</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1932 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Weltwirtschaftliches Archiv </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Jacob Viner </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.745 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> To John Stuart Mill, deeply as he disliked it, it formed along with "diminishing returns", the principal truth of Political Economy. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/136597" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/136597" target="_blank">What is Left of Adam Smith?</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1935 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The Canadian Journal of Economics and Political Science / Revue canadienne d'Economique et de Science politique </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Stephen Leacock </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.740 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Not all, of course, are equally serviceable to him; nor can he restrict himself to the doctrines most prominent in the canonical books of the economic scriptures, if only for the reason that it is precisely the interaction between the economic and nonleconomic aspects of society which, as the example of Adam Smith should be sufficient to remind us, is a central part of his theme. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2548857" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2548857" target="_blank">The Study of Economic History</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1933 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Economica </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> R. H. Tawney </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.738 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> It is possible that Mill overemphasized the unverifiability of the propositions of classical Political Economy. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1821691" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1821691" target="_blank">Werner Sombart and the "Natural Science Method" in Economics</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1933 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Journal of Political Economy </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Leo Rogin </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.737 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The economics of Adam Smith, therefore, if we attempt to apply it to the world of to-day fails utterly as an explanation of production, value, </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/136597" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/136597" target="_blank">What is Left of Adam Smith?</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1935 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The Canadian Journal of Economics and Political Science / Revue canadienne d'Economique et de Science politique </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Stephen Leacock </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.731 </td>
  </tr>
