  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Still this should not render us purblind to the fact that what he presented as a "matter-offact" inquiry into "brute" causation is substantially a critique of existing economic institutions and theories which rests upon thinly concealed value judgments, assumptions, and preconceptions concerning the past and the desirable course of future progress. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1910777" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1910777" target="_blank">Veblen and the Social Phenomenon of Capitalism</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1951 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The American Economic Review </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Abram L. Harris </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.794 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> To deny any influence to economic analysis is to deny any role to reason in the formation by a sensible man of his system of ends. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1807709" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1807709" target="_blank">Schumpeter's History of Economic Analysis</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1954 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The American Economic Review </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Jacob Viner </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.777 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> However, what emerges from such a conviction is not the use of physical or biological analogies in economics. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/40433455" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/40433455" target="_blank">The Concept of Energy in Economics</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1954 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Weltwirtschaftliches Archiv </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> S. D. Zagoroff </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.777 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> No one would deny to economists the right to define their subject in any manner they wish, but little common sense was needed to under- </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1831578" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1831578" target="_blank">The Influence of Keynesian Economics on Contemporary Thought</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1957 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The American Economic Review </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Dudley Dillard </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.774 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> This is shown by a perusal of his works, and he himself has declared to that effect.6) Accordingly, it will not be fair to adjudge his economic thought on the basis of his economic theory ; rather it would be more to the point to evaluate the situation from the following angle. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://www.jstor.org/stable/10.2307/43217075" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://www.jstor.org/stable/10.2307/43217075" target="_blank">SOCIAL THOUGHT OF R. H. TAWNEY</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1959 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Kyoto University Economic Review </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Yuzo Deguchi </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.768 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Thus economic theory does not by any means produce identical explanations and conclusions concerning economic events and processes. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/137857" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/137857" target="_blank">The Pragmatic Basis of Economic Theory</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1950 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The Canadian Journal of Economics and Political Science / Revue canadienne d'Economique et de Science politique </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> H. Scott Gordon </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.767 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Now of course there cannot be an absolute restriction of economics to a study of just the pattern of related, changing economic quantities and nothing else. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1882578" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1882578" target="_blank">Schumpeter and Marx: Imperialism and Social Classes in the Schumpeterian System</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1951 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The Quarterly Journal of Economics </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> O. H. Taylor </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.767 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The influence of this operation on the thinking of contemporary economists, however, has not been obvious-a fact which leads one to the conclusion that it was not a strong influence. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2976652" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2976652" target="_blank">The Development of the Concept of "Automatic Stabilizers"</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1956 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The Journal of Finance </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Norman F. Keiser </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.765 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> In his judgment the theory of economic change was at this stage; yet he felt that economists were treating it as if it were not, as if the phenomena were already sufficiently well known to provide a basis for generalization. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1827087" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1827087" target="_blank">Wesley C. Mitchell as an Economic Theorist</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1950 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Journal of Political Economy </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Milton Friedman </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.755 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Some students of the development of economic thought have even suggested that the various economic doctrines which have gained prominence were intended - deliberately or unconsciously - to rationalize and defend economic interests of specific classes of the population. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1879498" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1879498" target="_blank">Prolegomena to a History of Economic Reasoning</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1951 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The Quarterly Journal of Economics </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Karl Pribram </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.754 </td>
  </tr>
</tbody>
</table><table class="table table-striped table-condensed" style="font-size: 12px; margin-left: auto; margin-right: auto;">

  <tr>

  </tr>
 </thead>
<tbody>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> However, the nature of much basic economic theory is not directly evident from casual common sense reasoning. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://www.jstor.org/stable/10.2307/40472280" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://www.jstor.org/stable/10.2307/40472280" target="_blank">A Note on Quasi-Programming in Economic Principles Instruction</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1965 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Nebraska Journal of Economics and Business </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> John H. Wicks </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.819 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> A tendency arose, partly unconscious, to avoid the impression that economic theorists bore the responsibility to make their assumptions as realistic as they could, given practical limitations in knowledge, returns to additional theoretical invention, and time. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1828428" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1828428" target="_blank">Friedman and Machlup on the Significance of Testing Economic Assumptions</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1965 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Journal of Political Economy </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Jack Melitz </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.807 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> One school of thought holds that economic theories contain terms which upon close examination can be shown to lack any connection with factual or empirical reality. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1055334" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1055334" target="_blank">An Empirical Principle for Deductive Theory in Economics</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1967 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Southern Economic Journal </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Robert G. Fabian </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.788 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> This, however, does not mean that economic theory as a whole is not valuable. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/4223956" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/4223956" target="_blank">Axioms of Economics and the Claim to Efficiency</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1968 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Journal of Economic Issues </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Sherman Krupp </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.784 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> At times the attribution of policies to economic theory was dubious to say the least. </td>

  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> It might be supposed, even by economists who find the rationality assumption innocuous enough, that, if economics could have dispensed with this assumption, the epistemological foundations of the discipline would have been tightened and a considerable logical economy achieved. </td>

  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Yet to this principle certain economists take exception. </td>

   <td style="text-align:left;"> It is clear then that economic theory if it is to offer genuine explanations of economic events and processes cannot consist entirely of analytic statements. </td>

   <td style="text-align:left;"> This latter assumption probably does not have broad appeal among economists. </td>

   <td style="text-align:left;"> It may be argued that any conception of explanation applicable to economics at large cannot be very definite. </td>

  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Such an assumption is, for good reason, usually rejected by economists. </td>

  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Moreover, the torturous extremes to which some scholars in the past went to rule as off limits to an economist qua economist any sort of "what ought to be" judgments were, I think, a little silly. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/23481278" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/23481278" target="_blank">Presidential Address: The Cause of Economic Literacy and The Business Economist</a> </td>

  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Furthermore, in subjects like economics, it is seldom the case that rigid logical-deduction can be applied simplistically and with absolute certainty to the real world. </td>

  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> In orthodox or mainstream economics, for example, such 'assumptions', which may creep in unnoticed, are usually designed to achieve mathematical tractability, system closure or some such thing, rather than an understanding of the real causal mechanisms at work. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/23598149" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/23598149" target="_blank">Abstraction, tendencies and stylised facts: a realist approach to economic analysis</a> </td>

   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.781 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> So its a very different situation to have a full blown, well-developed mathematical economic theory that works well in explanation and prediction. </td>

  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The implications which one can derive from such models will often be contradicted by the economic behaviour which one can observe in presumably rational people. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://www.jstor.org/stable/10.2307/41950007" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://www.jstor.org/stable/10.2307/41950007" target="_blank">The Three Markets for Private Insurance</a> </td>

## Intertemporal cluster _4: risk_aversion, risk, aversion, absolute_risk_ 

  
The cluster gathers 16843 sentences from our corpus. It represents 5.08% of all the sentences selected over the whole period.

The community exists from 1930 to 1999. 

The most recurring authors are Mark J. Machina (138 sentences; 8 articles), Larry G. (74 sentences; 10 articles), John Broome (70 sentences; 8 articles), Chris Starmer (70 sentences; 11 articles), Uzi Segal (69 sentences; 10 articles), Wakker P.    <td style="text-align:left;"> If consumers do limit the field of choice in this way, then it is quite possible that somewhat different criteria apply to the different classifications of purchase decisions. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1054710" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1054710" target="_blank">Prolegomena to the Testing of Utility Theory</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1955 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Southern Economic Journal </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> R. W. Pfouts </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.809 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The consumer tends to enjoy his new taste for its own sake even if a prohibitive price of X prevents him from gratifying this new taste-except for a limiting case. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2295773" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2295773" target="_blank">Welfare Economics of Variable Tastes</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1953 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The Review of Economic Studies </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> John C. Harsanyi </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.807 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The particular actions which constitute the "best" behavior for a consumer depend upon facts referring to an enormously broad sweep of considerations-including, at least, what is good taste, what can be done with goods, and the availability of goods. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1054247" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1054247" target="_blank">The Disciplines of Economics and Business</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1957 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Southern Economic Journal </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Clarence E. Philbrook </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.804 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Some of the problems of consumer's choice have been unnecessarily clouded by the practice of regarding substitutability (or complementarity) between consumer's goods always as a matter of wants or tastes even when it is a matter of technology. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1812290" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1812290" target="_blank">Professor Hicks' Revision of Demand Theory</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1957 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The American Economic Review </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Fritz Machlup </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.803 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Most conventional theories of consumer behavior implicitly contain Axiom (1), the exceptions being theories which allow the consumer a choice from several bundles toward which he is indifferent. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1905494" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1905494" target="_blank">An Eclectic Approach to the Pure Theory of Consumer Behavior</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1956 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Econometrica </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Harvey M. Wagner </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.801 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> It is, however, possible to avoid this conflict and still have a consistent theory of consumer's choice, such as that presented here. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1881875" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1881875" target="_blank">Choice, Expectations and Measurability</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1954 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The Quarterly Journal of Economics </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Nicholas Georgescu-Roegen </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.800 </td>
  </tr>

  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Given some degree of ignorance and preference, risk becomes a donminant element in the behavior of man. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://www.jstor.org/stable/10.2307/251157" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://www.jstor.org/stable/10.2307/251157" target="_blank">Doctoral Education for Risk and Insurance in Leading U.S. Universities</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1969 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The Journal of Risk and Insurance </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Mark R. Greene </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.864 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Consequently, one might hypothesize that most people would be more adverse to pure risks than to speculative risks and that, as a result, they might take steps to avoid pure risks while accepting speculative risks. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://www.jstor.org/stable/10.2307/251231" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://www.jstor.org/stable/10.2307/251231" target="_blank">Attitudes toward Speculative Risks as an Indicator of Attitudes toward Pure Risks</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1966 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The Journal of Risk and Insurance </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> C. Arthur Williams, <suffix>Jr.</suffix> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.842 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> It is acknowledged that this gain may not be as sweeping as it first appears, for the empirical determination of a decision maker's utility function may involve the determination of his attitude toward risk situations as measured by what is essentially the insurance premium. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://www.jstor.org/stable/10.2307/250988" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://www.jstor.org/stable/10.2307/250988" target="_blank">Some Mathematical Views of Risk</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1966 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The Journal of Risk and Insurance </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> James C. Hickman, Douglas A. Zahn </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.841 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Such behavior has been observed enough to warrant a theoretical explanation by Professors Friedman and Savage who, in a classic article on utility theory, have explained why the same person might buy insurance and still be interested in accepting speculative risks.6 The Friedman-Savage article, however, does not explain this behavior in terms of varying attitudes toward pure and speculative risks, but by the shape of the individual's utility function. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://www.jstor.org/stable/10.2307/251231" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://www.jstor.org/stable/10.2307/251231" target="_blank">Attitudes toward Speculative Risks as an Indicator of Attitudes toward Pure Risks</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1966 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The Journal of Risk and Insurance </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> C. Arthur Williams, <suffix>Jr.</suffix> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.836 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Since many formulations of decision-making under risk exist in the literature, and since no one can be judged correct under all circumstances, it is important to see whether this conclusion is always true. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2296663" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2296663" target="_blank">Some Effects of Taxes on Risk-Taking</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1968 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The Review of Economic Studies </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> B. Näslund </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.834 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The very practical recognition given to risk as an element complicating the choices which a decision maker, acting in partial ignorance, must render is regarded by some educators as a decided strength of this approach. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://www.jstor.org/stable/10.2307/250470" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://www.jstor.org/stable/10.2307/250470" target="_blank">Curricular Concepts in Risk and Insurance</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1962 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The Journal of Insurance </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> NA </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.826 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Nonetheless, the authors intuitively feel that it is plausible to hold that uncertainty can give rise to risk under certain conditions. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://www.jstor.org/stable/10.2307/250861" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://www.jstor.org/stable/10.2307/250861" target="_blank">The Meaning of Risk</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1967 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The Journal of Risk and Insurance </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Ronald C. Horn, Robert M. Crowe </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.826 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The results themselves, however, are in no way dependent on any special assumptions with respect to risk or "risk aversion"; and readers wlho find our rationalization in terms of these categories unsatisfactory are free to sulbstititte their own. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1823774" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1823774" target="_blank">Some Estimates of the Cost of Capital to the Electric Utility Industry, 1954-57</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1966 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The American Economic Review </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Merton H. Miller, Franco Modigliani </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.817 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Given some degree of ignorance and preference, risk becomes a dominant element in the behavior of man. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://www.jstor.org/stable/10.2307/250470" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://www.jstor.org/stable/10.2307/250470" target="_blank">Curricular Concepts in Risk and Insurance</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1962 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The Journal of Insurance </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> NA </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.816 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Since different decisionmakers have varying attitudes toward risks, we shall study in particular how these attitudes, as reflected by utility functions, affect the optimality of the independent approach to assessing different risk situations. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://www.jstor.org/stable/10.2307/251543" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://www.jstor.org/stable/10.2307/251543" target="_blank">Comparison of Independent and Joint Decision-Making for Two Insurance Decisions</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1968 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The Journal of Risk and Insurance </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> G. A. Whitmore, C. A. Williams, <suffix>Jr.</suffix>, J. Neter </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.811 </td>
  </tr>

  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The paper attempted to argue that if a person were neither dissaving nor saving, he had reached his desired consumption level given his personal discount differential, his consumption preferences, and his lifetime budget constraint. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1818419" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1818419" target="_blank">The Optimum Lifetime Distribution of Consumption Expenditures: Reply</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1970 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The American Economic Review </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Lester C. Thurow </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.787 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The fundamental assumption involved here is that any individual consumer does not have a preference till such time as his commodity require ments are enquired into. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://www.jstor.org/stable/10.2307/25824883" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://www.jstor.org/stable/10.2307/25824883" target="_blank">Quantum Economics</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1978 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Pakistan Economic and Social Review </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> ASGHAR QADIR </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.783 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> In both cases, this is achieved by the addition (to the assumptions used in [2]) of two easily interpreted and verified assumptions: one to the effect that consumption and production can be truncated, and one to the effect that consumers discount consumption in distant or improbable states. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2526035" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2526035" target="_blank">A Note on Price Systems in Infinite Dimensional Space</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1972 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> International Economic Review </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Edward C. Prescott, Robert E. Lucas, <suffix>Jr.</suffix> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.775 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> In the theory of demand it is usually assumed that an individual's utility function depends on his own consumption, but not on the consumption of others. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1829929" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1829929" target="_blank">Habit Formation and Dynamic Demand Functions</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1970 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Journal of Political Economy </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Robert A. Pollak </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.772 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Thus, we propose as a criterion for rational choice over time that the consumption plan must be consistent and free from regret. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/25602944" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/25602944" target="_blank">Social Welfare Functions for the Future</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1974 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The American Economist </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> William Schulze </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.770 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Introduction of an interest rate or of a subjective rate of discount on future utility would eliminate the constancy of consumption over time but would not eliminate the correspondence of the time pattern of consumption for the two cases. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1828707" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1828707" target="_blank">On Uncertain Lifetimes</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1977 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Journal of Political Economy </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Robert J. Barro, James W. Friedman </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.767 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> As is well known, the choice of a constant consumption level is optimal for a utility maximizing individual provided his subjective time preference is equal to the rate of interest. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/0047-2727(78)90051-8" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/0047-2727(78)90051-8" target="_blank">A model of social security and retirement decisions</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1978 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Journal of Public Economics </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Sheshinski E. </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.765 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> It is possible, according to the theorem, that some of the consumers may find they have available within their budget sets some points which are strictly preferred to the consumption that the theorem allocates to them. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/0022-0531(72)90103-2" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/0022-0531(72)90103-2" target="_blank">Approximate equilibrium in economies with indivisible commodities</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1972 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Journal of Economic Theory </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Broome J. </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.765 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> One of the implications of this supposition is that for each consumer, the bundle of goods chosen for current consumption and the stock-bill portfolio chosen to hold during the first period are, at current prices, most preferred among all possibilities in his budget set. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/0304-405X(74)90002-6" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/0304-405X(74)90002-6" target="_blank">Stock prices, inflation, and the term structure of interest rates</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1974 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Journal of Financial Economics </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Long J. </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.762 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The main implication of this condition (13) is that tastes of an individual for intertemporal consumption (in addition to beliefs and prices) is involved in his decision. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1805275" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1805275" target="_blank">Market Efficiency in an Arrow-Debreu Economy: A Closer Look</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1978 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The American Economic Review </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Kose John </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.762 </td>
  </tr>

 </thead>

  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The desirability of choices made is evaluated in terms of preferences each individual is assumed to have among the alternatives. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1913838" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1913838" target="_blank">Construction of Outcome Functions Guaranteeing Existence and Pareto Optimality of Nash Equilibria</a> </td>

   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.847 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Under varying sets of assumed preferences, different results would emerge. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://doi.org/10.1177/109114217500300301" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://doi.org/10.1177/109114217500300301" target="_blank">Utility Interdependence and Redistribution: Methodological Implications for Welfare Economics and the Theory of the Public Household</a> </td>

   <td style="text-align:left;"> Johnston J.F. </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.832 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> This général formulation23) implies the possibility of choosing between différent Utility functions U (B). </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/23805838" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/23805838" target="_blank">Bernoulli's Utility Theory and Historical Ramifications</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1972 </td>

   <td style="text-align:left;"> Hans-Werner Gottinger </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.817 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> It is this property that makes the expected utility model attractive for normative purposes in difficult decision problems when the decision maker's preferences are not fully developed in a consistent fashion because of the complexities in comparing the alternatives. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://www.jstor.org/stable/10.2307/251402" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://www.jstor.org/stable/10.2307/251402" target="_blank">Acceptability of Three Normative Methods in Insurance Decision Making</a> </td>

   <td style="text-align:left;"> C. Arthur Williams, <suffix>Jr.</suffix>, John Neter </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.817 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Suppose the individual's choice behavior obeys Axioms 2.1, 2.2, 2.3, and 3.1 and, as guaranteed by Theorem 1, his choice behavior is represented by functions U and u,. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1913656" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1913656" target="_blank">Temporal Resolution of Uncertainty and Dynamic Choice Theory</a> </td>

   <td style="text-align:left;"> David M. Kreps, Evan L. Porteus </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.815 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The underlying idea is that certain preference considerations are more duly allowed for in some kinds of decisions than in others. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/0047-2727(78)90036-1" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/0047-2727(78)90036-1" target="_blank">Implicit social preferences in the Norwegian system of indirect taxation</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1978 </td>

## Intertemporal cluster _5: monopoly, competition, prices, pure_competition_ 

  
The cluster gathers 9511 sentences from our corpus. It represents 2.87% of all the sentences selected over the whole period.

The community exists from 1900 to 1989. 

The most recurring authors are <suffix>Jr.</suffix> (111 sentences; 77 articles), Franklin M. Fisher (36 sentences; 12 articles), Julio J. Rotemberg (36 sentences; 10 articles), F. H. Hahn (31 sentences; 10 articles), Stephen J. Turnovsky (31 sentences; 23 articles), Paul A. Samuelson (29 sentences; 16 articles), William Fellner (26 sentences; 10 articles), Joseph E. Stiglitz (26 sentences; 17 articles), Louis J. Maccini (26 sentences; 5 articles), William J. Baumol (25 sentences; 17 articles), Robert J. Gordon (25 sentences; 9 articles), Nicholas Kaldor (24 sentences; 10 articles), Lucile Sheppard Keyes (24 sentences; 6 articles), Aubrey Silberston (24 sentences; 1 articles), Bennett T. McCallum (23 sentences; 12 articles), Dennis W. Carlton (23 sentences; 8 articles).

The most recurring journals are The American Economic Review (886 sentences; 599 articles), The Quarterly Journal of Economics (472 sentences; 308 articles), Journal of Political Economy (451 sentences; 320 articles), The Economic Journal (415 sentences; 277 articles), Econometrica (357 sentences; 222 articles), The Review of Economic Studies (348 sentences; 207 articles).

### Closest sentence from 'rational' and 'rationality' of the backbone community

<table class="table table-striped table-condensed" style="font-size: 12px; margin-left: auto; margin-right: auto;">
 <thead>
  <tr>
   <th style="text-align:left;"> Sentence </th>
   <th style="text-align:left;"> Title </th>
   <th style="text-align:right;"> Year </th>
   <th style="text-align:left;"> Journal </th>
   <th style="text-align:left;"> Authors </th>
   <th style="text-align:right;"> Words Similarity </th>
  </tr>
 </thead>
<tbody>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> It is also sometimes silently assumed the all necessary information for decisionmaking can be contained in "rational" prices. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/40729354" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/40729354" target="_blank">MARKET SOCIALISM</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1989 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Acta Oeconomica </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> A. NOVE </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.727 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Only if the quasi rationals become informed can the correct price be assured. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1818646" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1818646" target="_blank">The Relevance of Quasi Rationality in Competitive Markets</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1985 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The American Economic Review </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Thomas Russell, Richard Thaler </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.719 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> In this case, if price expectations are formed rationally, it may be more appropriate to focus on the stabilization of prices rather than income. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1885503" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1885503" target="_blank">The Optimum Monetary Aggregate for Stabilization Policy</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1980 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The Quarterly Journal of Economics </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Don E. Roper, Stephen J. Turnovsky </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.710 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Therefore, this is the price system with the aid of which - under these conditions - management can be "rational" or "optimal". </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/40727781" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/40727781" target="_blank">DUAL CONCEPT OF THE ECONOMY IN MARX'S "CAPITAL"</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1967 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Acta Oeconomica </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> A. Bródy </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.709 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Yet to assume that prices are not conditional on quality would be counter to a rational expectations equilibrium. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2297283" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2297283" target="_blank">Prices and Qualities in Markets with Costly Information</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1982 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The Review of Economic Studies </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Yuk-Shee Chan, Hayne Leland </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.708 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> As well, under the rationality assumptions in force, the mean of the unanticipated part of the general price level should be zero and the differential will only vary if the variance of r1 changes.' </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2297762" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2297762" target="_blank">Assessing the Variability of Inflation</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1983 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The Review of Economic Studies </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> A. R. Pagan, A. D. Hall, P. K. Trivedi </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.706 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> (c) When, in extending the classical theory, the assumptions of perfect competition were removed, even the definition of rationality became ambiguous. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1809901" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1809901" target="_blank">Theories of Decision-Making in Economics and Behavioral Science</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1959 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The American Economic Review </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Herbert A. Simon </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.703 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> In either event, the price decisions should be put on a rational basis. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1152246" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1152246" target="_blank">Economic and Social Factors Affecting the Development of Smallholder Agriculture in Eastern Nigeria</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1965 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Economic Development and Cultural Change </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> C. Davis Fogg </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.698 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> 2 demand curves result not so much from rational behavior per se as from a general principle which includes a wide class of irrational behavior as well. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1827018" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1827018" target="_blank">Irrational Behavior and Economic Theory</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1962 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Journal of Political Economy </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Gary S. Becker </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.697 </td>
  </tr>

   <td style="text-align:left;"> H. J. Davenport </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.752 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Therefore, if prices generally were fixed it would have been questionable economics to attempt to restrict a producer to one product if he could have produced another more economically. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1884491" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1884491" target="_blank">Price Fixing and the Theory of Profit</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1919 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The Quarterly Journal of Economics </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Kemper Simpson </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.752 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Turning to a direct examination of the reasoning it seems difficult to escape the fact that a rise in the cost of a commodity causes, other things being equal, a fall in the demand for it. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2220851" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2220851" target="_blank">Economic Theory and Proposals for a Legal Minimum Wage</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1907 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The Economic Journal </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> H. B. Lees Smith </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.747 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> He does not think, however, that price fixing on " the basis described is the same as that which would obtain if normal forces were working under normal conditions." </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1884491" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1884491" target="_blank">Price Fixing and the Theory of Profit</a> </td>

  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> And since nothing can be told as to price determination from a knowledge of the cost principle (diminishing, increasing, or constant) and since these principles cannot be said to attach peculiarly to any type of business undertaking and are themselves constantly being modified and counteracted by complex qmalitative readjustments whose effects are often far more important in the explanation of concrete situations, it would appear that an exaggerated importance has been attached to those principles as explanations of price determination. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/739" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/739" target="_blank">Graphic Illustration of the Laws of Price</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1924 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The American Economic Review </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Norman J. Silberling </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.807 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> It might be said that a commission charged with price fixing need therefore only consider the expense of producing the supply and that the principle of the adjustment of price to natural determination will follow; but this might or might not be true. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1804382" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1804382" target="_blank">The Economic Basis for Business Regulation</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1921 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The American Economic Review </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Rexford G. Tugwell </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.798 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> It is, however, of importance that in all attempts to explain price </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1804896" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1804896" target="_blank">The Circuit Velocity of Money</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1923 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The American Economic Review </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Hudson B. Hastings </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.794 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The problem of explaining price must be separated from other considerations. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1822751" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1822751" target="_blank">A Suggestion for Simplifying the Statement of the General Theory of Price</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1928 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Journal of Political Economy </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Frank H. Knight </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.765 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> In the second place, we must recognize that the prices in the market are not determined by what one might call the real or ultimate facts of demand and supply, but rather by the opinions of those in the market in regard to these ultimate facts. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1230332" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1230332" target="_blank">Market Price Analysis</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1924 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Journal of Farm Economics </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Warren C. Waite </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.764 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> It is, in my judgment, the case for deliberate price variation which can be most clearly made in principle, primarily on the ground of what has come somewhat loosely to be called the " discontinuous " nature of the adjustments involved. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2548386" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2548386" target="_blank">Mr. Robertson's Views on Banking Policy: A Reply to Mr. Harrod</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1928 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Economica </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> M. Tappan </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.764 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Changes in the value relation of various goods may be at least partially explained, then, by changes in their cost of production, even tho we have no unit of cost applicable to all or to any two of them. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1885553" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1885553" target="_blank">The Doctrine of Comparative Cost</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1926 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The Quarterly Journal of Economics </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Edward S. Mason </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.761 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> In accepting competitive prices as a criterion, however, one must not overlook the fact that under this system production follows demands, not needs. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1885440" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1885440" target="_blank">Composite Demand and Joint Supply in Relation to Public Utility Rates</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1929 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The Quarterly Journal of Economics </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Raymond T. Bye </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.759 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> that consequently neither the objective nor the subjective theory, which respectively ascribes the prices to either the objective or the subjective factors exclusively, will hold water. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://www.jstor.org/stable/10.2307/43216707" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://www.jstor.org/stable/10.2307/43216707" target="_blank">ON THE COEFFICIENTS OF PRODUCTION</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1929 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Kyoto University Economic Review </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Yasuma Takata </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.759 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Or it is held, conversely, that with the producer receiving a particular price the consumer is forced to pay more than he should, or again that the producer may have goods to sell and the consumer desire to purchase them but the market machinery fails to bring about an exchange. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1808657" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1808657" target="_blank">Criteria of Marketing Efficiency</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1921 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The American Economic Review </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Fred E. Clark </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.757 </td>
  </tr>

  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> To concede, however, that the elasticity of demand for a given rigidly priced commodity is such that sales would not be significantly larger if prices were substantially lower is not to negate the argument-outlined in the second paragraph preceding-that rigid prices are a causal element in cyclical fluctuations. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1806302" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1806302" target="_blank">Dr. Tucker's "Reasons" for Price Rigidity</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1938 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The American Economic Review </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Ralph C. Wood </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.810 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The reasoning behind this view is sometimes no more elaborate than an assumption that prices must change with changing conditions of demand and supply, and that the penalty of price resistance to such changes is economic maladjustment, whatever that means. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1928401" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1928401" target="_blank">Public Utility Prices and the Business Cycle: A Study in the Theory of Price Rigidity</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1939 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The Review of Economics and Statistics </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> John D. Sumner </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.798 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The influence of price on the quantity demanded is then to be ascribed to the fact that a definite price increment prevents a certain group of people from buying their "full" quantity. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1907948" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1907948" target="_blank">Annual Survey of Significant Developments in General Economic Theory</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1934 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Econometrica </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> J. Tinbergen </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.787 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> a given chaiige in the price ratio will cause a given change in the relative quantities demanded, whichever of the two prices has moved relatively to the other) this is by no means the case when the lack of indifference is merely due to the inertia of buyers. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2549105" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2549105" target="_blank">Market Imperfection and Excess Capacity</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1935 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Economica </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Nicholas Kaldor </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.787 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The fact that the prices of products deviate from values means that the cost of production can no longer be considered in terms of value and that it must be considered in terms of productive price. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://www.jstor.org/stable/10.2307/43216771" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://www.jstor.org/stable/10.2307/43216771" target="_blank">THE MEANING OF THE THEORY OF VALUE IN THEORETICAL ECONOMICS</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1933 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Kyoto University Economic Review </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Kei Shibata </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.784 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Thus, we come to somewhat different conclusions as to the relation of two goods according as we rely upon the "price-demand" criterion, or reason in terms of the influences which seem to account for the relation. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1803729" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1803729" target="_blank">The Relation of Commodities in Demand</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1938 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The American Economic Review </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> E. E. Lewis </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.781 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> That demand should remain low or decline when a price is arbitrarily fixed at an artificially high level is easily understood if we can assume that people in general tend to act in a rational manner. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1052989" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1052989" target="_blank">Direct Price Fixing</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1936 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Southern Economic Journal </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Jules Backman </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.776 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> And if this long-term tendency to rise and fall is so largely independent of the rate of increase of the product, then it would likewise seem that the variation in prices, the broad level of prices, cannot possibly be due to variations in the "costs of production," expressed in labor time. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1806646" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1806646" target="_blank">On the Structure and Inertia of Prices</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1934 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The American Economic Review </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Carl Snyder </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.776 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> And if this long-term tendency to rise and fall is so largely independent of the rate of increase of the product, then it would likewise seem that the variation in prices, the broad level of prices, cannot possibly be due to variations in the "costs of production," expressed in labor time. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1806646" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1806646" target="_blank">On the Structure and Inertia of Prices</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1934 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The American Economic Review </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Carl Snyder </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.776 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> appear which are not in accord with such broad generalizations of accepted theory.7 A lower price very often leads not to increased demand but to an actual decrease in the quantity of a commodity that can be disposed of in a market. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1807517" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1807517" target="_blank">Speculation and the Growing Instability of Stock Prices</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1933 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The American Economic Review </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> M. J. Fields </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.776 </td>
  </tr>
</tbody>
</table><table class="table table-striped table-condensed" style="font-size: 12px; margin-left: auto; margin-right: auto;">
 <thead>
  <tr>
   <th style="text-align:left;"> Sentence </th>
   <th style="text-align:left;"> Title </th>
   <th style="text-align:right;"> Year </th>
   <th style="text-align:left;"> Journal </th>
   <th style="text-align:left;"> Authors </th>
   <th style="text-align:right;"> Similarity to HDSBSCAN Centroid </th>
  </tr>
 </thead>
<tbody>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The weight of the tradition that monopoly and competition are mutually exclusive alternatives is a heavy one indeed, and one may well despair of gaining really serious recognition for the idea that actual situations are typically a combination of the two -recognition which will go so far as to accept some appropriate theoretical structure in which both elements find their place. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1881679" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1881679" target="_blank">Monopolistic or Imperfect Competition?</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1937 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The Quarterly Journal of Economics </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Edward H. Chamberlin </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.828 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> 335-50) that the theory of competition is unequal to dealing with the problem, and that though monopoly in the ordinary sense does not prevail, recourse must be had to the theory of monopoly, which will yield a determinate result (loc. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2223643" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2223643" target="_blank">Increasing Returns and the Representative Firm</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1930 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The Economic Journal </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> D. H. Robertson, Piero Sraffa, G. F. Shove </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.820 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> This, however, is not compatible with the assumption of perfect competition. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2224727" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2224727" target="_blank">The Equilibrium of the Firm</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1934 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The Economic Journal </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Nicholas Kaldor </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.808 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> But it is important to remember that such an assumption is something quite different and logically much less satisfactory in the case of imperfect competition than in the case of perfect competition. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2548808" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2548808" target="_blank">Mrs. Robinson's "Economics of Imperfect Competition"</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1934 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Economica </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Nicholas Kaldor </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.790 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Apparently it is never seen that the familiar meaning of monopoly is perfectly satisfactory as soon as it is anchored to any commodzty whatever, however broadly or narrowly defined, and is wholly consistent with competition between that commodity and others. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1881679" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1881679" target="_blank">Monopolistic or Imperfect Competition?</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1937 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The Quarterly Journal of Economics </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Edward H. Chamberlin </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.783 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> I submit, however, that there is no evidence (at least that I have been able to find) that Mrs. Robinson thinks of monopoly (in its ordinary sense) and competition in any other way but as mutually exclusive.7 If I seem to exaggerate at all the importance of this difference in conception between us, it is because I have become convinced that it is the key to an understanding of many other differences in treatment of the problems involved. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1881679" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1881679" target="_blank">Monopolistic or Imperfect Competition?</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1937 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The Quarterly Journal of Economics </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Edward H. Chamberlin </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.778 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Thus, if a person, partnership, or corporation has a monopoly in a certain field, so that there is no competitor, his acts, no matter how deceptive or misleading and unfair to the consuming public, may not be restrained. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1824590" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1824590" target="_blank">The Federal Trade Commission Act as Amended in 1938</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1939 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Journal of Political Economy </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Martin L. Lindahl </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.777 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> But unless we go so far as to assume that a system of free competition fully does away with irrationality and inertia, we shall have to admit that flexibility and free competition are not the same things. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1822998" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1822998" target="_blank">Money and Production</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1935 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Journal of Political Economy </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Walter Egle </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.773 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Protection from monopoly may have motivated some legislation and judicial decisions in the past; it is not, however, the origin of the idea, nor is it the present significance. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/3139051" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/3139051" target="_blank">The Common Carrier-Public Utility Concept: A Legal-Industrial View</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1931 </td>

   <td style="text-align:left;"> Irwin S. Rosenbaum </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.773 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> power.7 The essential point is that a monopoly is not necessarily disarmed by the existence of substitutes even though over-reaching efforts to gain profits may be restrained. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1803814" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1803814" target="_blank">Competitive Significance of Substitutes for Public Utility Service</a> </td>

  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> see, can be attributed to a significant extent, not to any successful overt attempt to control prices artificially, but to certain inherent characteristics of supply and demand conditions and of the operation of the market. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1883726" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1883726" target="_blank">Dynamic Shortages and Price Rises: The Engineer-Scientist Case</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1959 </td>

   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.812 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> But even if one holds that price rigidity is not harmful, further examination should be made of the manner in which such prices are set, the considerations behind their determination, the economic effects of their being imposed at alternative levels, etc. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1823585" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1823585" target="_blank">Economic Concentration and Depression Price Rigidity</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1955 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The American Economic Review </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> John M. Blair </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.796 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> But they argue that "not much can be said in support of the idea that there is or ought to be a persisting relationship of the price of one commodity to any other." </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1233589" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1233589" target="_blank">Individual vs. Group Commodity Reserves for Price Stabilization</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1951 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Journal of Farm Economics </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Ralph J. Scanlan </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.789 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Evidently the important consideration is not what the firm which wishes to raise prices can supply, but what the others can supply." </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1884228" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1884228" target="_blank">Competition of the Few Among the Many</a> </td>

   <td style="text-align:left;"> Willard D. Arant </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.787 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> "9 It does not follow, however, that the effects of prices on quantities supplied and demanded can legitimately be disregarded or that these are purely matters of judgment in which one person's opinion is as good as another's. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1826345" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1826345" target="_blank">The Economic Development of Nigeria: A Reply</a> </td>

   <td style="text-align:left;"> P. T. Bauer </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.783 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Though we may find a convention to enable us to put 'prices' on the goods in question, these prices cannot play the parts which we have been ascribing to them. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2662090" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2662090" target="_blank">The Measurement of Real Income</a> </td>

   <td style="text-align:left;"> Oxford Economic Papers </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> J. R. Hicks </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.780 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> One of these, probably not the most important in the minds of those responsible, presumably is price, but the concept of the elasticity of demand is not certainly and consciously brought into play. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2228043" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2228043" target="_blank">The Position of Economics and Economists in the Government Machine</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1954 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The Economic Journal </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> R. L. Marris </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.775 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> One cannot rely upon the price mechanism alone to make the necessary adjustment. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1928527" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1928527" target="_blank">Trends and Cycles in Economic Activity</a> </td>

   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.773 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> This, it seems in this view, gives meaning to the involved theoretical discussions of price determination. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1910783" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1910783" target="_blank">Economic Theory and Quantitative Research: A Broad Interpretation of the Mitchell Position</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1951 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The American Economic Review </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Rutledge Vining </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.772 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Without this condition, which deprives the enterprise of direct influence on prices, there can be a tendency to seek profit by jacking up prices, there can be tendencies towards a peculiar monopolization. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2661900" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2661900" target="_blank">On the Role of the Law of Value in Socialist Economy</a> </td>

   <td style="text-align:left;"> Wlodzimierz Brus </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.771 </td>
  </tr>
