<tbody>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> But if one deems it profitable to argue on so general and yet so limited a basis (and I do not), it is to be observed that no reconciliation with the conventional theory of monopoly is necessary. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1818318" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1818318" target="_blank">The Economist Plays with Blocs</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1954 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The American Economic Review </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> George J. Stigler </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.799 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> For example, there is no reason to believe that a situation in which there is the same degree of monopoly in all industries will necessarily be in any sense superior to a situation in which the degree of monopoly varies as between industries. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2296233" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2296233" target="_blank">The General Theory of Second Best</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1956 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The Review of Economic Studies </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> R. G. Lipsey, Kelvin Lancaster </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.796 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> There can be little doubt that the essence of the monopoly argument is political, but it is not necessarily the worse for that. " </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2227057" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2227057" target="_blank">The Iron and Steel Act, 1949</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1950 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The Economic Journal </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> S. J. Langley </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.788 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The essential point was not the greater or less perfection of competition or monopoly, but the greater or less purity of the one or the other. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/29793005" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/29793005" target="_blank">The Theory of Monopolistic Competition: A General Theory of Economic Activity</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1955 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Indian Economic Review </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> F. Perroux </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.787 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> But when we refuse to employ a presumption for competition, we are not therefore logically bound to be indifferent to the implications of a policy for the competitive process. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1809767" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1809767" target="_blank">Policy Analysis</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1958 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The American Economic Review </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Charles E. Lindblom </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.782 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> It may be that certain acts which are detrimental to the public interest, given monopoly, are also the normal conduct of a firm pursuing what would be, given free competition, the socially desirable aim of maximizing profits. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/138735" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/138735" target="_blank">Some Empirical Issues in Canadian Combines Policy</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1957 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The Canadian Journal of Economics and Political Science / Revue canadienne d'Economique et de Science politique </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> J. N. Wolfe </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.780 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> This does not mean that perfect competition is necessarily the ideal. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1053722" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1053722" target="_blank">An Ideology for a Laboristic Economy</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1950 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Southern Economic Journal </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Rendigs Fels </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.776 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> But a general belief in the merits of competition in relation to efficiency is not necessarily relevant in the particular case. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2097749" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2097749" target="_blank">`Public Interest' and the Calico Printing Industry: A Review of the Monopolies and Restrictive Practices Commission's Judgment in the Report on the Process of Calico Printing</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1957 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The Journal of Industrial Economics </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> NA </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.774 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The important point is that monopoly is neither the universal nor an inevitable consequence, a point regularly overlooked or belittled in much recent literature. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1826109" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1826109" target="_blank">Monopoly, Bigness, and Progress</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1956 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Journal of Political Economy </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> G. Warren Nutter </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.770 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> I agree that this concept of competition is fundamental to my approach, but I do not apply it so naively as Mrs. Hall suggests. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2662075" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2662075" target="_blank">[Two Comments on 'Competition in Retail Trade']: A Reply</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1951 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Oxford Economic Papers </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> P. W. S. Andrews </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.769 </td>
  </tr>

 </thead>
<tbody>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Prices may be called upon to perform a variety of functions which, however, can often be met only in a contradictory way. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/40694543" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/40694543" target="_blank">PRICE CALCULATIONS AND THE ANALYSIS OF PROPORTIONS WITHIN THE NATIONAL ECONOMY</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1966 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Acta Oeconomica </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> S. Ganczer </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.812 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Yet there is a price, validly looked upon as depending on the confrontation of supply conditions and demand conditions. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2228764" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2228764" target="_blank">Recent Theories Concerning the Nature and Role of Interest</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1961 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The Economic Journal </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> G. L. Shackle </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.802 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> On the contrary, if we decide to reason in the long period, we admit the possibility that buyers, who are interested in a particular product, can modify their demand prices having regard to the evolution of the prices of other products which could be substituted for the one in which they are particularly interested (even if these products are technically different, for these very changes in relative prices mainly result from innovation and technical progress). </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2097733" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2097733" target="_blank">Common Markets: Towards a Theory of Market Integration</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1962 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The Journal of Industrial Economics </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Louis Phlips </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.793 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> A parallel situation exists on the price side. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2295812" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2295812" target="_blank">Notes on Jorgenson's Model</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1963 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The Review of Economic Studies </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> M. McManus </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.792 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> ments are not necessarily conclusive in determining the kind of price that will emerge. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1884199" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1884199" target="_blank">The Economics of Disequilibrium Price</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1961 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The Quarterly Journal of Economics </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Romney Robinson </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.782 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> On the other hand, market mechanisms may play a part in the decision. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://doi.org/10.2307/2329895" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://doi.org/10.2307/2329895" target="_blank">Portfolio analysis</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1967 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Sharpe W.F. </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.779 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> But this argument is valid only on the assumption that the market valuations of affected outputs are not prevented from representing actual worth to buyers, either because of the existence of other restrictions or because of pricing defects-e.g., where uniform prices have to be charged although discriminatory prices would result in larger revenues. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1055530" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1055530" target="_blank">Price Discrimination in Law and Economics</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1961 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Southern Economic Journal </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Lucile Sheppard Keyes </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.779 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Or, prices that are deemed "too high" or "too low" during one period may result in public action that will alter the market structure during a subsequent period. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1235691" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1235691" target="_blank">The Midwest-Eastern Seaboard Conflict of Interest in the Production and Distribution of Milk: The Role of Market Structures and Other Institutional Arrangements</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1960 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Journal of Farm Economics </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Irving Dubov, M. Lloyd Downen </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.775 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> if all prices were administered on the basis of markup over direct cost-then excess demand might exist in all markets, yet without effect on the price level." </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1926532" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1926532" target="_blank">Another View of Cost-Push and Demand-Pull Inflation</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1960 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The Review of Economics and Statistics </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Fritz Machlup </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.775 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Moreover, some other such hypotheses may be more useful in explaining those special cases in which a price does not follow the tendency described by the law and in explaining the composition of supply in cases other than pure competition and monopoly. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1055227" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1055227" target="_blank">Operations Research and the Theory of the Firm</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1962 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Southern Economic Journal </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Almarin Phillips </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.773 </td>
  </tr>

  <tr>

 </thead>
<tbody>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Where it occurs, it will be a fair approximation to take it that prices are related to costs, rather than determined by supply and demand. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2723390" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2723390" target="_blank">On Coddington's Interpretation: A Reply</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1979 </td>

   <td style="text-align:left;"> John Hicks </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.809 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> That assumption has somewhat more plausibility when prices are set by individuals conscious of disequilibrium than it does in other contexts. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2297080" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2297080" target="_blank">Quantity Constraints, Spillovers and the Hahn Process</a> </td>

  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> While, under the usual assumptions, with each price there is associated a unique quantity, the converse does not always hold. </td>

   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.801 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> It follows that from the industry's point of view, it is undesirable to have prices change with the frequent short-run changes in demand or cost conditions since such changes would open the possibility of disagreement and threaten the structure in an unpredictable fashion.7 As a consequence, a crucial component of noncompetitive, or what we will hereafter call administered pricing, is that it exhibits a certain amount of price stability in the face of variations in market conditions. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1808857" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1808857" target="_blank">Wage Determination, Inflation, and the Industrial Structure</a> </td>

  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The more difficult it is for the firm to judge different buyers' willingness to pay, the greater will be the incentive to have a freely fluctuating price for everyone.23 A second completely different explanation for price rigidity given in Section IVC postulates that the cost of detecting the need for a price change, changing price, and disseminating price information may be quite low but that the equilibrium price to any class of buyer does not vary much even though other product characteristics (such as delivery time) may vary considerably in equilibrium. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1833081" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1833081" target="_blank">Contracts, Price Rigidity, and Market Equilibrium</a> </td>

## Intertemporal cluster _6: bargaining, players, player, game_ 

  
The cluster gathers 175320 sentences from our corpus. It represents 52.91% of all the sentences selected over the whole period.

The community exists from 1950 to 2009. 

The most recurring authors are Matthew Rabin (520 sentences; 22 articles), Larry Samuelson (438 sentences; 26 articles), Drew Fudenberg (428 sentences; 32 articles), Battigalli P. (423 sentences; 9 articles), Vincent P. Crawford (412 sentences; 26 articles), David K. Levine (319 sentences; 19 articles), Robert Sugden (318 sentences; 18 articles), B. (281 sentences; 6 articles), Paul Weirich (279 sentences; 1 articles), Basak S. (276 sentences; 9 articles), Güth W. (274 sentences; 31 articles).

The most recurring journals are Journal of Economic Behavior and Organization (10513 sentences; 1200 articles), Games and Economic Behavior (8504 sentences; 989 articles), Journal of Economic Theory (8317 sentences; 1191 articles), Journal of Economic Dynamics and Control (6391 sentences; 973 articles), Econometrica (6325 sentences; 765 articles), Economic Theory (5839 sentences; 922 articles).

   <td style="text-align:left;"> The game theoretic formulation makes it clear, however, that other behavioral assumptions can lead to other solutions. </td>

  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> An equilibrium or a solution to the game is defined over the set of these decision rules, which depend on knowledge of earlier actions of rivals and correct expectations of the way rivals will act in the future. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://www.jstor.org/stable/10.2307/3003344" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://www.jstor.org/stable/10.2307/3003344" target="_blank">Preempting an Alert Rival: Strategic Timing of the First Plant by Analysis of Sophisticated Rivalry</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1979 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The Bell Journal of Economics </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> David P. Rutenberg, Ram C. Rao </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.764 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The situation need not, however, be fully consistent with equilibrium. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1818873" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1818873" target="_blank">The Theory of Economic Growth: A Critique and Reformulation</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1975 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The American Economic Review </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Donald J. Harris </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.763 </td>
  </tr>

  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> A particular equilibrium is played only if all players have appropriate beliefs about the strategies other players will play-see Aumann (1987). </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1912562" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1912562" target="_blank">Implicit Contracts, Incentive Compatibility, and Involuntary Unemployment</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1989 </td>

   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.835 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> In this game there may exist other equilibria as well at which the decisionmaker does not behave skeptically and the full-information decision is not reached. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2555625" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2555625" target="_blank">Relying on the Information of Interested Parties</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1986 </td>

   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.834 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> 6An interesting paper in which a general definition of equilibrium in games is proposed which explicitly involves certain beliefs of the players is Kreps and Wilson (I 982a). </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1808119" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1808119" target="_blank">Expectations and Reputations in Bargaining: An Experimental Study</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1983 </td>

   <td style="text-align:left;"> Alvin E. Roth, Francoise Schoumaker </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.828 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Equilibria in games of this sort strongly depend on out-of-equilibrium beliefs, and certain kinds of beliefs may seem unreasonable. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2555691" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2555691" target="_blank">Warranties as Signals under Consumer Moral Hazard</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1989 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The RAND Journal of Economics </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Nancy A. Lutz </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.826 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> When a game possesses more than one equilibrium point the theory cannot prescribe to a player what he ought rationally to do. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/0014-2921(89)90142-6" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/0014-2921(89)90142-6" target="_blank">Some theoretical considerations</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1989 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> European Economic Review </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Dasgupta P. </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.824 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> We give a second example, also having a unique Nash equilibrium outcome, in which any strategy that rationalizes the necessary out-of-equilibrium beliefs must entail deviations from the equilibrium in future moves. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1913559" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1913559" target="_blank">Structural Consistency, Consistency, and Sequential
              Rationality</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1987 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Econometrica </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> David M. Kreps, Garey Ramey </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.822 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> If the order in which the players respond to a non-equilibrium point and the information available to them at the time of their computation are not predetermined, then the notion of a stable equilibrium becomes more restrictive. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/0165-1889(88)90030-9" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/0165-1889(88)90030-9" target="_blank">Asynchronous algorithms in non-cooperative games</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1988 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Journal of Economic Dynamics and Control </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Başar T. </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.821 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Equilibrium Existence of Equilibrium Sequential equilibria are assessments in which the players in the game are sequentially rational and hold consistent beliefs (see Kreps and Wilson [1982b] for a theoretical analysis). </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1830472" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1830472" target="_blank">Innovation and Reputation</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1988 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Journal of Political Economy </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Robert A. Miller </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.821 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> It is instructive to observe that the standard conditions for existence of a pure strategy Nash equilibria-continuity and quasi-concavity in agents' own strategies-do not suffice. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/0022-0531(87)90118-9" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/0022-0531(87)90118-9" target="_blank">Local perfection</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1987 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Journal of Economic Theory </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Simon L.K. </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.816 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> If agents share the common belief that Nash equilibrium is normally realized, they no longer entertain the rationally admissible doubt that an opponent will fail to conform. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1911196" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1911196" target="_blank">Rationalizable Strategic Behavior</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1984 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Econometrica </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> B. Douglas Bernheim </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.815 </td>
  </tr>

<tbody>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> It is also assumed that yt is known to all agents before they decide on their own actions at time t. Denote by xt the ' We are very grateful to Richard Barnett and two anonymous referees for helpful comments. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1913514" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1913514" target="_blank">Dynamic Inconsistency, Rational Expectations, and Optimal Government Policy</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1984 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Econometrica </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Brian Hillier, James M. Malcomson </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.850 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> As discussed earlier, an agent's observed decision in any period t is not assumed to always equal its optimal choice in that period. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/0167-2681(89)90057-7" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/0167-2681(89)90057-7" target="_blank">The origin of predictable dynamic behavior</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1989 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Journal of Economic Behavior and Organization </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Heiner R. </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.840 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> It is assumed that, when the agent chooses a E A, he knows the probability function 7T but not the outcome which will result from his action. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1912246" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1912246" target="_blank">An Analysis of the Principal-Agent Problem</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1983 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Econometrica </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Sanford J. Grossman, Oliver D. Hart </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.813 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Now we allow for uncertainty and recognize that the k-th agent's preferences among actions will reflect his tastes, his expectations and his attitude toward risk. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/0176-2680(85)90004-7" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/0176-2680(85)90004-7" target="_blank">Money and transaction costs under uncertainty</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1985 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> European Journal of Political Economy </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Dusansky R. </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.811 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Our intent here has been to develop an explicit model where the observed decisions of other agents are relevant for the decision making of uninformed agents. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2328198" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2328198" target="_blank">Banking Panics, Information, and Rational Expectations Equilibrium</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1988 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The Journal of Finance </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> V. V. Chari, Ravi Jagannathan </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.808 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> In the first, we assume that agents initially know only their own parameters, have quite dif'- fuse priors regarding others' strategies, and are quite risk averse, so they follow maximin strategies. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1837224" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1837224" target="_blank">The Informational Efficiency of Experimental Asset Markets</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1984 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Journal of Political Economy </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Daniel Friedman, Glenn W. Harrison, Jon W. Salmon </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.807 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The agent's choice of action will differ from the firstbest one in predictable ways. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://www.jstor.org/stable/10.2307/3003413" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://www.jstor.org/stable/10.2307/3003413" target="_blank">Bonuses and Penalties in Incentive Contracting</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1980 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The Bell Journal of Economics </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Tracy R. Lewis </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.800 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> In order to make the behaviour of the agents well defined we have to make specific assumptions about the information that the agents have on each other's preferences. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/0022-0531(81)90076-4" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/0022-0531(81)90076-4" target="_blank">Prudence versus sophistication in voting strategy</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1981 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Journal of Economic Theory </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Moulin H. </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.797 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The main restrictive assumption of our study is the a priori-symmetry of agents in the case of incomplete information. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://www.jstor.org/stable/10.2307/41105836" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://www.jstor.org/stable/10.2307/41105836" target="_blank">A Comparison of Pricing Rules for Auctions and Fair Division Games</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1986 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Social Choice and Welfare </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> W. Güth, E. van Damme </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.796 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> This analysis disposes effectively of the problem of accounting for how agents behave before becoming certain of the new value of X, at least if we ignore the question of where their priors come from. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1804021" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1804021" target="_blank">Econometric Policy Evaluation: Note</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1984 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The American Economic Review </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Thomas F. Cooley, Stephen F. LeRoy, Neil Raymon </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.794 </td>
  </tr>
</tbody>
</table><table class="table table-striped table-condensed" style="font-size: 12px; margin-left: auto; margin-right: auto;">

 </thead>
<tbody>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The answer to the question posed by this paper is likely to be an important consideration in a number of actual bargaining situations. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/S0921-8009(99)00065-8" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/S0921-8009(99)00065-8" target="_blank">Bargaining to preserve a unique ecosystem: The role of anticipatory investments to establish stronger bargaining positions</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1999 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Ecological Economics </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Stranlund J. </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.889 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> To illustrate how much the conclusions to which one is led by such an approach can differ from the predictions of traditional game theory, we plan to discuss a very simple bargaining game in the next section. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/40753015" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/40753015" target="_blank">An Economist's Perspective on the Evolution of Norms</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1994 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Journal of Institutional and Theoretical Economics (JITE) / Zeitschrift für die gesamte Staatswissenschaft </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Ken Binmore, Larry Samuelson </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.870 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> When a player fails to frame the bargaining problem comprehensively as expected utility predicts, his or her view on the relative importance of probability and consequences will affect the agreement (Edwards, 1953). </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/S0928-7655(97)00026-2" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/S0928-7655(97)00026-2" target="_blank">Coasean bargaining with symmetric delay costs</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1998 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Resource and Energy Economics </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Shogren J.F. </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.867 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The starting point of this paper is a recognition that a complete range of rational bargaining strategies cannot be specified in advance even under perfect information about objective functions. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/S0927-5371(96)00009-7" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/S0927-5371(96)00009-7" target="_blank">Bargaining and strikes: Towards an evolutionary framework</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1996 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Labour Economics </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Varoufakis Y. </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.862 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> In the paper that stimulated this article, applied this idea to a noncooperative, two-person bargaining game. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://doi.org/10.1006/game.1998.0700" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://doi.org/10.1006/game.1998.0700" target="_blank">Bargaining with imperfect commitment</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1999 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Games and Economic Behavior </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Kambe S. </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.860 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> We first show how results change if, say, player B is endowed with the "whole bargaining power" (the power to make offers), but player A still chooses the final action. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://doi.org/10.1006/game.1996.0042" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://doi.org/10.1006/game.1996.0042" target="_blank">An exact formula for the lion's share: A model of preplay negotiation</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1996 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Games and Economic Behavior </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Bensaid B. </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.856 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The bargaining approach employed can either be interpreted as the axiomatic bargaining model of Nash (1950) or the strategic bargaining model of Rubinstein (1982), as under conditions to be made precise the latter converges to a version of the former as the time between rounds in the strategic game becomes small. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2077723" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2077723" target="_blank">Search, Bargaining, Money and Prices: Recent Results and Policy Implications</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1993 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Journal of Money, Credit and Banking </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Alberto Trejos, Randall Wright </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.856 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> [6] Most applications of the Nash bargaining solution assume that the disagreement payoffs are exogenous in the determination of the bargaining payoffs, but Nash (1953) recognized that the bargaining parties are motivated to manipulate these payoffs before completion of an agreement to manipulate the terms of the agreement to their advantage. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/3146998" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/3146998" target="_blank">Sunk Capital and Negotiated Resolutions of Environmental Conflicts</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1999 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Land Economics </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> John K. Stranlund </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.856 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> In this note, it is shown that this multitude of joint hypotheses can be reduced when investigating alterations of the bargaining structure. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/40724237" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/40724237" target="_blank">A note on the impact of procedures in strike models. The case of bargaining structure</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1998 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Recherches Économiques de Louvain / Louvain Economic Review </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Laszlo Goerke </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.853 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> In conjunction with other recent studies described in detail in the remarks following the main result, they show that the recent focus on the role played by the disagreement point in the theory of bargaining has been quite illuminating. ' </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/0899-8256(90)90018-P" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/0899-8256(90)90018-P" target="_blank">Nash solution and uncertain disagreement points</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1990 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Games and Economic Behavior </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Chun Y. </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.852 </td>

  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> In order to answer this question we must analyse the various equivocal implications which are hidden in the term " rationality" as it is applied to the level of every-day experience. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2549460" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2549460" target="_blank">The Problem of Rationality in the Social World</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1943 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Economica </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Alfred Schuetz </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.791 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The chief point to be made is that (I) there is no area of human conduct which is purely rational; (2) there is no class of human </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1825485" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1825485" target="_blank">The Institutional Man</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1940 </td>

   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.770 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> arises from the fact that his definition of rationality is wide enough to cover all actions except those which I called real irrationality, while when he speaks about the difference between the rationality of capitalist and pre-capitalist households he seems to think of the narrower meaning of rationality which also excludes the actions mentioned under points (2) and (3) above. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2295759" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2295759" target="_blank">The Meaning of Rationality: A Note on Professor Lange's Article</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1946 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The Review of Economic Studies </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> K. W. Rothschild </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.767 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> "Rationality" has been imputed to the consumer only in the sense that his preferences are assumed to be unambiguous and self-consistent. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1825792" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1825792" target="_blank">Professor Knight and the Theory of Demand</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1946 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Journal of Political Economy </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Robert L. Bishop </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.767 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> This short analysis shows that we cannot speak of an isolated rational act, if we mean by this an act resulting from deliberated choice, but only of a system of rational acts.' </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2549460" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2549460" target="_blank">The Problem of Rationality in the Social World</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1943 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Economica </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Alfred Schuetz </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.767 </td>

  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The existence of society in which men can live a life of reason is dependent finally on the existence of a body of tradition, sentiments, beliefs, and personal loyalties that can be understood and shared but which are not rational, not at least in the sense that a machine is rational. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/137200" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/137200" target="_blank">Physics and Society</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1940 </td>

   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.755 </td>

  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> lies upon no assumption that individuals will always act rationally. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1826801" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1826801" target="_blank">Professor Robbins' Definition of Economics</a> </td>

   <td style="text-align:left;"> Robert Scoon </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.755 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> It seems that we have to distinguish between the rationality of knowledge which is a prerequisite of the rational choice and the rationality of the choice itself. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2549460" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2549460" target="_blank">The Problem of Rationality in the Social World</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1943 </td>

   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.753 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> What I wish to emphasise is only that the ideal of rationality is not and cannot be a peculiar feature of every-day thought, nor can it, therefore, be a methodological principle of the interpretation of human acts in daily life. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2549460" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2549460" target="_blank">The Problem of Rationality in the Social World</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1943 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Economica </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Alfred Schuetz </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.750 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Economic rationality thus assumes different forms or is subordinated to the mores of different areas. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1826409" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1826409" target="_blank">National Patterns of Union Behavior</a> </td>

   <td style="text-align:left;"> Journal of Political Economy </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Adolf Sturmthal </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.750 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> beings who are strictly rational in a given area of conduct; and (3) there is therefore no class of individuals who are strictly economically rational, to say nothing of the population at large. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1825485" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1825485" target="_blank">The Institutional Man</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1940 </td>

   <td style="text-align:left;"> Harvey Pinney </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.747 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> I The criterion of "rationality" applied to the economic process refers to the optimum satisfaction of given wants with scarce means. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1882066" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1882066" target="_blank">The Planning Approach in Public Economy: A Reply</a> </td>

   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.745 </td>

  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The term " rationality ", or at least the concept it envisages, has, within the framework of social science, the specific role of a "key concept ". </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2549460" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2549460" target="_blank">The Problem of Rationality in the Social World</a> </td>

   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.743 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Rationality of knowledge is given only if all the elements from which the actor has to choose are clearly and distinctly conceived by him. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2549460" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2549460" target="_blank">The Problem of Rationality in the Social World</a> </td>

   <td style="text-align:left;"> Alfred Schuetz </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.740 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Similarly, the rational deliberation of an actor as to wbether the results of a given proposed course of action will or will not promote certaiin specific interests, and the correspondi dcecision, do not become one bit more understandable by taking 'psychological' coinsiderations into account. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2549708" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2549708" target="_blank">Some Remarks on "The Theory of Social and Economic Organization"</a> </td>

   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.737 </td>

  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Even this, however, does not necessarily imply rationality. </td>

   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2295759" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2295759" target="_blank">The Meaning of Rationality: A Note on Professor Lange's Article</a> </td>

   <td style="text-align:left;"> We may reasonably conclude, therefore, that not only the cost of reproduction of the physical property for railway purposes, but also its strategic location and the ability with which it is managed as indicated by the great or small density of its traffic and its relatively large or small operating expenses, must be given due weight in fixing its valuation for rate-regulation, and that any valuation for rate-regulation that does not give due weight to these and any other factors that enter into its utility as an instrumentality of transportation will not secure the approval of the Supreme Court of the United States. </td>

   <td style="text-align:left;"> The inference-and the worker is not slow to take it-is plain that, if society should see fit to allow the laborers through their unions to force upon employers regulations, curtailing the present proprietary rights of m;anagem-ent, there could be no, appeal by the employers except to that same physical force which the laborer recognizes as the main foundation of property rights. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1819493" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1819493" target="_blank">The Trade-Union Point of View</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1907 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Journal of Political Economy </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Robert F. Hoxie </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.832 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Union leaders would consequently be bound before the public to keep labor in line and yet would not be furnished with the authority to do this effectively.1 From the standpoint of sheer logic this attitude of Mr. Hutcheson's was not ill-taken, but, although the Carpenters and Joiners Union has never been a party to the creation or continuance of the Adjustment 1 It should not be inferred that the other labor officials who signed the memoran? </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1820672" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1820672" target="_blank">Labor Administration in the Shipbuilding Industry During War Time: I</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1919 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Journal of Political Economy </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> P. H. Douglas, F. E. Wolfe </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.799 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Such men will offer no more effective opposition than a muttered protest against reduced wage scales and lengthened hours; they have no "mistaken notions" about the employer's right "to run his own business," although their interest in the matter is as vital to themselves and the community at large as his is to himself. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1820081" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1820081" target="_blank">The Economic Basis of the Fight for the Closed Shop</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1912 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Journal of Political Economy </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Howard T. Lewis </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.795 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Let us look rather to a few items that seem to be the point of contention: Limitation as to the amount of work to be done in a day, Restrictions in the use of machinery, The arbitrary action of the business agent, Sympathetic strikes. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1817477" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1817477" target="_blank">Analysis of the Building-Trades Conflict in Chicago, from the Trades-Union Stand-Point</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1900 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Journal of Political Economy </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> S. V. Lindholm </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.791 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> It would seem from the records of labour movements as if the operative's fear-based as much on ignorance as on distrust-lest the longer day should mean no more pay, though the weekly product would be greater, has protected him against the injurious consequences of short-sightedness; but I am inclined to think that the dominant force in these labour movements has consisted in ideals of life, formed half instinctively, which are unconnected with views, fallacious or otherwise, concerning the mechanics of distribution. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2221102" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2221102" target="_blank">Hours of Labour</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1909 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The Economic Journal </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> S. J. Chapman </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.787 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Assuming (though the point is by no means settled) that it is beyond the power of the legislature to secure to laborers fair conditions of employment, such a limitation of the police power demands logically that laborers should be allowed to secure these conditions for themselves by their combined efforts, and it can be justified, if at all, only by the existence of the widest possible power of organization and association. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1817281" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1817281" target="_blank">Recent Illinois Decisions Regarding Injunctions Issued in the Course of Strikes</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1906 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Journal of Political Economy </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Ernst Freund </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.777 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Looked at in this light, the labor of the factory superintendents, of the men who sweep the floors, of the administrators, of the bookkeepers, of the public accountants, to whose competent advice and supervision in these modern times the success of the enterprise is often largely due, of the lawyers who examine and prepare the legal documents, of the doctors who bind up broken limbs -the labor of these is just as productive as that of the workmen who handle the looms, or who work at the machines. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1814920" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1814920" target="_blank">Cost Units</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1911 </td>

   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.774 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> A case similar to this, and with a like confusion of thought, has arisen in the industrial world under the assertion, "Every man has the right to labor." </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1882413" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1882413" target="_blank">The Right to Labor</a> </td>

   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.774 </td>

   <td style="text-align:left;"> And we ought also to ask: Even if it be true that the extraordinary tax on wealth introduced by the Decree is much preferable to a levy on capital, is it really a measure preferable to any other? </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2223520" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2223520" target="_blank">A Levy on Capital</a> </td>

   <td style="text-align:left;"> Corrado Gini </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.806 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> On the one hand it is claimed that the taxation of capital represents an abandonment of the "ability to pay" principle, since it is the current income of an individual which is the measure of his tax-paying capacity.3 In the case of a tremendous emergency like war, however, it may be more equitable to charge expenses upon resources rather than upon income-a contention which would probably be readily admitted if all resources were in the form of food and shells and guns.4 With the state, as with the individual or corporation, expenditure may be divided into revenue expenditure and capital expenditure. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1822182" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1822182" target="_blank">Proposals for the Taxation of Wealth in Great Britain</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1920 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Journal of Political Economy </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Alzada Comstock </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.805 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Still another instance of the support of present procedure by the use of arguments not followed to a conclusion is contained in the statement that the abolition of double taxation by the United Kingdom and foreign governments would involve a serious departure from the principle of "ability to pay." </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1809046" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1809046" target="_blank">British Income Tax Reform</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1920 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The American Economic Review </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Alzada Comstock </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.787 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> But he adds that, " if a tax is believed to be practicable over a considerable part of the field to which it is to be applied, and the impracticability is confined to a minor part, most States will embark upon the scheme, and by a sacrifice of logical principle at the point of difficulty and the adoption of a few conventions, will satisfy the equities roughly " (p. 97). </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2547962" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2547962" target="_blank">Some Recent Contributions to the Study of Public Finance</a> </td>

   <td style="text-align:left;"> Hugh Dalton </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.785 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> I have examined, and to some extent justified, this position in Chapter III of The Fundamental Principles of Taxation. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2223454" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2223454" target="_blank">The Taxable-Capacity of Ireland</a> </td>

   <td style="text-align:left;"> J. C. Stamp </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.783 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Will not the fear of a repetition of the levy prove a greater obstacle to the accumulation of wealth than is that burden of taxation which the capital levy seeks to diminish? </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2223520" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2223520" target="_blank">A Levy on Capital</a> </td>

   <td style="text-align:left;"> Corrado Gini </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.780 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Much of the opposition to the excess profits tax is due, I am convinced, to the purposes for which it is conceived to exist, among which may be mentioned the following: 1. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1803340" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1803340" target="_blank">Suggestions for Revision of the Federal Taxation of Income and Profits</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1920 </td>

   <td style="text-align:left;"> Fred Rogers Fairchild </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.779 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> And if it be said that this principle is not the only one to be considered but that other principles are of great importance to justice and wisdom in taxation, then the question immediately arises whether these other relevant principles may not support a system of taxation which is not at all in proportion to ability. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/3139129" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/3139129" target="_blank">Should Bare-Land Values Be Taxed More Heavily?</a> </td>

   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.778 </td>

  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> It ought to be remembered that when the wisest government has exhausted all the proper subjects of taxation, it must, in cases of urgent necessity, have recourse to improper ones" (Vol. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2548476" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2548476" target="_blank">Adam Smith on Twentieth Century Finance</a> </td>

   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1884092" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1884092" target="_blank">Should The Excess Profits Tax be Repealed</a> </td>

   <td style="text-align:left;"> A consideration of taxation and a minimum of subsistence leads one to the conclusion that ability to pay should be given more weight in formulating our tax policies, indefinite as this standard is. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/253" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/253" target="_blank">Taxation and the Minimum of Subsistence</a> </td>

   <td style="text-align:left;"> Alfred G. Buehler </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.798 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Until there is established a reasonable basis for a belief not only in the reality of the hypothesis that the curve of diminishing marginal utility of money income is steeper than a rectangular hyperbola but also in the reality of the eight preceding assumptions, the case for progressive taxation cannot be based upon the theory of equal sacrifice.56 A discussion of the sacrifice theories would be incomplete without mention of their ethical validity. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1824777" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1824777" target="_blank">Recent and Contemporary Theories of Progressive Taxation</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1938 </td>

   <td style="text-align:left;"> Elmer D. Fagan </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.792 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> derive from the tax, and that any appraisal of the desirability of a given tax ought to consider them. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1801984" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1801984" target="_blank">The Incidence and Effects of Taxation: Some Theoretical Aspects</a> </td>

   <td style="text-align:left;"> M. Slade Kendrick </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.788 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The points made respecting application of the principle of declining marginal utility to money, and the existence of sacrifice in progressive taxation hold for this view also. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1806989" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1806989" target="_blank">The Ability-to-Pay Theory of Taxation</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1939 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The American Economic Review </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> M. Slade Kendrick </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.782 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> In a certain ultimate and fundamental sense, taxation reform is of equal importance, to be sure; but expenditure control derives its greater significance from the psychological, political and fallacious economic obstacles to its realization. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1231484" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1231484" target="_blank">Tax Relief through Rational Expenditure Control</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1935 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Journal of Farm Economics </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Harley L. Lutz </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.779 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Although he would evidently confine the discussion of the effects of public expenditures to those taxes where the receipts clearly change the supply of or the demand for the taxed object, it appears more logical to the writer to recognize that the shifting and incidence of a tax may also be modified by the expenditure of funds obtained from other taxes, borrowing, or other sources. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1806303" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1806303" target="_blank">Public Expenditures and the Incidence of Taxes: Some Theoretical Considerations</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1938 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The American Economic Review </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Alfred G. Buehler </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.779 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> To do this satisfactorily and with acceptance would certainly not be easy, but it is precisely my case here, as elsewhere, that the difficulties of rational taxation ought to be faced: that we can no longer afford to turn our backs upon them and let things drift. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2224799" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2224799" target="_blank">Rates and Taxes</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1939 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The Economic Journal </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> H. O. Meredith </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.779 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> For the early steps in a purely theoretical discussion of sacrifice in taxation, this hypothesis is highly valuable if not indispensable. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1824777" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1824777" target="_blank">Recent and Contemporary Theories of Progressive Taxation</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1938 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Journal of Political Economy </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Elmer D. Fagan </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.776 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> This doctrine has been accepted by numerous economists in various forms and on various grounds; other economists have ignored it or openly rejected it; while the framers of our tax laws have considered the doctrine to the extent that politics demanded and have commonly compromised on the issue. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/253" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/253" target="_blank">Taxation and the Minimum of Subsistence</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1933 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The American Economic Review </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Alfred G. Buehler </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.776 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> This may be looked at also in the light of a distinction of old standing in the theory of taxation, between the basis, the source, and the application of resources. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2224061" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2224061" target="_blank">Taxation of Co-operative Dividend</a> </td>

   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.774 </td>

  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The modern tendency to find mental satisfaction in measuring everything by a fixed rational standard, and the way it takes for granted that everything can be related to everything else, certainly receives from the apparently objective value of money, and the universal possibility of exchange which this involves, a strong psychological impulse to become a fixed habit of thought, whereas the purely logical process itself, when it only follows its own course, is not subject to these influences, and it then turns these accepted ideas into mere probabilities.' </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2113261" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2113261" target="_blank">On the Economic Significance of Culture</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1944 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The Journal of Economic History </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Harold A. Innis </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.738 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Moreover, the judgment, in valuation, logically (if not psychologically) implies a selection or several selections from two or more possible alternatives; yet these selections or judgments are impossible without reference to some means and ends, usually (if not always) those of the agent or researcher himself. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/3483397" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/3483397" target="_blank">The Place of Value-Judgments in the Social Sciences</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1945 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The American Journal of Economics and Sociology </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Melvin J. Williams </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.738 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> If it were generally recognized, for example, that decisions which had to be taken often involved considerations other than those of the most immediate profits of a particular firm, the decisions which were made, even without governmental control or regulation, might be wiser. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1814503" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1814503" target="_blank">Economic Planning and the Problem of Full Employment</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1940 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The American Economic Review </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Calvin B. Hoover </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.735 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> "63 One cannot disagree with this statement any more than with the statement that the price of butter measures the marginal utility of butter to each member of the community.64 Both statements are either tautologies or definitions of rational behavior. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1905567" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1905567" target="_blank">Liquidity Preference and the Theory of Interest and Money</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1944 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Econometrica </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Franco Modigliani </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.726 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Perhaps they did not completely realize the complexity of human motivation, but they cannot be accused, as Dickinson rightly points out, of a ridiculous blindness to ideal motives.8 However, they held that none of the altruistic and other possible motives were of such typical and general significance as the desire of wealth, and that, therefore, it was legitimate to disregard them, or at least to give them secondary consideration only, particularly in the initial stages of economic analysis.' </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1052713" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1052713" target="_blank">Rational Human Conduct and Modern Industrial Society</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1943 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Southern Economic Journal </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Karl W. Kapp </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.721 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> It would not be difficult to find similar situations in other fields of practice; but perhaps these two are enough to illustrate the point that, in so far as the theory of value assumes choice, the relation of scarce means to ends, and orders of preference, it is dealing with features of conduct that are not specifically economic but general throughout all practice. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1826801" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1826801" target="_blank">Professor Robbins' Definition of Economics</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1943 </td>

   <td style="text-align:left;"> Robert Scoon </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.721 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> It is a fact to be taken account of in describing the logical implications of our pecuniary system motivated by money profit expectations. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1884723" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1884723" target="_blank">A Process Analysis of Bank Credit Expansion</a> </td>

   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.719 </td>

  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> himself of formulating a satisfactory theory of value in terms of cause and effect which would illumine, if it did not solve, the problems of the real world; and partly to his own impatience with rigid definition and an excessive tendency to let the context explain his meaning. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2226236" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2226236" target="_blank">The Evolution of Marshall's Principles of Economics</a> </td>

## Intertemporal cluster _8: land, farmer, farm, farmers_ 

  
The cluster gathers 2421 sentences from our corpus. It represents 0.73% of all the sentences selected over the whole period.

The community exists from 1900 to 1979. 

The most recurring authors are Harry Gunnison Brown (49 sentences; 15 articles), <suffix>Jr.</suffix> (39 sentences; 31 articles), Richard T. Ely (24 sentences; 9 articles), Earl O.
