### Closest sentence from 'rational' and 'rationality' of the backbone community

<table class="table table-striped table-condensed" style="font-size: 12px; margin-left: auto; margin-right: auto;">
 <thead>
  <tr>
   <th style="text-align:left;"> Sentence </th>
   <th style="text-align:left;"> Title </th>
   <th style="text-align:right;"> Year </th>
   <th style="text-align:left;"> Journal </th>
   <th style="text-align:left;"> Authors </th>
   <th style="text-align:right;"> Words Similarity </th>
  </tr>
 </thead>
<tbody>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> In short, farmers are assumed to hold rational expectations, which Muth (I96I) defines as those which would be predicted by the relevant economic theory, given the information currently available. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2231500" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2231500" target="_blank">The Theory of Commodity Price Stabilisation Rules: Welfare Impacts and Supply Responses</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1979 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The Economic Journal </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> D. M. G. Newbery, J. E. Stiglitz </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.702 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> If the farm-firm problems are defined in a specific manner, then the management process will be more "rational." </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1237067" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1237067" target="_blank">A Systematic Conceptualization of Farm Management</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1967 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Journal of Farm Economics </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Willard T. Rushton, E. T. Shaudys </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.698 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> They implicitly assume that activities which are not rational by business standards are irrational, and that the peasant cultivator would be better off if he changes his practices to conform with the rationale of business. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1151638" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1151638" target="_blank">Economic Accounting and Family Farming in India</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1959 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Economic Development and Cultural Change </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Walter C. Neale </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.691 </td>
  </tr>

   <td style="text-align:left;"> Our conclusion seems to be that owners of land are entitled to a return on their investments in improvements, such as special assessments for cutting streets, in the same sense and to the same degree that they are entitled to a return on the cost of building houses or factories; that, however, they are no more entitled to a socially guaranteed return in the one case than in the other;' and that there is no reason why they should be allowed more than enough, on the basis of such expenditures, to make the expenditures worth while. </td>

  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> In considering broad problems of agricultural policy, it does not suffice to rely upon a general background of theory and merely qualitative observations. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1927345" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1927345" target="_blank">New Indices of Agricultural Supplies and Carry-Over</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1937 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The Review of Economics and Statistics </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> E. J. Working </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.813 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The farmer may have a fairly clear picture of the facts with regard to his own farm and yet be utterly without the necessary information to make such adjustments in his farm operations as may become necessary due to the competition of farmers in other areas or due to changes in market conditions. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1231780" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1231780" target="_blank">A Century of Agricultural Statistics</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1939 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Journal of Farm Economics </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Henry C. Taylor </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.810 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> What a farmer decides to do is largely a result of his reaction to prices received or to those he expects to receive, . </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://www.jstor.org/stable/10.2307/44643520" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://www.jstor.org/stable/10.2307/44643520" target="_blank">EXTENSION IN AGRICULTURAL ECONOMICS</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1934 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Proceedings of the Annual Meeting (Western Farm Economics Association) </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> L.M. Vaughan </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.809 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> It would seem that regardless of the objective and technique with which farm 31 Equally and probably more important (as noted by Elkinton) is to help the farmer arrive at more rational expectations before he has allocated or reallocated his stream of assets into the form of more or less fixed resources. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1232142" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1232142" target="_blank">Theory of the Firm and Farm Management Research</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1939 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Journal of Farm Economics </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> T. W. Schultz </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.792 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> If farmers should change from commercial to self-sufficient types of production, the unsoundness of some widely accepted and used economic philosophies might be recognized more generally. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://www.jstor.org/stable/10.2307/44643437" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://www.jstor.org/stable/10.2307/44643437" target="_blank">"BEST" USE OF AGRICULTURAL RESOURCES</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1939 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Proceedings of the Annual Meeting (Western Farm Economics Association) </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Harold F. Hollands </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.790 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The last is not an easy task, but it is believed that this approach comes closer to the farmer's own mode of thinking on the subject than any other method of presenting the proble </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1231242" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1231242" target="_blank">The Theory of Combination of Enterprises on Individual Farms</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1933 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Journal of Farm Economics </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Sherman E. Johnson </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.789 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> As I shall point out later on, however, there exist, of course, strong natural and economic factors in agriculture which tend to promote variety of agricultural management by obstructing the tendency of simplification of production. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://www.jstor.org/stable/10.2307/43216776" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://www.jstor.org/stable/10.2307/43216776" target="_blank">HORIZONTAL AND VERTICAL DIFFERENTIATIONS IN THE AGRICULTURAL PRODUCTION OF JAPAN</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1934 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Kyoto University Economic Review </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Yoshinosuke Yagi </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.788 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> In line with this determining principle, the argument of an influential group of agricultural economists today is to the effect that too large a proportion of the American people is on the farms. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1053520" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1053520" target="_blank">The Effects of Urbanization on Agriculture</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1935 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Southern Economic Journal </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Wilson Gee </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.785 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The farmer wishes to know the relevance of this principle to his total business and not only in one but in all its possible aspects. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1231179" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1231179" target="_blank">A Statistical Analysis of Farm Accounts</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1934 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Journal of Farm Economics </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Walter H. Jones </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.782 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> In the light of the individualistic tendency of farmers, this action may at first seem strange, but if sympathy toward years of extension efforts, plus governmental financial backing, could not sway the farmer, then there would be little hope of every having concerted action on the part of the agricultural class. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1231184" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1231184" target="_blank">The Relationship between the Agricultural Adjustment Administration and Agricultural Economics Extension Work in the South</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1934 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Journal of Farm Economics </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> J. F. Criswell </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.782 </td>
  </tr>

  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> "7 The economic basis of land value must be sought "in the use to which it is or may be put. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/3139048" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/3139048" target="_blank">Valuation of Land by Public Utility Commissions</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1931 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The Journal of Land &amp; Public Utility Economics </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Ernest M. Fisher </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.817 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> It is sad but characteristic of this blundersome human race that the matters of land use, possibly the most important to our economic existence, have never been settled by any logical study; in fact, they have been logically approached only in a few comparatively trifling details. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/3158108" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/3158108" target="_blank">Physical Aspects of Country Planning</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1937 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The Journal of Land &amp; Public Utility Economics </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Frank A. Waugh </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.807 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> lands, have in general received more consideration in the selection of areas than in the use for which the land is to be employed. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1231107" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1231107" target="_blank">The Social and Economic Implications of the National Land Program</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1936 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Journal of Farm Economics </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> L. C. Gray </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.802 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> We may bo convinced that much land has been settled which ought not to have been settled or that much land is wrongly used, but we must start by recognizing that the present position, good or bad, exists and that the best mode of changing it is to mould rather than to disrupt. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://www.jstor.org/stable/10.2307/44643498" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://www.jstor.org/stable/10.2307/44643498" target="_blank">PLANNING THE LAND OF THE FUTURE</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1934 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Proceedings of the Annual Meeting (Western Farm Economics Association) </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> L. Dudley Stamp </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.797 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Common lands, he records, let for only about one-third as much as enclosed lands, because of "the many several interests: whence it is, that men can not agree to employ it to its properest use, and best advantage." </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1822286" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1822286" target="_blank">The Place of Agriculture in British National Economy Prior to Adam Smith</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1931 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Journal of Political Economy </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> S. J. Brandenburg </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.796 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> (5) The sometimes observed decrease in the relative return from a certain plot of land is not to be blamed on a law of Nature, but rather appears to be a result of our limited knowledge of Nature, as well perhaps as of agricultural production, and the lack of interest in these; or due to purely economic relationships. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1230418" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1230418" target="_blank">The Law of Diminishing Fertility of the Soil, from the Point of View of Some of the Russian Economists of Today</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1931 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Journal of Farm Economics </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> John W. Boldyreff </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.790 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The problem is much less simple when we come to consider the alternative uses of land and the extent to which the rent of land under one use may be said to enter into the cost of production of rival products. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2225276" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2225276" target="_blank">Davenport on the Economics of Alfred Marshall</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1937 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The Economic Journal </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> C. W. Guillebaud </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.789 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> This is stated, not so much as a suggestion to branches of federal and state governments buying land where there is no question of its being covered with artificial lakes or subjected to other immediate marked changes in condition, but as a means of making clear a broader principle. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/3158325" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/3158325" target="_blank">Strategy in Protecting the Public's Interest in Land: With Special Reference to Strip Mining</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1939 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The Journal of Land &amp; Public Utility Economics </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Charles L. Stewart </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.782 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> In discussing measures of land-use control it is assumed that the social interest in the private ownership and use of land is sufficient to justify the adoption of measures to protect that interest where recalcitrant individual owners fail to do so. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://www.jstor.org/stable/10.2307/44643422" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://www.jstor.org/stable/10.2307/44643422" target="_blank">SOME CONSIDERATIONS INVOLVED IN AN APPRAISAL OF MEASURES FOR LAND-USE CONTROL</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1938 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Proceedings of the Annual Meeting (Western Farm Economics Association) </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> James H. Marshall </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.778 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> But there appear to be good reasons, both in theory and practice, which need not be discussed here, for treating certain forces on the supply side of land, defining "land" as a potential capacity for producing food and raw materials. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1230927" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1230927" target="_blank">The Use of Farm Organization and Budgetary Data as a Basis for Land Valuation</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1935 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Journal of Farm Economics </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> M. H. Saunderson </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.773 </td>
  </tr>
</tbody>
</table><table class="table table-striped table-condensed" style="font-size: 12px; margin-left: auto; margin-right: auto;">

  <tr>

 </thead>
<tbody>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> A farmer in a particular situation may be better off but, in the formulation of hypotheses, care must be taken not to translate one possible situation in terms of the whole of agriculture. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1234487" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1234487" target="_blank">Social Security in Agriculture: A Preliminary Appraisal of Its Operation, Implications, and Emerging Problems</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1956 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Journal of Farm Economics </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Gene Wunderlich </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.854 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> In interpreting a farmer's decision making in light of the proposed framework, it is necessary to recognize that the applicable sets of possible events, actions and strategies are subjective. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1234713" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1234713" target="_blank">Problems of Uncertainty in Farm Planning</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1957 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Journal of Farm Economics </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> C. Hildreth </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.825 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Due to particular circumstances, some farmers may not be able to act in the manner that appears most rational. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1234012" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1234012" target="_blank">The Wheat Supply Function</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1955 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Journal of Farm Economics </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> B. J. Bowlen </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.821 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> At any given time the essence of the farmer's problem is less likely to be one of allocating resources to the point of equi-marginal returns than one of how to perform a necessary sequence of operations once he is committed to a particular productive organization or investment. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1233307" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1233307" target="_blank">Industrial Management Techniques in Agriculture</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1954 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Journal of Farm Economics </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> J. E. Wills </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.820 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> It would be incorrect to conclude that price was not an important consideration in farmers' decision making process, but rather the direction and extent to which farmers respond is influenced by a most diverse set of conditions among areas, among farms within an area and over time. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1234012" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1234012" target="_blank">The Wheat Supply Function</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1955 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Journal of Farm Economics </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> B. J. Bowlen </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.814 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> We may believe that a certain type of farm organization or certain economic action is more desirable for a farmer to take than another. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1234290" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1234290" target="_blank">Developing a Set of Basic Principles for Economic Extension</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1954 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Journal of Farm Economics </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> J. Carroll Bottum </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.811 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The assertion that the farmer alone "has to accept prices offered while others fix theirs" may be persuasive political dogma but as evidence it is weakened by many exceptions and limitations. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1233489" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1233489" target="_blank">What Sort of a Farm Price Policy Is Practical in the U.S.A.?</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1952 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Journal of Farm Economics </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> O. B. Jesness </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.809 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Although our understanding of farmers' objectives and their economic behavior is substantially incomplete, a few safe generalizations can be made. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1234598" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1234598" target="_blank">Price Support Programs and Interregional Competition</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1956 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Journal of Farm Economics </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Vernon L. Sorenson </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.806 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> It may be reasoned that too little attention is given to the wants, preferences and goals of farm families; that human, financial and related resources are inadequately evaluated; and that data, information and inductive teaching are emphasized, rather than working through the decision making process realistically. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1234005" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1234005" target="_blank">Possible Implications of Decision Making Studies for Farm Management Teaching and Research</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1955 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Journal of Farm Economics </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Lowell S. Hardin </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.805 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> When one takes a broad view of decision making, it is apparent that economic logic is only one form of logic in farm management and that it alone is far too narrow to handle the range of problems encountered by farm managers." </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1235024" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1235024" target="_blank">Farmers' Decisions in the Use of Fertilizer</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1958 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Journal of Farm Economics </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Moyle S. Williams </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.805 </td>
  </tr>
</tbody>
</table><table class="table table-striped table-condensed" style="font-size: 12px; margin-left: auto; margin-right: auto;">

  <tr>

 </thead>
<tbody>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Namely, all problems of agricultural economics, may they be related to prices, production relations, labour or technology, have an aspect from the point of view of agricultural policy; and any well-founded decision of agricultural policy depends on how far the actual problem has been cleared up in its own place. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/40694549" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/40694549" target="_blank">THEORETICAL PROBLEMS OF FARM ORGANIZATION AND MANAGEMENT</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1966 </td>

### Closest sentence from 'rational' and 'rationality' of the backbone community

<table class="table table-striped table-condensed" style="font-size: 12px; margin-left: auto; margin-right: auto;">
 <thead>
  <tr>
   <th style="text-align:left;"> Sentence </th>
   <th style="text-align:left;"> Title </th>
   <th style="text-align:right;"> Year </th>
   <th style="text-align:left;"> Journal </th>
   <th style="text-align:left;"> Authors </th>
   <th style="text-align:right;"> Words Similarity </th>
  </tr>
 </thead>
<tbody>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> On one hand, a fully rational person will realize that other people participating in a nonhypothetical experiment get some enjoyment out of stating their value; thus, a fully rational person's inferred valuation would be expected to equal the expected nonhypothetical valuation, that is, WTP1 = F^WTP ], so long as people can predict others' behavior reasonably well. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/27759692" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/27759692" target="_blank">An Inferred Valuation Method</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 2009 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Land Economics </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Jayson L. Lusk, F. Bailey Norwood </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.724 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The neo-classical economic theory of choice provides the underlying theoretical foundation for contingent valuation and requires that individuals participating in CV are rational in the sense that their preferences are complete, transitive, and invariant, and that individuals have invested optimally in the acquisition of information (Kahneman, 1986). </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ecolecon.2005.11.031" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ecolecon.2005.11.031" target="_blank">Contingent valuation: Environmental polling or preference engine?</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 2006 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Ecological Economics </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> MacMillan D. </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.709 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> that a rational agent will be able to express a unique monetary valuation. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/27647701" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/27647701" target="_blank">Incommensurability and Monetary Valuation</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 2006 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Land Economics </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Jonathan Aldred </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.699 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The more narrowly the entire system of competitive valuation specifies the economic quantity that is being priced, the more rational the choices can be among the different ways of organizing production to achieve a given bill of goods. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://www.jstor.org/stable/10.2307/44012653" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://www.jstor.org/stable/10.2307/44012653" target="_blank">EXAMINING SELECTED FEATURES OF COMMODITY MARKETS THROUGH BALANCE SHEETS</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1964 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Proceedings of the Annual Meeting (Western Farm Economics Association) </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Allen B. Paul </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.699 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> (1992) argued that if there is uncertainty regarding the utility (payoff) of a transaction, values would depend on the “viewpoint”. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.joep.2004.07.002" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.joep.2004.07.002" target="_blank">Effects of study design characteristics on the WTA-WTP disparity: A meta analytical framework</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 2005 </td>

  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The important point is that the co1lception of value, from being the esteem in wllich a commodity ought to be held, an esteem the degree of which could be interpreted by experts only, had come to be its power in exchange. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://www.jstor.org/stable/10.2307/2485740" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://www.jstor.org/stable/10.2307/2485740" target="_blank">The Theory of Value before Adam Smith</a> </td>

  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> t should be sufficiently evident that I do not want the value concept limited to " rate of exchange " or any other relative notion, nor do I regard such concepts as ultimate nor oppose the use of concepts of social value. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1883305" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1883305" target="_blank">The Concept of Value: A Rejoinder</a> </td>

  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The second of the current tendencies which threaten to drag value theory from its place of authority is the growing realization by value theorists of the inadequacy or incompleteness of their work. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1822591" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1822591" target="_blank">The Place of Value Theory in Economics: II</a> </td>

  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> We have now to see what considerations established the worth of a thing in itself or its " true " value, as they conceived of it. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://www.jstor.org/stable/10.2307/2485740" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://www.jstor.org/stable/10.2307/2485740" target="_blank">The Theory of Value before Adam Smith</a> </td>

  <tr>

   <td style="text-align:left;"> This review of the various theories of valuation shows that none of them can be applied in its purity without considerable violation of ethical principles or without encountering insurmountable practical difficulties. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1882669" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1882669" target="_blank">Ethical and Economic Elements in Public Service Valuation</a> </td>

   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1882669" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1882669" target="_blank">Ethical and Economic Elements in Public Service Valuation</a> </td>

   <td style="text-align:left;"> The consideration of these various manifestations of value has brought into prominence two characteristics of the problem of valuation which deserve further consideration. </td>

   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1884621" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1884621" target="_blank">Progress and Poverty in Current Literature on Valuation</a> </td>

   <td style="text-align:left;"> Another group, intelligent enough to see that "physical value" is a self-contradictory and unmeaning term, admits that cost is not the same thing as value, but claims that it is a sufficiently good measure of value to warrant them in calling cost assessment by the name valuation. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1811558" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1811558" target="_blank">The Meaning of Valuation</a> </td>

   <td style="text-align:left;"> The valuations of the market are no more absolute and have no greater validity than those which result from the workings of any other institution of pecuniary valuation. </td>

  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The fundamental considerations of the nature of value are often imperfectly comprehended or are overlooked or disregarded. </td>

   <td style="text-align:left;"> Much of the confusion as to valuation methods is ascribed to the fact that different concepts of value require different methods of valuation; that the </td>

  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The theory of value, it is claimed, has to be reconstructed so that no doubt is left as to the fundamental immeasurability of total and marginal utility, and if it should turn out that either of these two concepts, or both, cannot be fitted into the reshaped framework, it is concluded that they must be eliminated as "meaningless" and "unscientific." </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2549021" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2549021" target="_blank">The End of the Marginal Utility Theory?</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1938 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Economica </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> H. Bernardelli </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.812 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Here again there is an analogy with the traditional Theory of Value. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2967434" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2967434" target="_blank">The Theory of Money and the Analysis of Output</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1933 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The Review of Economic Studies </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Joan Robinson </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.811 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> It may well be necessary to rewrite the whole theory of value </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1884068" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1884068" target="_blank">Professor Pigou's Theory of Unemployment</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1935 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The Quarterly Journal of Economics </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> S. E. Harris </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.806 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> This leads to the conception of value. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2548905" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2548905" target="_blank">On the Subject-Matter and Method of Economic Science</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1933 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Economica </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Felix Kaufmann </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.804 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> We have then the principle of value: " .... </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1824519" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1824519" target="_blank">The Economics of Carl Menger</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1937 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Journal of Political Economy </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> George J. Stigler </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.802 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The theory of value, the theory of rent, even the theory of wagesthese are propositions which, with a little sympathetic understanding, can be regarded as having a limited validity. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2548861" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2548861" target="_blank">The Ricardian Theory of Profits</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1933 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Economica </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Victor Edelberg </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.802 </td>
  </tr>

  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> It is probably true that the concepts of value theory which usually are used can be indicted on these grounds, but this is only a reiteration of the preceding </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1818331" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1818331" target="_blank">The Value of Value Theory</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1954 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The American Economic Review </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Richard Ruggles </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.876 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The specific charges I shall cover are (1) that value theory is tautological; (2) that many of the concepts of value theory have no empirical counterparts; (3) that the necessity of using rigid ceteris paribus assumptions paralyzes the analysis so that it </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1818331" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1818331" target="_blank">The Value of Value Theory</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1954 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The American Economic Review </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Richard Ruggles </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.838 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> This problem has a bearing upon the value judgment controversy. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://www.jstor.org/stable/10.2307/43751278" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://www.jstor.org/stable/10.2307/43751278" target="_blank">THE BASIC IDEA OF FISCAL SCIENCE</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1953 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The Annals of the Hitotsubashi Academy </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Hanya Ito </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.823 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The Ambiguous Nature and True Role of Values Much of what I am trying to say is bound up in two very different meanings of the word "value," a truly disastrous ambiguity, and a fact not sufficiently taken into account by most writers. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1233167" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1233167" target="_blank">Comment on Professor Parsons' Article</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1950 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Journal of Farm Economics </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Frank H. Knight </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.812 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Value judgments must be made. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1233967" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1233967" target="_blank">Welfare Implications of Efficiency and Technological Improvements in Marketing Research and Extension</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1955 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Journal of Farm Economics </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Lawrence Witt </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.809 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> With respect to these more specific objectives, a number of fairly common charges regarding the limitations of value theory will be discussed, and from these, as a third part of the paper, some possible suggestions for future work in this area will be developed. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1818331" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1818331" target="_blank">The Value of Value Theory</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1954 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The American Economic Review </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Richard Ruggles </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.807 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> In the past, comparing judgments which are capable of objective verification with judgments which are not so verifiable, I have sometimes put my point in the form of a comparison between judgments of fact and judgments of value. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2550835" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2550835" target="_blank">Robertson on Utility and Scope</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1953 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Economica </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Lionel Robbins </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.807 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The extraction of Veblen's general theory of value might seem to be made difficult by his writing from, rather than about, his more general philosophic position; but, such extraction is not particularly difficult, for although statements of his philosophical position are scattered through his writings, they are quite explicitly stated. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/3484564" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/3484564" target="_blank">Thorstein Veblen, Radical Apologist for Conservatism</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1959 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The American Journal of Economics and Sociology </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Ernest W. Dewey </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.806 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> First, a suitable theory of value had to be formulated. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2296164" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2296164" target="_blank">Mr. Gottlieb on Marx: A Comment</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1952 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The Review of Economic Studies </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Ronald L. Meek </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.805 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> In the absence of an acceptable standard whereby to judge between two value preferences it seems more reasonable to assert equal value than to assert the superiority of one over the other. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/138513" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/138513" target="_blank">A Note on David Easton's Approach to Political Philosophy</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1954 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The Canadian Journal of Economics and Political Science / Revue canadienne d'Economique et de Science politique </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> R. C. Pratt </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.804 </td>
  </tr>

   <td style="text-align:left;"> "4 He points out the elusive nature of "value" and the need to use a valuation as a substitute for value and offers some criteria with which to appraise valuation methods. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1348861" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1348861" target="_blank">Inventory Valuation and Farm Income</a> </td>

   <td style="text-align:left;"> Illinois Agricultural Economics </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> William A. Tinsley </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.861 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> This I believe to be at the heart of the problem of valuation. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1812046" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1812046" target="_blank">Equity Yields, Growth, and the Structure of Share Prices</a> </td>

   <td style="text-align:left;"> Burton G. Malkiel </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.851 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> '5 Apart from the problems of estimating the quantities involved there is the conceptual question of valuation. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1926662" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1926662" target="_blank">Soviet National Income Accounts for 1955</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1962 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The Review of Economics and Statistics </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Morris Bornstein </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.824 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The choice among methods of valuation rests not on any proof of the correctness of any one valuation over another - but on questions of logic, usefulness, and measurability." </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1348861" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1348861" target="_blank">Inventory Valuation and Farm Income</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1961 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Illinois Agricultural Economics </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> William A. Tinsley </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.817 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> It follows that any distributive value judgments which are expressed in money terms must be regarded as derived, in principle, from value judgments concerning the collection of goods which people ought to be able to command, and as acceptable only as long as prices are stable or remain within certain bounds. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2552136" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2552136" target="_blank">Redistribution: A Reply</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1968 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Economica </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Lucien Foldes </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.812 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> why the routine and undramatic problem of value has elicited the supreme efforts of the greatest theorists. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1815008" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1815008" target="_blank">The Influence of Events and Policies on Economic Theory</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1960 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The American Economic Review </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> George J. Stigler </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.806 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The extent to which the valuation implies consideration of appreciation, depreciation, and a distinction between capital and revenue expenditures depends on the underlying assumptions made about the nature of "value." </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://www.jstor.org/stable/10.2307/3112299" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://www.jstor.org/stable/10.2307/3112299" target="_blank">The Origin and Evolution of Nineteenth-Century Asset Accounting</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1966 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The Business History Review </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Richard P. Brief </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.803 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> In this sense " value" depended simply on a definition; or as Mrs. Robinson says: " As I see it, the conflict between Volume I [values] and Volume III [prices of production] is a conflict between mysticism and common sense. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2601601" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2601601" target="_blank">Ricardo and Marx</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1961 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Economica </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> G. S. L. Tucker </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.801 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> It has been suggested, however, that the answer to the question posed above depends upon the definition of value. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1829595" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1829595" target="_blank">The Historical Roots of the Concept of Human Capital</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1966 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Journal of Political Economy </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> B. F. Kiker </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.799 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> There is, of course, a widely held methodological position which asserts that the theory of value should explain which commodities carry positive prices and which do not, rather than merely explaining the relations among positive prices. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2525415" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2525415" target="_blank">Some Properties of the Closed Linear Model of Production</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1965 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> International Economic Review </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Sidney G. Winter, <suffix>Jr</suffix> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.797 </td>
  </tr>
</tbody>
</table><table class="table table-striped table-condensed" style="font-size: 12px; margin-left: auto; margin-right: auto;">

 </thead>
<tbody>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Contingent valuation is prone to a number of biases that are the subject of extensive investigation (e.g. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/S0921-8009(03)00122-8" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/S0921-8009(03)00122-8" target="_blank">The existence value of biodiversity in South Africa: How interest, experience, knowledge, income and perceived level of threat influence local willingness to pay</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 2003 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Ecological Economics </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Turpie J. </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.894 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Contingent valuation has been under fire in the literature for years, and some observers have concluded that the weighty catalog of mechanisms by which stated valuations fail to equate with true economic preference implies that contingent valuation should be discarded. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.joep.2008.07.007" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.joep.2008.07.007" target="_blank">On assuaging positive bias in environmental value elicitation</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 2009 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Journal of Economic Psychology </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Posavac S.S. </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.876 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> A review of the theoretical and empirical basis of contingent valuation is presented in Mitchell and Carson (1989), Arrow et al. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ecolecon.2008.09.002" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ecolecon.2008.09.002" target="_blank">An econometric analysis of willingness-to-pay for sustainable development: A case study of the Volčji Potok landscape area</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 2009 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Ecological Economics </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Verbič M. </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.871 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The attraction of contingent valuation is that it facilitates the construction of a market in which the researcher can observe an economic decision directly related with the good in question [3]. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.culher.2004.09.001" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.culher.2004.09.001" target="_blank">Valuing cultural heritage: The social benefits of restoring and old Arab tower</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 2005 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Journal of Cultural Heritage </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Del Saz Salazar S. </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.869 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> As per the earlier discussion on previously delineated threats to the validity of contingent valuation, the positivity bias is but one of many potential problems that undermine the ability of contingent valuation to accurately reflect economic preference. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.joep.2008.07.007" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.joep.2008.07.007" target="_blank">On assuaging positive bias in environmental value elicitation</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 2009 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Journal of Economic Psychology </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Posavac S.S. </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.869 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Importantly in the present context, contingent valuation has been shown to be subject to a number of different forms of bias (see Baron, 1997, for a review). </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/S0167-4870(02)00139-3" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/S0167-4870(02)00139-3" target="_blank">The effect of providing misleading cost information on the perceived value of government services</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 2003 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Journal of Economic Psychology </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Kemp S. </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.862 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> This assumption has increasingly been scrutinized and challenged in the literature (Bowles, 1998; Norton et al., 1998) and has led researchers to consider preference construction as way to improve valuation procedures (e.g. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ecolecon.2007.08.012" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ecolecon.2007.08.012" target="_blank">Assessing information provision and respondent involvement effects on preferences</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 2008 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Ecological Economics </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Shapansky B. </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.858 </td>

   <td style="text-align:left;"> It is also true that investmentin a community such as ours-cannot be increased by increased desire to save, except as a consequence of the reduction in the rate of interest.3 But all that follows from this is that the immediate effect of an increase in savings by some individuals must be an equivalent amount of " dis-saving " (or reduction of savings) by others. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2967650" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2967650" target="_blank">Money Wage Cuts in Relation to Unemployment: A Reply to Mr. Somers</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1939 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The Review of Economic Studies </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Nicholas Kaldor </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.835 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> (I may say in passing that this dictum has no relation to Mr. Keynes' famous theorem regarding the equilibrium between savings and investment, which I believe to be fruitful, for he uses savings in a different and abnormal sense, and discussion of his theorem would lead us on to quite different terrain.) </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2549128" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2549128" target="_blank">[Mr. Harrod and the Expansion of Credit]: Rejoinder to Mr. Robertson</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1934 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Economica </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> R. F. Harrod </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.830 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Tightly wedged in between the conception of saving as merely refraining from expenditure and its conception as the accumulating of income-yielding things which results from income exceeding consumption, is an intermediate conception in which it appears to be the saving up or accumulation of money rather than the saving up or accumulation of other goods acquired in exchange for money. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2223770" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2223770" target="_blank">Saving and Usury: A Symposium</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1932 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The Economic Journal </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Edwin Cannan, B. P. Adarkar, B. K. Sandwell, J. M. Keynes, K. E. Boulding </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.823 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> This conception of saving seems to be quite logical regarded from the individual point of view, and, indeed, for a given individual in the stated circumstances it does have a very real meaning: the greater the rate of saving by an individual the greater the rate at which he is providing for his future wants. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/3693801" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/3693801" target="_blank">Dynamic Theory of Saving and Investment</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1938 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Southern Economic Journal </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Montgomery D. Anderson </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.823 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The classical argument that interest is necessary to evoke saving wears a different aspect when we appreciate that saving does not necessarily mean investment. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2224010" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2224010" target="_blank">Interest and Usury in a New Light</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1931 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The Economic Journal </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> H. Somerville </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.819 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> I have in mind an act of saving without an act of investment; and I see no reason for supposing that such an event must be followed later on by an act of investment without an act of saving.-Note by J. M. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2223770" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2223770" target="_blank">Saving and Usury: A Symposium</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1932 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The Economic Journal </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Edwin Cannan, B. P. Adarkar, B. K. Sandwell, J. M. Keynes, K. E. Boulding </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.818 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> "5 The weight of his emphasis, however, lies on the fact that saving habits are rather marks of rationality than of hedonistic conduct.6 But even this does not explain why the amount of saving should be increased indefinitely with an increasing rate of interest. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1883923" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1883923" target="_blank">Wants and Activities in Marshall</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1931 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The Quarterly Journal of Economics </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Talcott Parsons </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.815 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> If saving continues willy-nilly by reason of a fixed psychological propensity without regard to price factors, and if the marginal efficiency of capital in a wealthy community falls below the minimum interest rate, then of necessity a part of the planned individual savings cannot find outlet in realized investment. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1824136" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1824136" target="_blank">Mr. Keynes on Underemployment Equilibrium</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1936 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Journal of Political Economy </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Alvin H. Hansen </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.813 </td>
  </tr>
</tbody>

  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Thus the conditions under which funds are available, the prices of investment goods, and the level of profits prevailing around the time of the decision would seem more significant than those at the time of the investment itself. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1812287" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1812287" target="_blank">Interest Rates and Manufacturers' Fixed Investment</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1957 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The American Economic Review </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Franz Gehrels, Suzanne Wiggins </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.809 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> To illustrate this point, consider the problem of investment decisions. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2295889" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2295889" target="_blank">On the Use of the Theory of Probability in Economics</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1952 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The Review of Economic Studies </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> R. S. Weckstein </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.797 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Somehow or other investment decisions have to be taken. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2662121" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2662121" target="_blank">Some Problems of Definition and Measurement of Capital</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1959 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Oxford Economic Papers </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Joan Robinson </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.797 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> However, a cumulative rise in the willingness to invest is not an automatic accompaniment of the increase in the quantity of money; it must result from some sort of additional assumption being introduced into the analysis. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2295737" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2295737" target="_blank">Some Cambridge Controversies in Monetary Theory</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1951 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The Review of Economic Studies </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Harry G. Johnson </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.792 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Even though such investment may meet the basic requirement of not being made merely to permit larger outputs, we would be guilty of overstating the case were we to deny all influence on expectations, long and short run, of prosperity and depression. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2226449" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2226449" target="_blank">Income Growth in Secular Stagnation and Inflation</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1953 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The Economic Journal </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> D. Hamberg </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.782 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Otherwise the phenomenon of investment would be incomprehensible. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1803060" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1803060" target="_blank">An Investigation Into the Dynamics of Investment</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1954 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The American Economic Review </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> R. W. Clower </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.773 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> As was stated earlier, it is impossible to generalize about the appropriate choice of investment priorities; the arguments made here are such that each case has to be examined on its own merits. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1827310" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1827310" target="_blank">Maintenance Costs and Economic Development</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1959 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Journal of Political Economy </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Rudolph C. Blitz </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.773 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> As has already been indicated, however, the general solution of the investment decision problem cannot rely solely on either present-value or rate-of-return reasoning. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1826746" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1826746" target="_blank">Formal Criteria for Investment Decisions</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1959 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Journal of Political Economy </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Martin J. Bailey </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.769 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> But since decisions to invest are subjective decisions, decisions which seem unique to the entrepreneurs who make them, not conditioned by any behavior-pattern such as lies behind the consumption function, but rather determined by expectations regarding the future, the degree to which Investment will change is likely to be unpredictable. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2226899" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2226899" target="_blank">A Graphical Analysis of the Foreign Trade Multiplier</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1952 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The Economic Journal </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Romney Robinson </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.768 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> But it is important to realize that investment of this kind can only be practiced so long as investment decisions of quite another kind are being taken at the same time. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2661972" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2661972" target="_blank">Imperfect Knowledge and Economic Efficiency</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1953 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Oxford Economic Papers </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> G. B. Richardson </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.768 </td>
  </tr>

  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> After all, investment is presumably dependent upon current profit expectations whereas those who argue that finance is a limiting factor tend to confuse two propositions: (1) that imperfections in the capital market will affect investment decisions; and (2) that current investment decisions should be affected by whether or not the sums sets aside for depreciation are equivalent to current replacement costs. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/139463" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/139463" target="_blank">Investment Control in Post-War Britain, 1945-1955</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1963 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The Canadian Journal of Economics and Political Science / Revue canadienne d'Economique et de Science politique </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Marvin E. Rozen </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.817 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> This explanation may be perfectly correct in some instances; in others, however, such "investment" may result from preferences xvell founded in the expectation of profit or, conversely, of security against a danger of depreciation that might face other forms of asset-holding [1, p. 398]. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1812467" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1812467" target="_blank">Capital Formation in Underdeveloped Countries</a> </td>

   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.809 </td>

   <td style="text-align:left;"> R. K. HARVEy The Ohio State University IT HAS LONG BEEN RECOGNIZED that the capital investment decision has two aspects: (1) it requires a commitment of wealth at one point in time in exchange for the opportunity to obtain income at one or more future points in time, and (2) the future income to be obtained is uncertain. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2325922" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2325922" target="_blank">A Portfolio Model of Capital Budgeting Under Risk</a> </td>

   <td style="text-align:left;"> R. K. Harvey </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.806 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> As we shall see, it is likely to be valid when there is no direct relation between the amount to be allowed for risk on, and the yield expected from, each project; or when the supply price of investment goods varies directly, and appreciably, with the level of investment. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1813844" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1813844" target="_blank">The Elasticity of the Marginal Efficiency Function</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1961 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The American Economic Review </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Lorie Tarshis </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.805 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> In spite of the fact that the desired stock of capital can never be isolated, it is nonetheless fruitful to view investment decisions as part of the broader framework in which assets are allocated as functions of their relative costs and yields. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2977199" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2977199" target="_blank">The Demand for Physical Capital: Application of a Wealth Model</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1963 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The Journal of Finance </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Frederick S. Hammer </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.797 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> This does not deny that risk may enter into the selection among investment alternatives or that profitability may have some influence on the scale of investment. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1883062" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1883062" target="_blank">Security and a Financial Theory of Investment</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1960 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The Quarterly Journal of Economics </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Myron J. Gordon </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.796 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> of capital construction, the requirement for a certain minimum limit of lucrativeness will play a role, as will the principle of returns from invested means. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/4379314" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/4379314" target="_blank">Improvement of the Organization and Planned Management of the National Economy</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1965 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Eastern European Economics </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Josef Lenart </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.789 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> A prediction of investment based on profits, liquidity, capacity utilization, and other variables that enter into a firm's ability and incentives to invest is genuinely different from one that rests in part on new orders or capital spending intentions. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1910885" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1910885" target="_blank">The Predictive Value of Surveys of Business Intentions</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1962 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The American Economic Review </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Arthur M. Okun </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.784 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> On the one hand investment is determined by profits and some acceleration variable. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1928344" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1928344" target="_blank">The Allocation of Corporate Profits between Dividends and Retained Earnings</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1967 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The Review of Economics and Statistics </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Stephen J. Turnovsky </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.784 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> An alternative theory of investment is that desired capital is proportional to profit. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1815529" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1815529" target="_blank">A Comparison of Alternative Theories of Corporate Investment Behavior</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1968 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The American Economic Review </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Dale W. Jorgenson, Calvin D. Siebert </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.783 </td>
  </tr>

</table><table class="table table-striped table-condensed" style="font-size: 12px; margin-left: auto; margin-right: auto;">
