 </thead>
<tbody>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> If we combine with our empirical observations on saving as an increasing function of income the assumption that most consumers most of the time in most situations maximize a typical preference function, we are led to the conclusion that the predominant motive for saving cannot be provision for a fixed future sum."' </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1926830" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1926830" target="_blank">The Relationship of Saving to the Rate of Interest, Real Income, and Expected Future Prices</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1961 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The Review of Economics and Statistics </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> D. V. T. Bear </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.810 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Savings are not thought of as a residual but as the result of a choice made by the individual; the individual weighs the desirability of saving against the desirability of further consumption. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1055365" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1055365" target="_blank">A Welfare Criterion</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1964 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Southern Economic Journal </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Ralph W. Pfouts </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.808 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The common sense of our claim rests largely on two propositions: (a) that the major purpose of saving is to provide a cushion against the major variations in income that typically occur during the life cycle of the household as well as against less systematic short-term fluctuations in income and needs; (b) that the provisions the household would wish to make, and can afford to make, for retirement as well as for emergencies, must be basically proportional, on the average, to its basic earning capacity, while the number of years over which these provisions can be made is largely independent of income levels.42 Both theories suggest individual behavior such that a person's consumption 43 will not vary greatly over his lifetime unless his tastes change radically. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://www.jstor.org/stable/10.2307/251249" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://www.jstor.org/stable/10.2307/251249" target="_blank">The Implications of Retirement Security Systems for Consumer Behavior</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1965 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The Journal of Risk and Insurance </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Walter Williams </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.799 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> To deny the possibility of such an outcome would be foolish; on the other hand, to hypothesize, without any explanation, exactly offsetting changes in consumption and liquidity preference proper and to ascribe the latter change to the ex ante savings function is an infelicitous mode of expression which is more likely to obfuscate than to clarify. </td>

<tbody>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Some decisions, as between given pairs of alternatives, may be assumed to be imposed. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1828886" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1828886" target="_blank">A Difficulty in the Concept of Social Welfare</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1950 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Journal of Political Economy </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Kenneth J. Arrow </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.829 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> or the criteria by which the choice is to be made. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1823547" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1823547" target="_blank">Regional Economic Reaction Paths</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1955 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The American Economic Review </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> F. T. Moore </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.818 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Decisions are not made in a vacuum. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://www.jstor.org/stable/10.2307/250196" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://www.jstor.org/stable/10.2307/250196" target="_blank">The Insurance Curriculum: Retrospect and Prospect</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1959 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The Journal of Insurance </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> O. D. Dickerson </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.809 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Decisions are taken by a multitude of individuals. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2226527" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2226527" target="_blank">Expectations and Equilibrium</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1952 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The Economic Journal </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> F. H. Hahn </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.807 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Further, it is clear that not all possible outcomes do, or should, exert equal influence on the decision-maker. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1812912" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1812912" target="_blank">Utility Theory, Decision Theory, and Profit Maximization</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1959 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The American Economic Review </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Joseph E. Haring, Gorman C. Smith </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.803 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> It goes beyond the problem of making meaningful and correct statements and tries to furnish criteria for choosing a course of action. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://www.jstor.org/stable/10.2307/3111860" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://www.jstor.org/stable/10.2307/3111860" target="_blank">Are Business History and Economic Theory Compatible?</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1955 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The Business History Review </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Donald E. Stout </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.802 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Decisionmaking requires the exercise of judgment. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1802809" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1802809" target="_blank">A Generalized Uncertainty Theory of Profit</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1950 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The American Economic Review </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> J. Fred Weston </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.800 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The decision-maker is being faced continually with such choices, and the outcome of each decision affects his entire future. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1825390" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1825390" target="_blank">Criteria for Choice Among Risky Ventures</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1959 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Journal of Political Economy </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Henry Allen Latané </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.800 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> We shall think in terms of an individual confronted with conflicting criteria applied to a set of alternatives. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1909827" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1909827" target="_blank">Intransitivity, Utility, and the Aggregation of Preference Patterns</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1954 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Econometrica </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Kenneth O. May </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.797 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The very basis or criterion for making a decision is harder to determine. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1927408" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1927408" target="_blank">Economics and Military Operations Research</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1958 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The Review of Economics and Statistics </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Charles Hitch </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.796 </td>
  </tr>

 </thead>
<tbody>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> For it seems possible that different assumptions lead to different conclusions so that this theory is not necessarily applicable to all cases in general. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://www.jstor.org/stable/10.2307/43217139" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://www.jstor.org/stable/10.2307/43217139" target="_blank">ON THE "AVERAGE PERIOD" OF J. R. HICKS</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1966 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Kyoto University Economic Review </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Sempei SAWA </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.827 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> This assumption raises two issues of interest. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1926734" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1926734" target="_blank">The Valuation of Risk Assets and the Selection of Risky Investments in Stock Portfolios and Capital Budgets: A Comment</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1969 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The Review of Economics and Statistics </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Charles W. Haley </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.801 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> However, some points of reasoning may be noted. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/133829" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/133829" target="_blank">The Carter Commission Report</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1968 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The Canadian Journal of Economics / Revue canadienne d'Economique </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> R. A. Musgrave </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.788 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Aside from this, however, the problem of the degree of realism of assumptions arises in another and crucial way. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/3484736" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/3484736" target="_blank">The Chicago School on Economic Methodology and Monopolistic Competition</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1963 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The American Journal of Economics and Sociology </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Louis A. Dow, Lewis M. Abernathy </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.787 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> One may also question the criterion on the basis of principle quite apart from practical considerations. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1235739" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1235739" target="_blank">Water Resources Development: A Review of the New Federal Evaluation Procedures</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1963 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Journal of Farm Economics </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Emery Castle, Maurice Kelso, Delworth Gardner </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.784 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> These assumptions may or may not be satisfied in actual situations. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2550514" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2550514" target="_blank">On External Diseconomies and the Government-Assisted Invisible Hand</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1964 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Economica </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Stanislaw Wellisz </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.773 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> However, these valuable suggestions are restricted by their own methods, because the more rigid the analysis being tried the broader must be the assumptions </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://www.jstor.org/stable/10.2307/43295426" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://www.jstor.org/stable/10.2307/43295426" target="_blank">PROGRESS IN THE EMPIRICAL ANALYSIS OF CONSUMPTION FUNCTION IN JAPAN</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1964 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Hitotsubashi Journal of Economics </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Toshiyuki Mizoguchi </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.773 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> What is required, therefore, is a theoretical framework which can clarify the assumptions and conditions under which such alternative possibilities are valid. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2552028" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2552028" target="_blank">The Structure of Interest Rates and Recent British Experience: A Comment</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1967 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Economica </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> A. Buse </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.772 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Yet even this generalization must be qualified in light of the following considerations. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/3484775" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/3484775" target="_blank">Economic vs. Protective Values in Urban Land Use Change</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1960 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The American Journal of Economics and Sociology </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Sidney Willhelm, Gideon Sjoberg </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.770 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Consideration of a hypothetical development may clarify the problems. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/724787" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/724787" target="_blank">Promises Respecting the Use of Land</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1965 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The Journal of Law &amp; Economics </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Allison Dunham </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.768 </td>
  </tr>
</tbody>
</table><table class="table table-striped table-condensed" style="font-size: 12px; margin-left: auto; margin-right: auto;">
 <thead>
  <tr>
   <th style="text-align:left;"> Sentence </th>
   <th style="text-align:left;"> Title </th>

   <th style="text-align:right;"> Similarity to HDSBSCAN Centroid </th>
  </tr>
 </thead>
<tbody>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Decisions are often based on something else. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1236057" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1236057" target="_blank">Farm Fundamentalism: Its Future</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1962 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Journal of Farm Economics </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Don F. Hadwiger </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.857 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Nonetheless, there are considerations which, in certain instances, enable one to make a logical selection. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1816270" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1816270" target="_blank">Substitution, Technical Progress, and Returns to Scale</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1965 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The American Economic Review </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> C. E. Ferguson </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.854 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Decisions must be made; but to provide the basis for informed choice the consequences of pursuing alternative lines of action must be more clearly set forth than has been customary in the past. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/3144740" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/3144740" target="_blank">Resource Management and Conservation; The Approach of the Brandywine Valley Association</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1964 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Land Economics </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> George Macinko </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.825 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> This brings us to the question of the interdependence of decisions. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://www.jstor.org/stable/10.2307/3438580" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://www.jstor.org/stable/10.2307/3438580" target="_blank">The Locational Decision from the Point of View of the Individual Company</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1964 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Ekonomisk Tidskrift </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Albert Danielsson </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.816 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> It involves a host of decisions. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2552766" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2552766" target="_blank">"Fair Comparison": The Case of the United States White-Collar Civil Service</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1965 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Economica </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> H. M. Douty </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.810 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The decision is less by intuition and more by reasoned judgment. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://www.jstor.org/stable/10.2307/44013323" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://www.jstor.org/stable/10.2307/44013323" target="_blank">DISCUSSION: THE RANGE LIVESTOCK INDUSTRY IN A DYNAMIC INTER-USE ENVIRONMENT</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1962 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Proceedings of the Annual Meeting (Western Farm Economics Association) </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Roland C. Bevan </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.808 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> These differences in individuals, along with individual variations in decision-making skill, further condition the decision or "correct choice." </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1235589" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1235589" target="_blank">Teaching Managers How to Improve Their Decision-Making Processes</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1961 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Journal of Farm Economics </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Stephen J. Brannen </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.805 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> This process involves inquiry, reflective thinking, and some attempt to anticipate the consequences of alternatives.4 Decisions based on such processes will be called deliberate choices or decisions in this paper. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1055475" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1055475" target="_blank">The Deliberateness of Economic Choices</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1962 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Southern Economic Journal </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Eldon D. Smith </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.800 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> These involve decisions of choice, especially in the long run. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1235587" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1235587" target="_blank">The Management Resource and Agricultural Marketing</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1961 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Journal of Farm Economics </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Charles E. French </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.799 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> actual circumstances of decision making. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1055783" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1055783" target="_blank">A Behavioral Approach to the Business Enterprise</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1960 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Southern Economic Journal </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Harold L. Johnson </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.798 </td>
  </tr>
</tbody>
</table><table class="table table-striped table-condensed" style="font-size: 12px; margin-left: auto; margin-right: auto;">
 <thead>
  <tr>
   <th style="text-align:left;"> Sentence </th>
   <th style="text-align:left;"> Title </th>
   <th style="text-align:right;"> Year </th>
   <th style="text-align:left;"> Journal </th>
   <th style="text-align:left;"> Authors </th>
   <th style="text-align:right;"> Similarity to HDSBSCAN Centroid </th>
  </tr>
 </thead>
<tbody>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> These considerations are basically political in nature. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/3144582" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/3144582" target="_blank">Can People Be Trusted with Natural Resources?</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1962 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Land Economics </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> J. W. Milliman </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.802 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Certain policy conclusions may then be drawn. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2228672" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2228672" target="_blank">Production Functions, Market Imperfections and Economic Development</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1962 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The Economic Journal </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Gustav Ranis </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.795 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Decisions will be made not so much on economic as on other grounds. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1348972" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1348972" target="_blank">The Emerging Structure of U.S. Agriculture: Traditional or Industrial?</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1964 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Illinois Agricultural Economics </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Harold F. Breimyer </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.788 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> It is inevitable, too, that political considerations will sometimes play a part in policy decisions. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1910873" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1910873" target="_blank">The Postwar Business Cycle in Western Europe</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1962 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The American Economic Review </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Milton Gilbert </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.781 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Further, this argument has many policy implications. </td>

   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2296678" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2296678" target="_blank">On the Theory of "Second Best"</a> </td>

  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Rather it is that in the political and administrative setting in which policy decisions are made, general humanitarian considerations and rather vague and remote strategic considerations tend to be lost sight of in the inidst of the wide array of more direct and compelling demands arising mainly from domestic residents with votes. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/133700" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/133700" target="_blank">Canada's Economic Policies toward the Less Developed Countries</a> </td>

Insurer Risk Capacity and Financial Ratings: The Use of Financial Ratings of Insurance Reporting Services to Avoid Potentially Insolvent or Otherwise Delinquent Insurers</a> </td>

  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Moreover, we should recognize that many questionable policies or choices are </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1814561" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1814561" target="_blank">The Unseen Hand in Government</a> </td>

   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.767 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> In this way, conclusions for policy would have some relevance to the actual situation. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/724810" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/724810" target="_blank">The Problem of Social Cost</a> </td>

  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> But to point to the unrealism of any or all of these assumptions is not enough; their modification should make it possible to offer a more satisfactory explana? </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/29794042" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/29794042" target="_blank">Ownership and Distribution of Land</a> </td>

   <td style="text-align:left;"> There are several reasons for exploring the consequences of this assumption. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2525886" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2525886" target="_blank">Asymptotic Theory and Large Models</a> </td>

   <td style="text-align:left;"> International Economic Review </td>

   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.779 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The above conclusion can be queried on two different grounds. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2098311" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2098311" target="_blank">Utility and Profit Maximization by an Owner-Manager: Towards a General Analysis</a> </td>

   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.777 </td>

   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2230953" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2230953" target="_blank">Effects of the Kennedy Round Tariff Concessions on the Exports of Developing Countries</a> </td>

   <td style="text-align:left;"> Several alternative assumptions are available. </td>

   <td style="text-align:left;"> However there are, as we saw in the first part of this paper, many plausible assumptions which could be retained. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/40724183" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/40724183" target="_blank">European Policy Coordination: An Evaluation</a> </td>

   <td style="text-align:left;"> This leads to two alternative sets of assumptions. </td>

  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> We have examined in this paper how the conclusion is revised if the assumption is removed. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://www.jstor.org/stable/10.2307/43295720" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://www.jstor.org/stable/10.2307/43295720" target="_blank">ON THE INTERTEMPORAL NON-NEUTRALITY OF TAXES ON LAND: A DYNAMIC MARKET CLEARING MODEL</a> </td>

  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> In a theoretical case these assumptions should not be arbitrary in any way' (p. 344). </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://www.jstor.org/stable/10.2307/43315381" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://www.jstor.org/stable/10.2307/43315381" target="_blank">AGONISING OVER EQUILIBRIUM: HAYEK AND LINDAHL</a> </td>

   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.813 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Our main interest is to see whether there are some sets of conditions under which the conclusions derived from the simple version continue to hold in the general version. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1058373" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1058373" target="_blank">A Model of Real National Price Levels</a> </td>

   <td style="text-align:left;"> Southern Economic Journal </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Christopher K. Clague </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.812 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> This brief summary, how ever, does not do justice to the rich variety of problems and details of the theory, nor to the necessity of precise assumptions; there also exist attempts in the literature at making less restrictive assumptions, e.g. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/23596679" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/23596679" target="_blank">Economic arguments on the sufficiency of natural resources</a> </td>

   <td style="text-align:left;"> Hans Aage </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.808 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Problems associated with types of assumptions, fragility of inferences, and general applications are being recognized and admitted.' </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/0261-5606(84)90034-2" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/0261-5606(84)90034-2" target="_blank">External currency market data: An application from BIS series</a> </td>

   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.805 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> 2 for the limitations of such an assumption). </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1816460" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1816460" target="_blank">The Logic of Vertical Restraints</a> </td>

  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> It would be interesting to determine the extent to which our specific assumptions lead to the results of this paper. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/S0022-1996(97)00041-X" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/S0022-1996(97)00041-X" target="_blank">Country-bashing tariffs: do bilateral trade deficits matter?</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1998 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Journal of International Economics </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Cox W. </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.847 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> This section explores the implications of some generalizations of the model. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/S0047-2727(97)00066-2" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/S0047-2727(97)00066-2" target="_blank">School heterogeneity, human capital accumulation, and standards</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1998 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Journal of Public Economics </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Somanathan R. </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.820 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The implications of this assumption have been extensively analyzed by Goodhart and Huang (1995) and Svensson (1997a, b), among others. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/S0304-3932(98)00055-5" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/S0304-3932(98)00055-5" target="_blank">Optimal monetary policy rules in a rational expectations model of the Phillips curve</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1999 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Journal of Monetary Economics </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Clark P.B. </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.817 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> We shall discuss the limita tions of these assumptions below, but shall concentrate for the moment on the theory's strengths. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/24700539" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/24700539" target="_blank">Decentralizing Public Services : what can we learn from the Theory of the Firm? / Décentralisation des services publics : que nous enseigne la théorie de la firme?</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1996 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Revue d'économie politique </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Jacques Crémer, Antonio Estache, Paul Seabright </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.817 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> One of the by-products of our model is a theoretical argument in support of these empirical results. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/S0378-4266(98)00123-X" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/S0378-4266(98)00123-X" target="_blank">A theory of banking structure</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1999 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Journal of Banking and Finance </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Das S. </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.809 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Most such implications can only be derived if we make further assumptions; I shall try to select these further auxiliary assumptions by the criterion of empirical realism. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/40752851" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/40752851" target="_blank">Antitrust and the Division of Labor-Comment</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1991 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Journal of Institutional and Theoretical Economics (JITE) / Zeitschrift für die gesamte Staatswissenschaft </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Carl-Christian von Weizsäcker </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.807 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Various rationalizations of similar assumptions have been proposed by ), , and others. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/0304-3932(94)90050-7" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/0304-3932(94)90050-7" target="_blank">Flexibility, investment, and growth</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1994 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Journal of Monetary Economics </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Bertola G. </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.805 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> For the sake of argument this paper pursued the implications of two strong, but straightforward assumptions. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/S0047-2727(97)00043-1" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/S0047-2727(97)00043-1" target="_blank">The selection principle and market failure in systems competition</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1997 </td>

The cluster gathers 1897 sentences from our corpus. It represents 0.57% of all the sentences selected over the whole period.

The community exists from 1920 to 1979.

   <td style="text-align:left;"> Paul Einzig </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.765 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> And, whether we assume a Crusoe whose own labors are the direct source of the goods he consumes, or take the familiar case of a society in which division of labor and monetary incomes prevail, we shall find that successive hours of labor involve, generally speaking, increasing irksomeness, while the additional wants they make it possible to gratify are of decreasing urgency. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1883503" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1883503" target="_blank">Utility Curves, Total Utility, and Consumer's Surplus</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1927 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The Quarterly Journal of Economics </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Harry E. Miller </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.762 </td>
  </tr>
</tbody>
</table><table class="table table-striped table-condensed" style="font-size: 12px; margin-left: auto; margin-right: auto;">
 <thead>
  <tr>
   <th style="text-align:left;"> Sentence </th>
   <th style="text-align:left;"> Title </th>
   <th style="text-align:right;"> Year </th>
   <th style="text-align:left;"> Journal </th>
   <th style="text-align:left;"> Authors </th>
   <th style="text-align:right;"> Similarity to HDSBSCAN Centroid </th>
  </tr>
 </thead>
<tbody>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> But too often the economic theory held by the business man bears little relation to his own practices-it is only if the practices of himself and of others like him were different from what they are that their theories could be correct. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2223697" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2223697" target="_blank">The Relation of Home Investment to Unemployment</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1931 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The Economic Journal </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> R. F. Kahn </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.783 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> It is, of course, undeniable that most of the commercial activity in present-day society is carried on as profit-making activity, but the profit-making motive is by no means confined to commercial activity. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://www.jstor.org/stable/10.2307/43216720" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://www.jstor.org/stable/10.2307/43216720" target="_blank">THE ESSENTIAL FUNCTION OF COMMERCE AND COMMERCIAL ECONOMICS; AN ESSAY ON THE OBJECTS OF STUDY IN COMMERCIAL BUSINESS SCIENCE AND COMMERCIAL ECONOMICS</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1930 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Kyoto University Economic Review </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> K. Taniguchi </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.759 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> For example, where economic decisions depend on individual men whose "profits" are distinct from the net income of the enterprise, maximization of individual gain may frequently take precedence over maximization of the revenue of the firm. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1891096" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1891096" target="_blank">Stockholdings of Officers and Directors in American Industrial Corporations</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1936 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The Quarterly Journal of Economics </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> R. A. Gordon </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.758 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Whatever be the points of debate among economic theorists about the origin of profits, certain it is that, for individual enterprise, the maintenance of net earnings depends at least partly upon the ability of the management to displace the element of pure chance in every phase of the business. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1230356" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1230356" target="_blank">The Commercial Application of Forecasting Methods</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1930 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Journal of Farm Economics </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Donald R. G. Cowan </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.755 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> While the actions of the business man may be based in general on purely economic considerations, there is often an indeterminate zone in which his sense of public obligation and his respect for public opinion will be effective. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/137184" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/137184" target="_blank">Report of the Royal Commission on the Textile Industry</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1939 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The Canadian Journal of Economics and Political Science / Revue canadienne d'Economique et de Science politique </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> H. R. Kemp </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.755 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The decisions of business men are not wholly rational, nor are they based upon exact knowledge or upon foreknowledge. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1806430" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1806430" target="_blank">The Aims of Unemployment Insurance with Especial Reference to the Wisconsin Act</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1933 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The American Economic Review </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Walter A. Morton </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.755 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> For only a person familiar with the method of calculation and reasoning which is likely to guide unconsciously the actions of business men in their search for maximum profit can hope to obtain any valid results from a realistic study of problems of this character. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1883687" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1883687" target="_blank">Theoretical Remarks on Price Policy Hotelling's Case with Variations</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1933 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The Quarterly Journal of Economics </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> F. Zeuthen </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.751 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> These explanations assume that the business man will not behave rationally, that his behavior does not follow the same rules which it is supposed to follow in the theoretical system of economics. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1885790" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1885790" target="_blank">Equilibrium Economics and Business-Cycle Theory</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1930 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The Quarterly Journal of Economics </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Simon Kuznets </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.748 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> This notion, which is perhaps more commonly held among German business leaders than any other, is in keeping with classical theory in that it holds profits to be a fair index of efficiency ("rationality") of a business, and at the same time a fit measure of the worth of the enterprise to the community. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1883398" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1883398" target="_blank">The Meaning of Rationalization: An Analysis of the Literature</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1932 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The Quarterly Journal of Economics </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Robert A. Brady </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.735 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> For without too great inaccuracy entrepreneurs might be said to aim at maximising their money profits which seemed a definite enough criterion to decide their policies. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/41793308" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/41793308" target="_blank">Expectation and Rational Conduct</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1937 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Zeitschrift für Nationalökonomie / Journal of Economics </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> T. W. Hutchison </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.734 </td>
  </tr>
</tbody>
</table><table class="table table-striped table-condensed" style="font-size: 12px; margin-left: auto; margin-right: auto;">
 <thead>
  <tr>
   <th style="text-align:left;"> Sentence </th>
   <th style="text-align:left;"> Title </th>
   <th style="text-align:right;"> Year </th>
   <th style="text-align:left;"> Journal </th>
   <th style="text-align:left;"> Authors </th>
   <th style="text-align:right;"> Similarity to HDSBSCAN Centroid </th>
  </tr>
 </thead>
<tbody>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> This leads one to question whether or not profit maximization really is the motivating or overriding influence. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1235024" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1235024" target="_blank">Farmers' Decisions in the Use of Fertilizer</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1958 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Journal of Farm Economics </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Moyle S. Williams </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.820 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Profit maximization is not the same thing as rationality because other ends also may be pursued in a rational way. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1884444" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1884444" target="_blank">Recent Developments in Economics</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1954 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The Quarterly Journal of Economics </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> F. Zeuthen </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.808 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> But the ideal of "reasonable" or "just" profit is often at the root of the decision. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://www.jstor.org/stable/10.2307/23006581" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://www.jstor.org/stable/10.2307/23006581" target="_blank">THE SOCIAL SETTING OF GROWTH</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1959 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The Punjab University Economist </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> SIDNEY C. SUFRIN </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.787 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> To this end he must pursue profit, but he must avoid action which, though profitable in the present, will damage his future position....2 This seems to me a fair statement of the businessman's approach to the profit-maximizing process. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2662005" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2662005" target="_blank">Price Formation in Manufacturing Industry and Excess Capacity</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1955 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Oxford Economic Papers </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> H. R. Edwards </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.778 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Now it seems to methat the traditional attitude, which consists of distinguishing in the profits of businessmen a managerial salary, a monopoly rent, etc., while entirely legitimate, is insufficient. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1813587" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1813587" target="_blank">The Construction of a New Theory of Profit</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1951 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The American Economic Review </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Jean Marchal </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.774 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> It is not helpful to dismiss this lack of vision, of confidence, or of experimenting ambition as an example of a failure to attempt to maximize profits, for they are intimately connected with the nature of managerial ability itself and must be reckoned as a limitation on the supply of specific types of productive services. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1823582" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1823582" target="_blank">Limits to the Growth and Size of Firms</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1955 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The American Economic Review </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Edith Penrose </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.772 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> And what, indeed, are we to say of traditional theory when we find -as I am very sure we would find-that management in the giant corporation in fact does recognize and adopt profit for the enterprise as its guide for action, and does in fact pursue profit for the enterprise with its full skill and as vigorously as though its employment and its own compensation were directly at stake? </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2114069" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2114069" target="_blank">Development of Large-Scale Organization: The Soviet Steel Industry: Economic Implications</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1952 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The Journal of Economic History </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Ben W. Lewis </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.772 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> For instance, maximization of profits is not always the primary goal. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/40434299" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/40434299" target="_blank">Towards a Synthesis of Theory and Policy in Latin American Developmental Economics: The Dynamics of the Economic Policy Revolution in the Transformation of the Periphery</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1958 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Weltwirtschaftliches Archiv </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Pedro C. M. Teichert </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.772 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> It may be argued that all this amounts to no more than long-run profit maximization, and thus that management in the modern corporation does no more than business management has always tried to do, allowing for changed circumstances. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1831602" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1831602" target="_blank">The Social Significance of the Modern Corporation</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1957 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The American Economic Review </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Carl Kaysen </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.768 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> On the assumption that the businessman's primary forte should be decision-making rather than theory-construction, and that skill in making decisions comes from practice, emphasis is placed on the case situation as such rather than on compiling theories from a number of cases. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://www.jstor.org/stable/10.2307/250782" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://www.jstor.org/stable/10.2307/250782" target="_blank">The Case Method of Instruction in Insurance</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1958 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The Journal of Insurance </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Davis T. Ratcliffe </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.764 </td>
  </tr>
</tbody>
</table><table class="table table-striped table-condensed" style="font-size: 12px; margin-left: auto; margin-right: auto;">
 <thead>
  <tr>
   <th style="text-align:left;"> Sentence </th>
   <th style="text-align:left;"> Title </th>
   <th style="text-align:right;"> Year </th>
   <th style="text-align:left;"> Journal </th>
   <th style="text-align:left;"> Authors </th>
   <th style="text-align:right;"> Similarity to HDSBSCAN Centroid </th>
  </tr>
 </thead>
<tbody>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The managerial motives under discussion are not fully consistent with profits maximization. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1879325" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1879325" target="_blank">The Motives of Managers, Environmental Restraints, and the Theory of Managerial Enterprise</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1964 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The Quarterly Journal of Economics </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> William L. Baldwin </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.819 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Even if profits maximization is the most accurate single motivational assumption we can make in dealing with the modern corporation, it may be virtually useless as a basis for determination of a single most rational solution to many problems. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1879325" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1879325" target="_blank">The Motives of Managers, Environmental Restraints, and the Theory of Managerial Enterprise</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1964 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The Quarterly Journal of Economics </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> William L. Baldwin </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.796 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Pursuit of profit does not mean that management spends much of its time contemplating profit as such but that its time is spent on decisions regarding the planning, providing, pricing, and selling of products, which govern revenue, and on the organizing, equipping, and carrying on of production, together with the purchase of labor, supplies, and other requirements, which govern costs. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1880509" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1880509" target="_blank">Corporate Control and Capitalism</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1965 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The Quarterly Journal of Economics </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Shorey Peterson </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.796 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Therefore, even if we agreed with traditional theory that the owners of a firm wish to maximize profits (and we do agree in the case of owner-managed firms), we would contend that the difference between owner motivation and managerial motivation will cause systematic deviations from profit-maximizing behavior as long as the firm is large enough so that the owners themselves cannot supervise all facets of its activities. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1829037" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1829037" target="_blank">A Theory of Large Managerial Firms</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1965 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Journal of Political Economy </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> R. Joseph Monsen, <suffix>Jr.</suffix>, Anthony Downs </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.792 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> They can choose between profit maximization and other goals. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/41796158" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/41796158" target="_blank">The Changing Moral Temper of Economic Thought</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1961 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Zeitschrift für Nationalökonomie / Journal of Economics </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Walter A. Weißkopf </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.773 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Although it is not strong enough to provide a discrimination between the utilityand profits-maximizing theories, it does suggest that either firms are operated as indicated by the managerial model or, if "actual" profits are maximized, that reported profits are reduced by absorbing some fraction of actual profits in executive salaries and possibly in perquisites of a variety of sorts. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1812047" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1812047" target="_blank">Managerial Discretion and Business Behavior</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1963 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The American Economic Review </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Oliver E. Williamson </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.771 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> If managers do not attempt to maximise profits, however, then some other guiding principle of entrepreneurial behaviour must be posited before a unique supply schedule can be derived. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2228715" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2228715" target="_blank">More on the Aggregate Supply Function</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1962 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The Economic Journal </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Paul Davidson </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.770 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Then rational behavior would dictate that the firm's profits should be maximized and when the returns are in the owners and managers should sit down together and bargain for the spoils. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/40722874" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/40722874" target="_blank">A Neo-Classical Foundation for a Theory of Manager-Controlled Firms</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1969 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Recherches Économiques de Louvain / Louvain Economic Review </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> John R. Mc Kean, Robert Haney Scott </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.769 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The decisions of the firm thus are a compound of interest in profits and the impact of constraints on enterprise. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1055783" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1055783" target="_blank">A Behavioral Approach to the Business Enterprise</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1960 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Southern Economic Journal </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Harold L. Johnson </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.768 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> restraint in profit-seeking, may merely be estimates of the most that can safely be sought over the long term, or they may just be handy rules-of-thumb by which company goals can be communicated operationally throughout the complex hierarchy of a great firm, perhaps as part of what is now quaintly called profit-planning. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1880509" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1880509" target="_blank">Corporate Control and Capitalism</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1965 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The Quarterly Journal of Economics </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Shorey Peterson </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.765 </td>
  </tr>
</tbody>

  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Thus, in the case when profit maximization is assumed to be the goal of the firm, it is possible to bridge the gap between the behavioral and conventional theories and to put behavioral content into the profit maximization hypothesis by postulating a set of decision rules under which the firm operates. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/3439287" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/3439287" target="_blank">The Measurement of Efficiency in Production: An Application to Swedish Manufacturing Industries 1968</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1972 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The Swedish Journal of Economics </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Bo Carlsson </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.809 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> One may then ask whether there is any reason to believe that managers (and in particular managers of lzrge firms) wish to maximize something else than the profits of the firm. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/0014-2921(76)90058-1" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/0014-2921(76)90058-1" target="_blank">Profit rates and structural variables in French manufacturing industries</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1976 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> European Economic Review </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Jenny F. </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.799 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Although profits are an important factor, in many cases it is not the only one or necessarily the overriding one. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://www.jstor.org/stable/10.2307/41258257" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://www.jstor.org/stable/10.2307/41258257" target="_blank">The Effects of Tax Holiday on Investment Decisions: An Empirical Analysis</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1974 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The Pakistan Development Review </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Sharouh M. Sharif, B. A. Azhar </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.796 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Thus, it has been claimed that "although the firm's interest centres on its profitability, this cannot be the only criterion in judging the work of the directors and the activities of the firm".' </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2551998" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2551998" target="_blank">The Economic Reform in Hungary</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1970 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Economica </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Bela Balassa </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.790 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> "A realistic analysis", it has been said of modern business, "must avoid the presumption of a profit motive, let alone a maximization of profit motive. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2594761" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2594761" target="_blank">Gentlemen and Players</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1973 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The Economic History Review </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> D. C. Coleman </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.790 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> On the other hand, and even more: profit-maximizing behaviour can never be more than a general tendency even in an economic mechanism most perfectly stimulating it; therefore, it can never be expected in a concrete case that the enterprise will by all means decide to choose the most profitable version. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/40728641" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/40728641" target="_blank">SOME GENERAL PROBLEMS OF THE HUNGARIAN INVESTMENT SYSTEM</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1978 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Acta Oeconomica </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> K. A. SOÓS </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.789 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> First, it has been hypothesized that managers treat as distinct decisions the maximization of "true" profits and the maximization of managerial utility (hereafter referred to as the "severable" decision model). </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1828333" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1828333" target="_blank">Managerial Objectives in Regulated Industries: Expense-Preference Behavior in Banking</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1977 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Journal of Political Economy </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Franklin R. Edwards </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.785 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The output which maximizes profit will not always be the output preferred by the authorities. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1056854" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1056854" target="_blank">Bonus Formulae and Soviet Managerial Performance</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1970 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Southern Economic Journal </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Wayne A. Leeman </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.784 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The general consequence is that the managers are able to pursue their own goals within certain limits and, thus, tend to direct the firm away from the profit maximizing position that represents the owners' desideratum.12 This basic interpretation can be extended in various ways and, indeed, many new models have been developed to account for different possible business goals. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2721541" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2721541" target="_blank">Property Rights and Economic Theory: A Survey of Recent Literature</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1972 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Journal of Economic Literature </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Eirik G. Furubotn, Svetozar Pejovich </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.784 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The point, then, is that the profit maximizing behavior may no longer be a "plausible" assumption of behavior. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/40749513" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/40749513" target="_blank">An Algorithm for Revenue Maximization Subject to a Profit Constraint</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1972 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Zeitschrift für die gesamte Staatswissenschaft / Journal of Institutional and Theoretical Economics </td>

   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.858 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Thus expectations are assumed to be "rational," albeit in a limited sense. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1992386" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/1992386" target="_blank">More on the Speed of Adjustment in Inventory Models</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1986 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Journal of Money, Credit and Banking </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Alan S. Blinder </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.857 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> It requires, however, that expectations are formed rationally, as we have maintained for the 'true' model (11) (12) and . </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/0304-4076(86)90033-3" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/0304-4076(86)90033-3" target="_blank">A comparison of alternative methods for the estimation of dynamic factor demand models under non-static expectations</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1986 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Journal of Econometrics </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Prucha I. </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.856 </td>
  </tr>
</tbody>
</table><table class="table table-striped table-condensed" style="font-size: 12px; margin-left: auto; margin-right: auto;">

 </thead>
<tbody>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> However, the qualitative conclusion that more heterogeneity of beliefs leads to greater deviations of prices from traders' fundamental valuations would be robust.2 The pricing scheme p* characterized in Theorem 2 is not the only one satisfying equation (7): there exists in addition a continuum of pricing schemes with a "Ponzi scheme" added on top of the "minimal pricing scheme" [Harrison and Kreps 1978]. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2946709" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/2946709" target="_blank">Speculative Investor Behavior and Learning</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1996 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The Quarterly Journal of Economics </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Stephen Morris </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.809 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Finally, it is shown that the investors' beliefs supporting the equilibrium are not contradicted by the Intuitive Criterion. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/S1386-4181(98)00013-5" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/S1386-4181(98)00013-5" target="_blank">Reputation and performance fee effects on portfolio choice by investment advisers</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1999 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Journal of Financial Markets </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Huddart S. </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.806 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> First, note that there exists a unique market equilibrium in which: (1) investors choose their demand for securities to maximize their utility based on their available information and (common) conjectures about the (linear) relations between prices and aggregate information available at times 1 and 2; (2) markets clear at times 1 and 2; and (3) investors’ price conjectures are self-fulfilled. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/S0165-4101(98)00013-5" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/S0165-4101(98)00013-5" target="_blank">Pre-announcement and event-period private information</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1997 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Journal of Accounting and Economics </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Kim O. </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.799 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Hence, the Intuitive Criterion does not rule out any investor beliefs, including those which support the equilibrium, namely that deviators are uninformed.□ </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/S1386-4181(98)00013-5" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/S1386-4181(98)00013-5" target="_blank">Reputation and performance fee effects on portfolio choice by investment advisers</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1999 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Journal of Financial Markets </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Huddart S. </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.791 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> In fact, our purpose is precisely to show that the initial and final security prices may depend on beliefs about beliefs even when there is no asymmetric information about anything else that affects prices. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/S1386-4181(97)00006-2" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/S1386-4181(97)00006-2" target="_blank">Endogenous sunspots, pseudo-bubbles, and beliefs about beliefs</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1998 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Journal of Financial Markets </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Kraus A. </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.790 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> It is now generally accepted that this type of trading depends on market incompleteness , , , ]. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/0167-2681(92)90003-T" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/0167-2681(92)90003-T" target="_blank">Non-Walrasian equilibria with speculation</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1992 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Journal of Economic Behavior and Organization </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Benninga S. </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.788 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Finally, it must be shown that the beliefs of investors in the event an adviser deviates from the equilibrium, namely that the deviator is uninformed, survive the Intuitive Criterion. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/S1386-4181(98)00013-5" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/S1386-4181(98)00013-5" target="_blank">Reputation and performance fee effects on portfolio choice by investment advisers</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1999 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Journal of Financial Markets </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Huddart S. </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.784 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> For the Intuitive Criterion to restrict off-equilibrium investors' beliefs, it must be that some type, either informed or uninformed, prefers the equilibrium payoff to the best payoff (over all possible reallocation choices by investors) that could be earned by a deviation, namely allocating all funds to the deviator in the second period. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/S1386-4181(98)00013-5" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/S1386-4181(98)00013-5" target="_blank">Reputation and performance fee effects on portfolio choice by investment advisers</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1999 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Journal of Financial Markets </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Huddart S. </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.783 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Making these conjectures is not an extraneous exercise for investors: each investor must reflect some belief about the future price P 1 in her portfolio choice and each investor realizes that the future price depends on the portfolio choices of other investors which are based on their beliefs. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/S1386-4181(97)00006-2" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/S1386-4181(97)00006-2" target="_blank">Endogenous sunspots, pseudo-bubbles, and beliefs about beliefs</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1998 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Journal of Financial Markets </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Kraus A. </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.783 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> 8, 9) argue that in a non-fully revealing equilibrium even informed investors “may find it less costly to infer valuations, albeit imperfectly, from changes in market prices than to incur the direct costs of processing information” and that errors in such inferences can become contagious. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/S0378-4266(98)00023-5" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/S0378-4266(98)00023-5" target="_blank">US day-of-the-week effects and asymmetric responses to macroeconomic news</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1998 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Journal of Banking and Finance </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Chang E.C. </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.783 </td>
  </tr>
</tbody>
</table><table class="table table-striped table-condensed" style="font-size: 12px; margin-left: auto; margin-right: auto;">
