 </thead>
<tbody>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> We would like to comment on the form of the rational expectations hypotheses we can handle in this framework. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/S0304-4076(99)00004-4" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/S0304-4076(99)00004-4" target="_blank">Testing exact rational expectations in cointegrated vector autoregressive models</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1999 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Journal of Econometrics </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Johansen S. </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.891 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Rational expectations are said to exist when agents do not make systematic errors in forecasting the future (see , for the "weak version" of the hypothesis) or when agents form expectations on the basis of complete knowledge of the "model of the economy" or its "reduced form" mechanics, (for the "strong version" of the hypothesis, see . </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://doi.org/10.1108/01443589210015926" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://doi.org/10.1108/01443589210015926" target="_blank">Towards a Neoclassical Theory of Institutional Failure</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1992 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Journal of Economic Studies </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Pitelis C. </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.877 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Expectations are assumed to be rational, conditioned on current information. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/135582" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/135582" target="_blank">Interest Parity, Cointegration, and the Term Structure in Canada and the United States</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1991 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The Canadian Journal of Economics / Revue canadienne d'Economique </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Paul Boothe </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.876 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Let us begin by contrasting our model with the rational expectations models. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/S0022-1996(96)01471-7" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/S0022-1996(96)01471-7" target="_blank">A simultaneous trade model of the foreign exchange hot potato</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1997 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Journal of International Economics </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Lyons R.K. </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.869 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Over time, economists have come to realize that rational expectations models can have more than one equilibrium. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/s0165-1889(97)00096-1" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/s0165-1889(97)00096-1" target="_blank">Chaotic dynamics in a cash-in-advance economy</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1998 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Journal of Economic Dynamics and Control </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Michener R. </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.869 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> In Section 4, the rational expectations model is discussed. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/s0161-8938(97)00053-7" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/s0161-8938(97)00053-7" target="_blank">Private investment and the demand for loanable funds in the Greek Agricultural Sector</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1999 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Journal of Policy Modeling </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Baltas N.C. </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.869 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The "rational" expectations change with the model we start with. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/3532997" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/3532997" target="_blank">ET Interview: Professor G. S. Maddala</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1999 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Econometric Theory </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Kajal Lahiri, G. S. Maddala </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.864 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> When expectations are formed according to the full information rational expectations mechanism, the probability of a large error may be much smaller than when expectations are formed in a backward-looking manner. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/S0164-0704(98)00046-9" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/S0164-0704(98)00046-9" target="_blank">Multiple equilibria and rules of thumb</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1998 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Journal of Macroeconomics </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Ellis C. </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.862 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Under the joint hypothesis of rational expectations and of a correctly specified model, the error term e t +1 has zero mean, is serially uncorrelated, and is uncorrelated with any information known at the beginning of time t, when expectations are formed. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/s0264-9993(98)00044-3" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/s0264-9993(98)00044-3" target="_blank">Modelling consumption: Permanent-income or rule-of-thumb behaviour?</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1999 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Economic Modelling </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Hatzinikolaou D. </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.860 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The hypothesis of rational expectation encompasses those assumptions, but it is not the purpose of this paper to discuss their realism. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/4538501" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://http://www.jstor.org/stable/4538501" target="_blank">Real-World Agents, REH Agents, and the Econometrician</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 1996 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Journal of Post Keynesian Economics </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Amal Sanyal </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.860 </td>
  </tr>
</tbody>
</table><table class="table table-striped table-condensed" style="font-size: 12px; margin-left: auto; margin-right: auto;">
 <thead>
  <tr>
   <th style="text-align:left;"> Sentence </th>
   <th style="text-align:left;"> Title </th>
   <th style="text-align:right;"> Year </th>
   <th style="text-align:left;"> Journal </th>
   <th style="text-align:left;"> Authors </th>
   <th style="text-align:right;"> Similarity to HDSBSCAN Centroid </th>
  </tr>
 </thead>
<tbody>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> In recent years the rational expectations hypothesis has become the most popular way to close the dependency of an economic system to agents’ expectations. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/S0165-1889(02)00109-4" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/S0165-1889(02)00109-4" target="_blank">Adaptive expectations coordination in an economy with heterogeneous agents</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 2003 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Journal of Economic Dynamics and Control </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Negroni G. </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.877 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Muth (1961) defines expectations as rational “if they are essentially the same as the predictions of the relevant economic theory” instead of identically the same. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jacceco.2004.09.001" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jacceco.2004.09.001" target="_blank">Loss function assumptions in rational expectations tests on financial analysts' earnings forecasts</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 2004 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Journal of Accounting and Economics </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Basu S. </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.861 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Instead of starting off by assuming that agents have rational expectations, we merely see rational expectations as a possible long run outcome of a learning process of boundedly rational agents using simpler rules. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jedc.2007.06.003" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jedc.2007.06.003" target="_blank">Informational differences and learning in an asset market with boundedly rational agents</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 2008 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Journal of Economic Dynamics and Control </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Diks C. </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.858 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Recent work takes a more traditional rational approach to expectation formation by modeling it as an economic decision. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/S0165-1889(01)00027-6" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/S0165-1889(01)00027-6" target="_blank">Local convergence properties of a cobweb model with rationally heterogeneous expectations</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 2002 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Journal of Economic Dynamics and Control </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Branch W. </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.857 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> An important implication of our results relates to the rational expectations hypothesis. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jmoneco.2009.03.013" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jmoneco.2009.03.013" target="_blank">A structural decomposition of the US yield curve</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 2009 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Journal of Monetary Economics </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> De Graeve F. </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.857 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> In general terms, the learning approach suggests that expectations might not always be fully rational, and the REE of interest should satisfy a natural stability criterion in expectations formation. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jmoneco.2004.02.003" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jmoneco.2004.02.003" target="_blank">Are non-fundamental equilibria learnable in models of monetary policy?</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 2004 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Journal of Monetary Economics </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Honkapohja S. </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.852 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Rational expectations are a nested special case of the proposed beliefs, and the analysis is centrally concerned with the conditions under which agents’ beliefs converge to those predicted by a rational expectations equilibrium analysis of the model. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jedc.2007.12.009" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jedc.2007.12.009" target="_blank">Adaptive learning and the use of forecasts in monetary policy</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 2008 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Journal of Economic Dynamics and Control </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Preston B. </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.852 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Another strand of literature closely related to the present paper is based on rational expectations models. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jdeveco.2002.09.001" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jdeveco.2002.09.001" target="_blank">Industrial targeting, experimentation and long-run specialization</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 2004 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Journal of Development Economics </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Klimenko M.M. </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.851 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Section 2 reviews two rational-expectations models from the existing literature. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/S0165-1889(01)00015-X" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/S0165-1889(01)00015-X" target="_blank">Stabilizing properties of monetary feedback rules: A representative-agent approach</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 2002 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Journal of Economic Dynamics and Control </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Biederman D. </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.850 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The hypothesis of rational expectations states that the agents’ knowledge of their economic environment is such that the objective distributions of the relevant variables are known to them. </td>

## Intertemporal cluster _14: voting, voters, voter, vote_ 

  
The cluster gathers 11430 sentences from our corpus. It represents 3.45% of all the sentences selected over the whole period.

The community exists from 1960 to 2009. 

The most recurring authors are Alberto Alesina (115 sentences; 22 articles), James M. Buchanan (82 sentences; 20 articles), Dennis C. Mueller (81 sentences; 13 articles), Bernard Grofman (80 sentences; 24 articles), <suffix>Jr.</suffix> (75 sentences; 27 articles), Geoffrey Brennan (69 sentences; 10 articles), John G. Matsusaka (67 sentences; 9 articles), Donald G. Saari (65 sentences; 16 articles), Otto H. Swank (58 sentences; 12 articles), Martimort D. (58 sentences; 6 articles), Roger D. Congleton (52 sentences; 9 articles), Stephen Coate (51 sentences; 12 articles), Callander S. (51 sentences; 4 articles), Peter C. Ordeshook (50 sentences; 9 articles), Martin J. Osborne (50 sentences; 4 articles).

The most recurring journals are Public Choice (2909 sentences; 906 articles), Journal of Public Economics (919 sentences; 242 articles), Social Choice and Welfare (836 sentences; 233 articles), European Journal of Political Economy (728 sentences; 190 articles), The American Economic Review (491 sentences; 159 articles), Journal of Economic Theory (316 sentences; 99 articles).

   <td style="text-align:left;"> Whenever power is divided among many elected officials, a theory of rational voting must take account, not only of the probability of helping one candidate to win rather than another, but also the probability that helping a particular candidate to win would actually affect government policies in a way that benefits the voter. </td>

   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/S0176-2680(03)00031-4" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/S0176-2680(03)00031-4" target="_blank">Divided government and dominance solvability</a> </td>

  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> The precise interpretation of these conditions may need to be re-evaluated in voting theory because the result presented here indicate that strategic voting may well be beneficial. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://doi.org/10.1007/s11238-007-9028-4" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://doi.org/10.1007/s11238-007-9028-4" target="_blank">The welfare consequences of strategic voting in two commonly used parliamentary agendas</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 2007 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Theory and Decision </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Lehtinen A. </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.844 </td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> A sincere voting equilibrium is a strategy for candidates, δ*; a sincere voting strategy for voters α*; and belief functions, P*; such that (i) each candidate ρ locates to maximize discounted utility given their own ideology and voter strategies, α*; (ii) each voter θ votes sincerely given candidate strategies δ*; and (iii) beliefs of voters and candidates are consistent with their strategies and are updated according to Bayes' rule. </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;width: 3.5cm; "> <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jpubeco.2003.10.008" target="_blank"></a><a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jpubeco.2003.10.008" target="_blank">Term limits and pork barrel politics</a> </td>
   <td style="text-align:right;"> 2004 </td>
   <td style="text-align:left;"> Journal of Public Economics </td>

   <td style="text-align:right;"> 0.843 </td>
